title: Understanding the First Trimester
description: Weeks 1 to 12 are when your baby’s organs form and your body builds a placenta from scratch. That work is why you can feel exhausted, nauseous and emotional before you even look pregnant. This guide explains what is happening week by week, which symptoms are expected, what your first antenatal visits involve, and which signs need prompt attention.
glance: The first trimester runs from the first day of your last period to the end of week 12. Pregnancy is dated from your last period, so at “6 weeks” the embryo is about 4 weeks old.
Most early symptoms, including nausea, tiredness, tender breasts and frequent urination, are driven by rising pregnancy hormones and a rapidly increasing blood supply.
Book your first antenatal appointment early, ideally before 10 weeks. It is where blood tests, blood pressure and a dating scan are usually arranged.
One-sided abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, or being unable to keep fluids down needs same-day medical care.

blocks.p: In the first 12 weeks your baby develops from a cluster of cells into a fetus with all of its major organs in place. The neural tube, which becomes the brain and spinal cord, forms around weeks 4 to 6. A heartbeat can often be seen on an ultrasound from around 6 to 7 weeks. By the end of week 12, the fetus is roughly 5 to 6 cm long, its organs are formed, and from here on the main work is growth and maturing.

At the same time, your body is building the placenta, a completely new organ that will pass oxygen and nutrients to your baby and remove waste. Until the placenta takes over hormone production, around the end of the first trimester, your ovaries and the early pregnancy tissue produce the hormones that keep the pregnancy going. This is a large amount of biological work, and it explains why so many women feel unwell during weeks that look, from the outside, like nothing has changed.

blocks.h: Why you feel the way you do

ul: **hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin)** is the hormone a pregnancy test detects. It rises quickly and usually peaks around weeks 8 to 11. Its rise is closely linked with nausea, which is why sickness often peaks in the same window.
**Progesterone** relaxes smooth muscle throughout the body to keep the uterus calm. It also slows your gut, causing bloating, wind and constipation, and it has a sedating effect, adding to tiredness.
**Oestrogen** rises steeply. It contributes to breast tenderness, a heightened sense of smell and food aversions.

**Blood volume** starts increasing early and keeps rising through pregnancy. Your heart works harder and your kidneys filter more fluid, so you may need to pass urine more often, even before the uterus presses on your bladder.

**Emotions** can swing sharply. Hormonal shifts, poor sleep, nausea and the sheer weight of the news can make you tearful, irritable or anxious. Mixed feelings about being pregnant are common, including in planned pregnancies.

**Nausea and vomiting (“morning sickness”)** can happen at any time of day. It usually starts around week 6 and, for most women, eases between weeks 12 and 20. Eat small amounts every 2 to 3 hours, because an empty stomach often makes nausea worse. Plain, dry foods such as rusks, crackers, toast or plain roti before getting out of bed can help. Sip fluids between meals rather than with them, and notice which smells set you off (cooking oil, tarka, perfume) and avoid them where you can. Cold foods often smell less than hot ones.
**Exhaustion** is often at its worst now. Treat it as a physical need, not laziness: rest early in the evening, nap if you can, and reduce non-essential housework for these weeks.
**Tender, heavier breasts** are caused by hormones preparing milk-producing tissue. A soft, supportive bra without underwire usually helps.
**Light cramping** can happen as the uterus begins to grow. Mild, period-like cramps that come and go are common. Severe or one-sided pain is not, and needs checking.
**Spotting** (a few drops of blood) can happen early in pregnancy and is often harmless, but always mention any bleeding to your doctor so it can be assessed.
**More vaginal discharge**, thin and milky white with little smell, is normal. Discharge that itches, burns, smells strongly or is green or yellow should be checked.

blocks.p: Make contact with a doctor, hospital antenatal clinic or Lady Health Visitor as early as you can. The WHO recommends at least eight antenatal contacts during pregnancy, with the first in the first 12 weeks. At early visits you can usually expect:

ul: Questions about your health, previous pregnancies, medical conditions, medicines you take and your family history.
Blood pressure, weight and height, which give a baseline for comparing later readings.

Blood tests, commonly for your blood group and Rh factor, haemoglobin (to check for anaemia, which is common in pregnancy in Pakistan), blood sugar, and infections such as hepatitis B and C, HIV and syphilis.
A urine test for protein, sugar and infection.
An ultrasound scan to confirm the pregnancy is in the uterus, check the heartbeat, see whether there is more than one baby, and estimate your due date.

Guidance on supplements. Folic acid is routinely advised before conception and during early pregnancy because it lowers the risk of neural tube problems, and iron is commonly advised too. Ask your doctor which supplements and doses are right for you rather than choosing your own.

blocks.note: Bring your antenatal card or a folder to every visit, and write your questions down beforehand. First-trimester appointments are often short, and it is easy to forget what you wanted to ask.

ul: **Boil unpasteurised milk** before drinking it, including milk delivered by a doodhwala. Raw milk can carry listeria and other infections that are more dangerous in pregnancy.
**Cook meat, chicken and eggs thoroughly.** Avoid runny eggs, rare kebabs and street food that has been sitting out in the heat.
**Limit liver.** It is very high in vitamin A, and large amounts can harm a developing baby.

**Limit caffeine.** Chai, coffee, cola and energy drinks all count. Many health services advise keeping caffeine under 200 mg a day, which is roughly two mugs of instant coffee or three to four cups of ordinary tea.
**Wash fruit and vegetables well**, especially those eaten raw.

myth: “You must eat for two now.”
You do not need extra calories in the first trimester. Needs rise only modestly later in pregnancy. Focus on quality and on keeping something down.
“Ripe papaya and pineapple will cause a miscarriage.”

Normal amounts of ripe fruit are not known to cause miscarriage. Unripe or semi-ripe papaya contains latex, so many health providers suggest avoiding it, but ripe fruit in ordinary amounts is part of a healthy diet.
“Telling people too early brings bad luck.”

Many families wait until after 12 weeks to share the news, and that is a valid personal choice. It has no effect on the pregnancy itself. What matters is that you are not left without support if you feel unwell or worried.

blocks.p: Early pregnancy loss is, sadly, common, and most first-trimester miscarriages happen because of chromosomal differences in the pregnancy that nothing could have prevented. Everyday activities such as working, walking, climbing stairs, lifting a toddler, having sex, eating spicy food or feeling stressed do not cause miscarriage. Many women blame themselves or are blamed by relatives, and that blame is not supported by evidence. The chance of loss falls considerably once a heartbeat has been seen, and falls further as the weeks pass.

soon: Vomiting most days and struggling to eat, even if you can keep some fluids down
Light spotting, or any bleeding at all, so it can be assessed
A burning feeling when passing urine, or needing to go urgently with pain (this can be a urine infection, which needs treating in pregnancy)
Discharge that itches, smells or has changed colour
You take regular medicines for a long-term condition such as epilepsy, diabetes, thyroid disease, high blood pressure or depression. Do not stop them suddenly; ask your doctor to review them.
urgent: Pain on one side of the lower abdomen, especially with bleeding, dizziness or fainting
Pain in the tip of your shoulder, which can be a sign of internal bleeding from an ectopic pregnancy
Heavy bleeding, soaking a pad in an hour, or passing clots
Being unable to keep any fluids down for 12 hours or more, passing very little dark urine, or feeling faint when you stand (signs of hyperemesis gravidarum and dehydration)
Fever with shivering, or feeling very unwell

blocks.p: The first trimester is often lived in secret. You may feel dreadful while carrying on with work, guests and household duties as if nothing has changed. You may feel joy one hour and fear the next, or feel nothing much at all and worry that this means something is wrong. It does not. If you have had a previous loss, early weeks can be especially tense, and it is reasonable to ask your doctor whether earlier reassurance scans are an option for you.

In many Pakistani households, a pregnancy quickly becomes a family matter, with opinions on food, rest and even the baby’s sex arriving before your first scan. It is fine to share the news with only one or two trusted people until you feel ready, and to ask your husband to help manage what is shared.

takeaway: The first trimester can feel like the hardest part of pregnancy because your body is doing its most intense building work while you look the same as always. Rest, small frequent meals and early antenatal care are the foundations. Know the warning signs, especially one-sided pain, heavy bleeding and being unable to keep fluids down, and do not wait to get them checked.
prompt: Which symptom is affecting your day the most right now, and what is one task you could hand over or drop for the next two weeks to make room for rest?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Navigating the Second Trimester
description: Weeks 13 to 27 are often called the most comfortable stretch of pregnancy. Nausea usually fades, energy returns, your bump appears and you will likely feel your baby move for the first time. It is also when the detailed anomaly scan and diabetes screening usually happen, and when new aches begin. This guide explains what to expect and how to make the most of it.
glance: For most women, nausea eases and energy improves between weeks 12 and 20, but not for everyone.
First movements (quickening) are usually felt between 16 and 24 weeks, often later in a first pregnancy.
A detailed anomaly scan is commonly offered around 18 to 21 weeks, and screening for gestational diabetes around 24 to 28 weeks.
Round ligament pain, heartburn, nasal congestion, bleeding gums and leg cramps are common and usually manageable.

blocks.h: What is happening with your baby

blocks.p: The second trimester is about growth and refinement. Your baby’s organs, already formed, now mature. The skeleton hardens, the baby starts to hear sounds (including your voice and heartbeat), develops sleep and wake cycles, and begins practising movements such as swallowing, sucking and kicking. By the end of this trimester, your baby is several times larger than at week 13, and the lungs have begun the long process of preparing to breathe air.

ul: **Energy and appetite usually return.** As the placenta takes over hormone production and hCG falls from its peak, nausea and exhaustion often lift. Many women describe feeling like themselves again. If sickness continues past 20 weeks, mention it, as it is less common and worth assessing.

**Your bump appears.** The top of the uterus rises above the pubic bone after about 12 weeks and reaches around the level of your navel near 20 weeks. In a first pregnancy, abdominal muscles are firmer, so the bump may show later than in later pregnancies.

**First movements.** Early movements feel like flutters, bubbles, a fish swimming or a gentle tap, and are easy to mistake for wind. As weeks pass, they become unmistakable kicks and rolls. If the placenta lies at the front of the uterus (an anterior placenta), it cushions movements and you may feel them later or less sharply.

**Skin changes.** A dark line down the belly (linea nigra), darker nipples and patches of pigmentation on the face (melasma) are common, caused by hormones stimulating pigment cells. They usually fade after birth.
**Lower blood pressure.** Blood pressure often dips in mid-pregnancy as blood vessels relax. Standing up quickly, standing for a long time, or a hot room can leave you dizzy.

**Round ligament pain** is a sharp, brief pain or pulling in the groin or low belly, often on one side, when you stand up, turn over in bed, cough or sneeze. The ligaments supporting the uterus are being stretched. Moving more slowly, bending slightly toward the painful side and supporting your bump when you turn usually help.

**Heartburn** happens because progesterone relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach and the growing uterus pushes upward. Eat smaller meals, leave 2 to 3 hours between eating and lying down, and notice whether fried, oily or very spicy foods make it worse.

**Stuffy nose and nosebleeds** come from increased blood flow to the delicate lining of the nose. Steam, saline rinses and a humid room can help. Pinch the soft part of the nose and lean forward for 10 minutes for a nosebleed.
**Bleeding gums** are common because gums swell with extra blood flow. Keep brushing gently twice a day and floss. Pregnancy is a good time for a dental check.
**Leg cramps**, often at night, are sudden and painful. Flexing your foot so your toes pull toward your knee and stretching your calves before bed often helps.
**Dizziness:** stand up slowly, avoid standing still for long periods, eat regularly and keep cool.

blocks.h: The tests usually offered in this trimester

ul: **Anomaly scan (around 18 to 21 weeks).** A detailed ultrasound that checks your baby’s brain, spine, heart, kidneys, limbs, face and growth, and the position of the placenta. Most scans show a healthy baby. If something needs a closer look, you will usually be offered a follow-up scan or a specialist referral. Ask the sonographer to explain what they are checking if you would like to understand it.

**Glucose test (around 24 to 28 weeks).** Gestational diabetes is a form of diabetes that develops in pregnancy as placental hormones make the body less responsive to insulin. Women of South Asian heritage are at higher risk, so screening is especially relevant. It is often managed with diet and activity changes, sometimes with medicine, and usually resolves after birth.
**Blood pressure and urine checks** continue at each visit to watch for pre-eclampsia, a condition that can develop from the second half of pregnancy.
**Haemoglobin may be rechecked** to see whether you need iron support.
**Vaccinations.** Ask which vaccines are recommended in pregnancy where you live, such as tetanus.

blocks.h: Making the most of the energy window

ul: **Gentle, regular activity.** If your pregnancy is uncomplicated, aim to build towards around 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as brisk walking. See the guide on gentle physical activity for details.
**Get practical tasks done while you feel well:** choosing a hospital, finding out its policies on birth companions and pain relief, arranging transport, and thinking about who will help after birth.
**Start sleeping on your side.** It becomes important to go to sleep on your side from around 28 weeks, so building the habit now is easier.
**Talk with your husband** about how roles at home will shift, both during late pregnancy and after the birth.

myth: “If you can’t feel the baby moving by 20 weeks, something is wrong.”
The timing varies widely, especially in a first pregnancy or with an anterior placenta. If you have not felt anything by 24 weeks, contact your antenatal team so they can check.
“Heartburn means the baby will have lots of hair.”
Heartburn is explained by hormones and the growing uterus. There is no reliable link to hair.
“The shape of your bump shows whether it is a boy or a girl.”
Bump shape depends on your muscle tone, height, the baby’s position and whether you have been pregnant before. Only a scan or birth tells you the sex.

soon: Sickness still making it hard to eat or drink after 20 weeks
Burning or stinging when passing urine
Itchy, smelly or coloured discharge
Persistent headache that does not settle with rest and fluids
You have not felt movements by 24 weeks
urgent: Vaginal bleeding of any amount
A gush or steady trickle of clear fluid from the vagina (possible waters breaking)
Regular tightenings or period-like pains that come in waves before 37 weeks (possible preterm labour)
Severe headache, blurred vision, flashing lights, pain under the ribs on the right side, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet (possible pre-eclampsia)
A clear change or slowing in your baby’s movements once you have a regular pattern. Do not wait until the next day.

blocks.p: Feeling better can bring a wave of relief, but this trimester also makes the pregnancy public. The bump invites comments, touching without asking, predictions about the baby’s sex and advice about everything. The anomaly scan can bring anxiety beforehand and either relief or worry afterwards. Some women feel properly connected to the baby for the first time when movements begin; others feel strange about something moving inside them. Both are common. If you are expected to resume full household or work duties just because you “look fine now”, it is reasonable to explain that pregnancy still demands real energy and that rest is part of a healthy pregnancy.

takeaway: The second trimester usually brings relief and energy, but it is also a time of important checks. Go to your anomaly scan and glucose test, start side-sleeping, get your birth practicalities organised while you feel well, and learn your baby’s movement pattern so you notice if it changes.
prompt: What would you like to have arranged or decided by the time you reach 28 weeks, and who could help you with it?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Preparing for the Third Trimester
description: Weeks 28 to 40 are about growth, getting into position and your body preparing for birth. Tiredness, breathlessness, heartburn and broken sleep often return. This guide explains why, how to monitor your baby’s movements, how to tell practice contractions from labour, which warning signs need urgent attention, and how to prepare practically in a Pakistani hospital setting.
glance: Your baby gains most of its birth weight now, and its lungs and brain mature rapidly.
Know your baby’s usual movement pattern. A reduction or change needs a same-day check, not waiting.
Go to sleep on your side from 28 weeks.
Plan the hospital, transport, money, documents and blood donor arrangements before 36 weeks.

blocks.h: What is happening with your baby

blocks.p: In the third trimester your baby lays down fat, which helps regulate temperature after birth, and gains weight rapidly. The lungs produce surfactant, a substance that keeps tiny air sacs open, which is why babies born closer to term usually breathe more easily. The brain grows quickly. Most babies settle head-down by around 36 weeks. If your baby is in a breech (bottom or feet first) position near term, your doctor will discuss options with you.

ul: **Breathlessness:** the uterus pushes up against your diaphragm, and progesterone increases your drive to breathe. Feeling breathless on stairs is common. Sitting upright and slowing down helps. When the baby moves down into the pelvis (“drops”) in the last weeks, breathing often eases.
**Heartburn and indigestion** get worse as the stomach has less room. Small meals, sitting upright after eating and propping up your head at night help.
**Frequent urination** returns as the baby’s head presses on your bladder. Do not cut down on fluids to avoid it. Do reduce drinks in the last hour before bed.
**Pelvic and back pain:** the hormone relaxin loosens ligaments for birth, and your centre of gravity shifts forward. See the guide on posture and mobility for specific techniques.

**Swelling of feet and ankles,** especially by evening and in hot weather, is common because of extra fluid and pressure on the veins from the uterus. Raise your feet, avoid standing still for long periods, and keep moving your ankles.

**Braxton Hicks contractions** are painless or mildly uncomfortable tightenings of the uterus, often irregular, that ease with rest, a change of position or a drink of water. They are your uterus practising.
**Poor sleep:** discomfort, needing the toilet, heartburn, leg cramps and a busy mind all add up. The guide on sleep and rest has specific strategies.

blocks.h: Your baby’s movements: the most important thing to monitor

blocks.p: Babies do not move less as they near birth. Movements may feel different, more rolls and pushes than sharp kicks, but your baby should continue to move in its usual pattern right up to and during labour. A reduction or change in movements can be an early sign that a baby is not well.

ol: Get to know your baby’s pattern: when it is usually active and what the movements feel like. There is no set number that applies to every baby.
If you notice the movements have slowed, changed or stopped, lie on your left side and focus on movements for up to two hours. If you are worried before then, do not wait.
If movements are still reduced, or you are unsure, contact your hospital or maternity unit straight away, at any time of day or night. Do not wait until the next morning or your next appointment.
Do not rely on home heartbeat monitors or apps. Hearing a heartbeat does not show that a baby is well.

blocks.note: If your family tells you it is normal for babies to go quiet before birth, it is reasonable to say that doctors now advise checking every reduction, and to go anyway.

ul: **Braxton Hicks:** irregular, do not get closer together, usually ease with rest, water or changing position, and are felt mostly at the front.
**Labour contractions:** become regular, longer, stronger and closer together over time, do not ease with rest, and often start in the back and wrap around to the front.

**Other signs labour may be starting:** a “show” (a plug of jelly-like mucus, sometimes streaked with pink or brown), backache, or your waters breaking, which can be a gush or a trickle you cannot control.

blocks.p: For when to go to hospital, follow your own hospital’s instructions. Commonly, first-time mothers are advised to go when contractions are regular, about five minutes apart and lasting around a minute, or sooner if the waters break, there is bleeding, or you are worried.

blocks.h: Practical preparation for birth in Pakistan

ul: **Hospital:** confirm where you will deliver, what the emergency entrance is, whether you need to register in advance, and what the hospital’s policies are on birth companions and on pain relief such as epidurals.
**Transport at any hour:** decide who will drive, keep fuel in the car, and save two backup numbers for a taxi, a relative and an ambulance.
**Documents:** CNIC, antenatal card and test reports, ultrasound reports and blood group record.
**Blood:** many hospitals ask families to arrange blood donors or replacement. Know your blood group and identify two or three willing relatives with compatible groups in advance.
**Money:** keep cash and a card accessible, since deposits are often requested on admission.

**Hospital bag (packed by around 36 weeks):** comfortable loose clothes that open at the front for feeding, maternity pads, several pairs of old cotton underwear, a dupatta or shawl, toiletries, phone charger, snacks and water for labour; for baby, soft clothes, a cap, socks, a blanket and nappies.
**Support after birth:** decide who will stay with you in hospital and who will help at home in the first weeks.

soon: Itching, especially on the palms of your hands and soles of your feet, often worse at night (this can be obstetric cholestasis, a liver condition of pregnancy that needs blood tests)
Swelling that is gradual but worsening, or a persistent headache
Signs of a urine infection
Feeling very low, anxious or unable to cope
urgent: Reduced, changed or stopped baby movements
Any vaginal bleeding
Your waters break, especially if the fluid is green, brown or bloody, or before 37 weeks
Regular contractions before 37 weeks
Severe headache, vision problems, pain below the ribs, vomiting, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet (possible pre-eclampsia)
Constant severe abdominal pain, or a uterus that stays hard and painful between contractions
Fever, or feeling very unwell
A painful, swollen, red calf, chest pain or sudden breathlessness (possible blood clot)

blocks.p: As birth approaches, many women feel a mixture of impatience, excitement and fear. Nesting energy, the urge to clean and organise, can alternate with deep tiredness. The last weeks can bring constant calls asking “Any news yet?”, which can feel like pressure. Only a small minority of babies arrive on their due date, and anything from 37 to 42 weeks is considered term, so it helps to tell people your due “month” rather than an exact date. If you are frightened of birth, see the guides on fear of childbirth and preparing emotionally for labour. Fear responds well to information and support.

takeaway: The third trimester is about watching closely and preparing well. Learn your baby’s movement pattern and act on any reduction the same day, sleep on your side, know the signs of labour and of pre-eclampsia, and have your hospital, transport, documents, money and blood donors arranged by 36 weeks.
prompt: If labour started at 3 a.m. tonight, what would happen next? Walk through it step by step and notice where the gaps are.
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Emotional Changes Throughout Pregnancy
description: Pregnancy changes your emotional life as much as your body. Hormones, sleep, physical discomfort, worries about the baby and shifting family expectations all play a part, and feelings tend to follow a recognisable pattern across the trimesters. This guide explains what drives emotional changes, what is typical at each stage, and how to tell ordinary ups and downs from antenatal depression or anxiety.
glance: Emotional changes in pregnancy have real biological drivers, not just “being sensitive”.
Mixed feelings, including doubt and fear, are common even in a wanted, planned pregnancy.
Depression and anxiety can start during pregnancy, not only after birth, and are treatable.
Low mood or worry lasting most days for two weeks or more is a reason to speak to your doctor.

ul: **Hormones.** Oestrogen and progesterone rise to many times their usual levels. These hormones act on brain chemicals involved in mood, including serotonin, which is one reason emotions can feel louder, faster and harder to manage.
**Sleep and tiredness.** Fatigue lowers your threshold for coping. Small frustrations feel larger when you are exhausted.
**Physical discomfort.** Constant nausea, pain or heartburn wears down patience and mood.
**Uncertainty.** You are waiting for news about your baby’s health, and preparing for birth and a life you cannot fully picture yet.
**Shifting relationships.** How your husband, in-laws, parents and employer treat you may change, sometimes in welcome ways and sometimes not.
**Your history.** Previous pregnancy loss, fertility struggles, a difficult earlier birth, or past depression or anxiety can bring feelings back to the surface.

blocks.h: A typical emotional pattern across pregnancy

ul: **First trimester:** excitement, disbelief, fear of loss, irritability and tearfulness are common, made heavier by nausea and exhaustion. You may feel unexpectedly flat or uncertain about the pregnancy. That ambivalence is common and does not predict how you will feel about your baby.
**Second trimester:** mood often steadies as energy returns. Seeing the baby on a scan or feeling movements can make the pregnancy feel real. Anxiety may rise before scans and appointments.
**Third trimester:** impatience, nesting, vivid dreams, fear of labour and worries about coping often grow as birth gets closer. Poor sleep amplifies everything.

blocks.h: What is common and usually manageable

ul: Crying more easily, including at things that would not usually move you
Feeling irritated by noise, smells, people or being touched
Anxious thoughts about the baby’s health, birth or money that come and go
Vivid or disturbing dreams, often in the third trimester, linked to broken sleep and a mind processing big change
Forgetfulness and difficulty concentrating
Moments of grief for the life you are leaving behind, alongside excitement for what is coming

blocks.h: When emotional changes may be something more

blocks.p: Depression and anxiety during pregnancy (antenatal or perinatal depression and anxiety) are recognised conditions, not personal failures. They are associated with real, treatable changes in brain function, and getting help protects both you and your baby. Signs include:

ul: Low mood, emptiness or hopelessness on most days for two weeks or more
Losing interest in things you usually enjoy, or feeling nothing about the pregnancy
Constant worry you cannot switch off, panic attacks, or fear that stops you doing ordinary things
Changes in sleep or appetite beyond what pregnancy explains, such as being unable to sleep even when you are exhausted
Feeling worthless, guilty or like a burden
Withdrawing from people

blocks.p: Effective help includes talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), support groups and, where appropriate, treatment that a doctor will weigh carefully for pregnancy. In Pakistan, the WHO-endorsed “Thinking Healthy” programme, a CBT-based approach developed and tested with Pakistani mothers, shows that structured psychological support can make a real difference.

ol: **Name the driver.** When your mood dips, ask: am I hungry, exhausted, in pain, or worried about something specific? Each needs a different response, such as food, rest, comfort or information.
**Eat regularly.** Long gaps between meals cause blood sugar dips that worsen irritability and anxiety.
**Protect sleep where you can.** See the guide on sleep and rest during pregnancy.
**Move daily.** A 20 to 30 minute walk has measurable effects on mood and stress.
**Give worries a shape.** Write them down and sort them into questions for your doctor, practical tasks, and fears to talk through with someone.
**Tell one person the truth.** Choose your husband, a sister or a friend, and say how you actually feel, not the version you think you should feel.
**Limit sources that make you anxious,** whether frightening stories from relatives, forums or social media accounts.

myth: “A happy mother makes a happy baby, so feeling sad will harm the baby.”

Ordinary sadness, stress and crying do not harm your baby. Long-lasting, severe depression or anxiety is worth treating, for your own sake and because it can affect sleep, eating and self-care, and that is exactly why help is available.
“Pregnancy is a blessing, so you should only feel grateful.”
Gratitude and difficulty can exist together. Feeling overwhelmed does not make you ungrateful.

soon: Low mood, hopelessness or loss of interest lasting two weeks or more
Anxiety or panic that is affecting your sleep, eating or daily life
A history of depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder or other mental health conditions. Tell your doctor early so they can plan support.
Feeling unable to talk to anyone at home about how you feel
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life
Feeling that your family would be better off without you
Hearing or seeing things others do not, or beliefs that feel unusually strong or frightening to others

blocks.h: The emotional side of being seen

blocks.p: Many women in Pakistan describe pressure to appear content during pregnancy, partly because others may not have had the chance to conceive, and partly because complaining can be seen as ungrateful. That pressure can make you hide exactly the feelings that most need attention. You can be grateful for this pregnancy and still find it hard. Saying so to a trusted person, or a professional, is a sign of looking after yourself and your baby.

takeaway: Emotional changes in pregnancy are real, driven by hormones, sleep, discomfort and huge life change. Most ups and downs pass, and they respond to rest, food, movement and honest conversation. Low mood or anxiety that lasts two weeks or more, or that stops you functioning, is treatable and deserves a conversation with your doctor.
prompt: If you were completely honest, what feeling about this pregnancy have you been keeping to yourself, and who is one person who could hear it without judging you?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Physical Changes During Pregnancy
description: Pregnancy reshapes almost every system in your body: heart, lungs, kidneys, digestion, joints, skin and brain. Knowing why each change happens makes symptoms less frightening and helps you recognise what is normal adaptation and what is a warning sign. This guide walks through each system in plain language.
glance: Your blood volume rises substantially, by around half by late pregnancy, so your heart pumps harder and faster.
Progesterone and relaxin loosen muscles and ligaments, which explains heartburn, constipation and pelvic aches.
Breathlessness is partly caused by hormones, not just the bump pressing up.
Most changes reverse after birth over weeks to months; some, such as foot size and stretch marks, may last.

blocks.p: Your blood volume increases steadily through pregnancy, by roughly half by the third trimester, to supply the placenta and protect you from blood loss at birth. Your heart pumps more blood with each beat and beats a little faster at rest. This explains:

ul: **Feeling your heart race** or pound occasionally, especially when you lie down or climb stairs
**Dizziness**, especially in mid-pregnancy when blood vessels relax and blood pressure dips

**“Dilutional” anaemia:** plasma, the liquid part of blood, increases faster than red blood cells, so haemoglobin readings fall a little even in healthy women. True iron deficiency is also common, which is why haemoglobin is checked.
**Varicose veins and swollen ankles:** pressure from the uterus slows blood returning from the legs, and hormones relax vein walls
**A higher risk of blood clots**, which is your body protecting you from bleeding at birth but means calf pain and swelling need attention

blocks.p: Progesterone makes the brain more sensitive to carbon dioxide, so you breathe a little more deeply and frequently. This begins early, which is why some women feel breathless before they have a bump. Later, the uterus pushes your diaphragm upward. Breathlessness on exertion is normal; breathlessness at rest, with chest pain, or that comes on suddenly is not.

ul: **Slower gut:** progesterone relaxes the muscles that move food through your intestines. Food sits longer, so you absorb more nutrients, but you also get bloating, wind and constipation.
**Heartburn:** the valve at the top of the stomach relaxes, and later the uterus presses upward, letting acid move into the oesophagus.
**Changed taste and smell:** many women notice a metallic taste or strong aversions, especially in the first trimester.
**More saliva:** some women produce excess saliva, which can come with nausea.

blocks.p: Your kidneys filter more blood and produce more urine. Early in pregnancy this, more than pressure on the bladder, explains frequent urination. Later, the baby’s head presses on the bladder. Hormonal relaxation of the urinary tract makes urine infections more likely, and these need treating promptly in pregnancy because they can travel up to the kidneys.

The hormone relaxin, together with progesterone, softens ligaments throughout the body, especially around the pelvis so it can widen slightly for birth. Combined with the forward pull of the bump, this causes back pain, pelvic girdle pain, a waddling walk late in pregnancy, and sometimes wider feet. Your abdominal muscles stretch and may separate down the middle (diastasis recti). See the guide on posture and mobility.

Hormones stimulate pigment cells (darker nipples, linea nigra, melasma), increase blood flow (a “glow”, but also spider veins and red palms), and keep more hairs in the growing phase, so hair often looks thicker. Stretch marks appear when skin stretches faster than it can adapt. See the guide on skin, hair and appearance changes.

Breast changes start within weeks: tenderness, growth, darker and larger areolas, visible veins and small bumps on the areola (Montgomery’s glands). From the second trimester, some women leak small amounts of colostrum. See the guide on breast changes.

Many women report forgetfulness or “pregnancy brain”. Research using brain imaging has found that pregnancy is associated with changes in brain structure, thought to relate to adapting to caregiving and reading a baby’s needs. Poor sleep and a mind full of planning also play a part. Carpal tunnel syndrome, tingling or numbness in the fingers, can develop because fluid retention compresses a nerve at the wrist.

Your immune system adjusts so that your body accepts the pregnancy. As a result, some infections, such as flu, can affect you more strongly, and some autoimmune conditions change in activity. Food safety, hand washing and recommended vaccines matter more now.

Swollen, bleeding gums, nasal congestion and nosebleeds come from increased blood flow. Fluid retention can change the shape of the eye slightly, making contact lenses feel uncomfortable, but sudden blurred vision or flashing lights in later pregnancy can be a sign of pre-eclampsia and needs urgent checking.

blocks.h: What stays and what goes after birth

ul: **Usually resolves within weeks to months:** blood volume, breathing changes, swelling, heartburn, carpal tunnel symptoms, most pigmentation
**Can take longer:** abdominal muscle separation, pelvic floor recovery, joint laxity (especially if breastfeeding)
**May be permanent:** stretch marks (which fade to silvery lines), changes in breast shape, sometimes a larger shoe size

soon: Haemoglobin results showing anaemia, or signs such as unusual breathlessness, paleness, palpitations or extreme tiredness
Signs of a urine infection
Tingling or numbness in the hands that disturbs sleep or makes it hard to grip
Varicose veins that are painful, hot or red
urgent: Breathlessness at rest, chest pain, or coughing up blood
A painful, swollen, warm calf on one side
Sudden swelling of the face or hands, with headache or vision changes
Fainting

takeaway: Most pregnancy symptoms are the side effects of sensible adaptations: more blood, looser ligaments, slower digestion and a reprogrammed immune system. Understanding the reason makes them less frightening. The changes that need urgent attention are the ones that are sudden, one-sided, severe, or involve chest pain, breathing at rest, or vision.
prompt: Which change in your body has surprised you most, and does understanding why it happens change how you feel about it?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Understanding Pregnancy Fatigue
description: Pregnancy fatigue is a heavy, whole-body tiredness that sleep does not always fix. It usually peaks in the first trimester, eases in the second and returns in the third. This guide explains what causes it, how to tell it apart from anaemia, thyroid problems or depression, and gives practical ways to conserve energy in a busy household.
glance: First-trimester fatigue is driven by progesterone, a rising blood volume and the energy cost of building the placenta.
Third-trimester fatigue comes from carrying extra weight, broken sleep and discomfort.
Iron-deficiency anaemia is common in pregnancy and worsens tiredness. A blood test can check for it.
Tea or chai with meals reduces iron absorption. Drink it between meals instead.

blocks.h: Why pregnancy makes you so tired

ul: **Progesterone** has a sedative effect on the brain. Its sharp rise in early pregnancy is one reason you may feel you could fall asleep at any moment.
**Your circulation is working harder.** Expanding blood volume and a faster heart rate increase your body’s baseline workload.
**Building the placenta** is an intense biological project in the first 12 weeks.
**Blood sugar shifts:** pregnancy changes how your body handles sugar, and long gaps between meals can leave you drained.
**Nausea and poor eating** reduce the fuel available.
**Later in pregnancy,** the extra weight, the physical effort of moving, and broken sleep from needing the toilet, heartburn and discomfort all add up.
**Emotional load:** worry, planning and keeping up appearances use energy too.

blocks.h: What normal pregnancy tiredness looks like

ul: Feeling sleepy in the afternoon or early evening, sometimes overwhelmingly so
Needing more sleep than usual, and still waking tired
Low stamina for activities that used to be easy
Improvement in the second trimester for most women, then a return in the last weeks

blocks.h: When tiredness may be something else

ul: **Iron-deficiency anaemia** is very common in pregnancy in Pakistan. Watch for breathlessness on mild effort, a racing or pounding heart, pale skin or inner eyelids, dizziness, headaches, cold hands and feet, restless legs, and cravings for ice, clay or chalk. Ask for your haemoglobin to be checked if you have not had a recent test.
**Thyroid problems** can cause tiredness, low mood, feeling cold and constipation. They are diagnosed with a blood test.
**Depression** can feel like tiredness: heaviness, no motivation, sleeping a lot or being unable to sleep, with low mood or loss of interest.
**Gestational diabetes** can cause tiredness along with thirst and passing more urine.
**Sleep apnoea** (loud snoring with pauses in breathing) is more likely later in pregnancy and causes daytime sleepiness.
**Eat every 3 to 4 hours,** including a protein source each time: eggs, daal, chana, yoghurt, milk, chicken, fish, meat or nuts.

**Combine iron sources with vitamin C** to improve absorption. Plant iron (from daal, chickpeas, kidney beans, spinach and other leafy greens) is absorbed much better alongside lemon juice, tomatoes, guava, oranges or kinnow. Red meat provides iron that is absorbed easily.
**Move your chai away from meals.** Tea and coffee contain compounds that reduce iron absorption. Have your cup an hour before or after a meal rather than with it.
**Drink enough water.** Even mild dehydration causes tiredness and headaches, especially in hot weather.
**Swap sugary energy spikes** (mithai, sugary drinks) for steadier options. Sugar gives a short boost then a dip.

blocks.h: Conserving energy in a busy home

ol: **Rank your tasks** each morning into essential, nice to do, and can wait. Do the essentials when your energy is highest, often the morning.
**Sit for tasks you usually do standing,** such as chopping vegetables, ironing and folding laundry.
**Batch and simplify cooking:** cook larger amounts of daal or salan once and use it for two meals.
**Accept or ask for help with heavy tasks** like mopping, carrying water, washing clothes by hand, and lifting heavy pots.
**Rest lying on your side** for 20 to 30 minutes in the afternoon. Even if you don’t sleep, resting helps.
**Go to bed earlier** for these weeks, and let guests and late-night socialising wait.
**Gentle movement helps:** a short walk often improves energy more than resting longer, especially in the second and third trimesters.

myth: “Tiredness means you are lazy, and pregnant women used to do everything in the old days.”
Pregnancy fatigue has clear biological causes. Women in the past also needed rest, and many got it from extended family. Rest now is part of a healthy pregnancy.
“Drinking more tea will give you energy.”
Caffeine gives a short lift but disrupts sleep and, with meals, reduces iron absorption. Keep it moderate and away from meal times.

soon: Tiredness with breathlessness, palpitations, dizziness or paleness
Cravings for non-food items such as clay, chalk, ice or raw rice (this is called pica and is often linked with iron deficiency)
Tiredness with low mood or loss of interest lasting two weeks or more
Loud snoring with gasping or pauses in breathing
Excessive thirst with frequent urination
urgent: Fainting or feeling about to faint
Breathlessness at rest or chest pain
Sudden, extreme weakness with severe headache or vision changes

blocks.p: Fatigue can make you feel unlike yourself, guilty about what is not getting done, and sensitive to comments about resting “too much”. In joint families, you may feel watched. It can help to explain to your husband, or ask your doctor to explain to family, that tiredness in pregnancy is physical and expected. Resting is not neglecting your responsibilities; it is meeting the biggest one.

takeaway: Pregnancy fatigue is real, biologically driven and usually temporary. Eat regularly with iron and protein, keep chai away from meals, rest without guilt and hand over heavy tasks. If tiredness comes with breathlessness, palpitations, cravings for clay or ice, or low mood, ask for a check-up, because anaemia, thyroid problems and depression are common and treatable.
prompt: Which one or two tasks drain the most energy from your day, and what would it take to hand them over for the next few weeks?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Sleep and Rest During Pregnancy
description: Sleep often gets harder as pregnancy progresses, through nausea, needing the toilet, heartburn, leg cramps, an active baby, a racing mind and simply finding a comfortable position. This guide explains why sleep changes, why side-sleeping matters from 28 weeks, and gives specific, practical fixes for each common sleep problem.
glance: From 28 weeks, go to sleep on your side, either left or right. Waking on your back is not a cause for alarm; just turn back onto your side.
A pillow between your knees and another under your bump can ease hip and back pain.
Heartburn, leg cramps and night-time urination each have specific fixes.
Do not take sleeping tablets or herbal sleep remedies without asking your doctor.

ul: **First trimester:** progesterone makes you sleepy during the day, while nausea, tender breasts and frequent urination break up the night.
**Second trimester:** sleep often improves, though vivid dreams and nasal congestion can disturb it.
**Third trimester:** the bump makes positions uncomfortable, the baby is often active at night, and heartburn, leg cramps, restless legs, needing the toilet and anxiety about birth all increase.

blocks.p: Research has found that going to sleep on your back in the third trimester is associated with a higher risk of stillbirth, likely because the weight of the uterus can press on major blood vessels and reduce blood flow to the baby. This is why going to sleep on your side, left or right, is advised from 28 weeks. The advice applies to going to sleep, including daytime naps. Everyone shifts in the night, so if you wake up on your back, simply turn onto your side again. You have not done anything wrong.

ul: **A pillow between your knees** keeps your hips level and reduces strain on your back and pelvis.
**A pillow or rolled towel under the bump** supports its weight.
**A pillow behind your back** stops you rolling onto your back.
**Raise the head of your bed or use extra pillows** if heartburn or breathlessness is worse lying down.
**A firm mattress, or a thin mattress on a flat surface,** can be more comfortable for back pain than a very soft one.
**Turning over:** bend your knees, keep them together and roll your whole body as one unit, which is gentler on a sore pelvis.

**Heartburn:** finish your evening meal 2 to 3 hours before bed, keep dinner lighter and less oily or spicy, and raise your upper body. Many Pakistani households eat dinner late; eating earlier, or having a smaller portion late, can help a lot. Ask your doctor or pharmacist what is safe if symptoms persist.

**Needing to urinate:** drink well during the day, then reduce fluids in the last hour before bed. Lean forward when you urinate to empty the bladder fully. Keep a dim light on the route to the bathroom, since bright light makes it harder to fall back asleep.
**Leg cramps:** stretch your calves before bed. During a cramp, straighten your leg and pull your toes toward your knee, or stand on a cool floor. Regular walking helps.
**Restless legs** (an uncomfortable urge to move your legs at rest): it can be linked to low iron, so ask for an iron check. Stretching, a warm bath and massage can help.
**Blocked nose:** steam inhalation before bed, saline rinses and raising your head.
**Racing mind:** write down tomorrow’s tasks and any worries before bed. Use slow breathing with a longer out-breath than in-breath (see the breathing guide).
**Baby kicking at night:** babies are often active when you lie still. Accepting this, rather than fighting to sleep, can make it less frustrating.

ol: Aim for a regular time to sleep and wake, even if it is not perfect.
Dim lights and reduce screen use in the last 30 to 60 minutes. Phone light and endless scrolling keep the brain alert.
Do something calming: a warm shower or bath (not very hot), gentle stretching, prayer, recitation or quiet reading.

Keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet. Use a fan in summer and avoid overheating in winter, and make sure any gas heater is turned off before you sleep. Gas heaters in a closed room can cause carbon monoxide poisoning.
If you have been awake for around 20 minutes and are getting frustrated, get up, do something quiet in dim light, and return when sleepy.

blocks.p: Naps of 20 to 30 minutes, or lying down to rest on your side, can make a real difference. If you share a room with others or the household is noisy, ask for a quiet time each afternoon or use earplugs and an eye mask.

myth: “Sleeping on your back once means you have harmed your baby.”
The advice is about the position you go to sleep in. Moving in your sleep is normal. Simply return to your side when you notice.
“You must only sleep on your left side.”
Research suggests left and right are both fine. The important thing is to avoid going to sleep on your back from 28 weeks.

soon: Loud snoring with gasping or pauses in breathing
Severe insomnia most nights for several weeks
Restless legs that disturb sleep most nights
Worry or low mood that is keeping you awake regularly
urgent: Waking with a severe headache, vision changes or pain under the ribs
Breathlessness when lying flat that does not improve when you sit up, or chest pain
Noticing reduced baby movements at night or on waking

blocks.p: Lying awake at night can make every worry feel larger. Anxiety and poor sleep feed each other. If your mind races about birth, money or the baby, that is common and treatable. Speaking to your doctor about persistent insomnia or anxiety is worthwhile, and talking therapies such as CBT for insomnia are effective and safe in pregnancy.

takeaway: Sleep in pregnancy is often broken, but it can be improved. Go to sleep on your side from 28 weeks, use pillows generously, fix the specific problem that wakes you (heartburn, cramps, bladder or worry), and rest during the day when you can. Persistent insomnia, snoring with pauses, or restless legs deserve a medical check.
prompt: What wakes you most often at night, and which of the fixes above could you try this week?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Pregnancy Discomfort and Everyday Wellbeing
description: Most pregnancy discomforts are common, explainable and manageable once you know what is causing them. This is a practical, symptom-by-symptom guide covering nausea, heartburn, constipation, piles, back and pelvic pain, swelling, headaches, carpal tunnel and itching, with what helps each one and when it needs a doctor.
glance: Most discomforts come from hormones relaxing muscles and ligaments, a growing uterus, and extra blood and fluid.
Simple adjustments to eating, posture, movement and rest often help significantly.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist before taking any medicine or herbal remedy, including over-the-counter products.
Severe headaches, sudden swelling, intense itching of palms and soles, or one-sided calf pain need prompt medical attention.

blocks.p: **Why:** linked with rising hCG and oestrogen, and with a heightened sense of smell. It usually peaks around weeks 8 to 11 and eases by weeks 12 to 20.

ul: Eat small amounts often, before you get very hungry.
Keep plain snacks by your bed and eat a little before getting up.
Try cold or room-temperature foods, which smell less.
Ginger, in food or tea, helps some women.
Rest, since tiredness makes nausea worse.
Fresh air and avoiding cooking smells can help significantly. Ask someone else to do the tarka if you can.

blocks.p: **Why:** progesterone relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach, and the growing uterus pushes upward.

ul: Eat smaller meals, eat slowly, and avoid lying down for 2 to 3 hours after eating.
Notice your triggers. Fried, oily, very spicy foods, citrus, chocolate, fizzy drinks and coffee are common culprits.
Raise the head of your bed and wear loose clothing around your waist.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist which remedies are safe in pregnancy if these steps are not enough.

blocks.p: **Why:** progesterone slows the gut, iron supplements can harden stools, and you may be moving less.

ul: Increase fibre gradually: whole wheat atta, daal, chickpeas, vegetables, fruit with skin, guava, and soaked dried figs or prunes.
Drink plenty of water; fibre needs fluid to work.
Move daily; walking stimulates the bowel.

Go when you feel the urge, and use a small stool under your feet on a Western toilet to raise your knees above your hips, which helps the bowel empty. A squatting toilet already gives a good position.
If iron supplements are making constipation severe, tell your doctor rather than stopping them.

blocks.p: **Why:** swollen veins around the anus, caused by pressure from the uterus, hormones relaxing vein walls, and straining.

ul: Prevent constipation (see above) and avoid straining.
Clean gently with water, which is easy with a lota or shattaf, and pat dry.
A cold compress wrapped in cloth can relieve swelling and itching.
Ask your doctor about treatments; do not use creams without advice.

blocks.p: **Why:** relaxin loosens ligaments, the bump shifts your centre of gravity forward, and your lower back arches more.

ul: Stand tall with your weight spread evenly between both feet, and avoid locking your knees.
When lifting, bend your knees, keep your back straight and hold the load close. Avoid lifting heavy buckets or toddlers onto your hip where possible.
Sit with your back supported and feet flat; place a cushion behind your lower back.
Gentle exercise, prenatal stretches, warm compresses and massage can help.
See the guide on posture, mobility and physical comfort for more detail.

blocks.p: **Why:** the joints of the pelvis move more than usual. It feels like pain at the front of the pubic bone, in the hips or the buttocks, and is often worse when walking, climbing stairs, turning in bed, or standing on one leg (for example, putting on shalwar).

ul: Keep your knees together when getting in and out of bed or a car.
Sit down to dress.
Take stairs one step at a time.
Avoid wide stances, heavy lifting and pushing heavy loads.
Ask for a referral to a physiotherapist. Specific exercises and support belts can help significantly, and the condition is treatable.

blocks.p: **Why:** extra fluid in your body, pressure on veins from the uterus, and heat.

ul: Raise your feet when sitting, avoid standing still for long periods, and walk regularly.
Rotate your ankles and flex your feet several times an hour.
Wear comfortable, wide shoes and remove tight rings.
Drink enough water. Cutting fluids does not reduce swelling.
Gradual swelling of feet and ankles by evening is common. Sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet is not, and needs urgent checking.

blocks.p: **Why:** hormones, dehydration, hunger, tiredness, eye strain, caffeine changes and stress.

ul: Drink water, eat regularly, rest in a quiet, dark room, and apply a cool cloth to your forehead.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist what pain relief is safe for you in pregnancy rather than taking what you used before pregnancy.
After 20 weeks, a severe headache that does not go away needs urgent assessment for pre-eclampsia.

blocks.p: **Why:** fluid retention compresses the nerve at the wrist, causing tingling, numbness or pain in the thumb and fingers, often worse at night.

ul: Avoid sleeping with your wrists bent.
Shake out your hands and gently move your fingers.
Ask about a wrist splint for night-time.
It usually improves after birth.

blocks.p: **Why:** stretching skin, dryness and hormones can cause mild itching, especially on the bump.

ul: Moisturise with a fragrance-free product, wear loose cotton clothing, and avoid very hot showers.
Intense itching, especially of the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, often worse at night and without a rash, can be a sign of obstetric cholestasis. This needs a blood test.

blocks.p: **Why:** pressure on leg veins and hormones relaxing vein walls. Veins may also appear on the vulva.

ul: Raise your legs, avoid crossing them, walk, and ask about support stockings.
Veins that become hot, red, hard and painful need checking.

soon: Nausea or vomiting that stops you eating most of the day
Constipation that lasts several days despite changes, or bleeding from the back passage
Pelvic or back pain that limits walking or sleeping
Intense itching, especially of the palms and soles
Tingling that weakens your grip
urgent: Severe headache that does not ease, vision problems, pain under the ribs, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet
A painful, red, swollen calf on one side, chest pain or sudden breathlessness
Severe abdominal pain, bleeding, or regular contractions before 37 weeks
Unable to keep fluids down for 12 hours or more

blocks.p: Constant small discomforts can wear you down more than one big problem. You may hear that “every pregnant woman goes through this”, which can make you feel you have no right to complain or ask for help. Being common does not mean you have to simply endure it. Most discomforts have specific, effective adjustments, and your doctor or a physiotherapist can help with those that persist.

takeaway: Pregnancy discomforts have specific causes and specific fixes. Adjust how you eat, move, sit, sleep and lift, and ask a physiotherapist or doctor about persistent pain. Never take medicines or herbal remedies without checking first. Know the few symptoms that need urgent attention: severe headache, sudden swelling, intense itching of palms and soles, and calf pain.
prompt: Which discomfort is affecting you most, and which specific change from this guide could you try for one week?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Understanding Your Changing Appetite
description: Appetite can change dramatically in pregnancy: aversions to foods you loved, intense cravings, a metallic taste, a heightened sense of smell, and big swings in hunger. This guide explains why these changes happen, how much extra food you actually need, how to eat well when appetite is unpredictable, and when a craving signals something to check.
glance: Food aversions and a heightened sense of smell are strongest in the first trimester and are linked to pregnancy hormones.
Extra energy needs are small and arrive mostly in the third trimester. You do not need to “eat for two”.
Craving non-food items such as clay (mitti), chalk, ice or raw rice is called pica and can signal iron deficiency. Tell your doctor.
When appetite is poor, focus on small, frequent, nutrient-dense foods rather than full meals.

ul: **Hormones:** rising hCG, oestrogen and progesterone affect taste and smell and are closely linked with nausea.
**A sharper sense of smell:** many women find smells overwhelming, especially cooking oil, meat, onion, garlic, perfume and tea. This can create strong aversions.
**Taste changes:** a metallic or bitter taste (dysgeusia) is common in early pregnancy.
**Slower digestion:** progesterone slows the gut, so you feel full sooner and may feel bloated.
**Space:** in late pregnancy, the uterus presses on your stomach, so large meals become uncomfortable.
**Emotions and tiredness** also affect hunger. Some women eat less when anxious, others more.

blocks.h: Cravings: what they mean and do not mean

blocks.p: Cravings for sour, salty, sweet or spicy foods are common: achaar, chaat, imli, mangoes, ice cream, pakoras. There is little evidence that ordinary cravings reflect a specific nutrient deficiency. They are more likely related to hormonal changes in taste and reward. Enjoying them in moderation is fine.

The exception is **pica**: cravings for non-food substances such as clay or soil (mitti), chalk, ash, ice, raw rice or paper. Pica is often associated with iron deficiency. Eating clay or soil can also expose you to infections, parasites and contaminants such as lead. If you have these cravings, tell your doctor and ask for your iron levels to be checked. It is not shameful; it is a known symptom.

blocks.h: How much extra do you need to eat?

blocks.p: Very little in the first two trimesters. Energy needs rise modestly in the third trimester, roughly the equivalent of an extra small snack, such as a glass of milk and a handful of nuts, or a roti with daal. What matters more than quantity is quality: protein, iron, calcium, folate, fibre and fluids. “Eating for two” in the sense of doubling portions often leads to heartburn, discomfort and more weight gain than recommended.

blocks.h: Eating well when you can’t face food

ul: **Eat little and often:** six small meals may work better than three large ones.
**Prioritise what you can keep down,** even if it is plain. Nutrition can improve once nausea settles.
**Choose foods that are nutrient-dense in small amounts:** eggs, yoghurt, milk, lassi, paneer, nuts, daal, chickpeas, dates and bananas.
**If meat or eggs repel you,** get protein from daal, chana, yoghurt, milk, nuts and seeds.
**If smells are the problem,** eat cold foods (yoghurt, fruit, sandwiches, cold chickpea chaat) and let someone else cook.
**Drink between meals** rather than with them, so you don’t fill up on fluids.
Half of the plate: vegetables and fruit, ideally including leafy greens and something rich in vitamin C
A quarter: protein such as daal, chickpeas, beans, eggs, chicken, fish or meat
A quarter: whole grains such as whole wheat roti, brown rice or daliya
Plus a source of calcium such as milk, yoghurt or paneer, and a small amount of healthy fat

blocks.p: When your stomach has less room, switch to smaller portions more often, and avoid eating large meals late at night, which worsens heartburn and disrupts sleep. Many women feel hungrier in the evening; plan a light, early dinner and a small protein snack if needed.

myth: “If you crave sweets, it’s a girl; if you crave salty food, it’s a boy.”
Cravings do not predict the baby’s sex.
“Not satisfying a craving will harm the baby or leave a mark on it.”
Cravings are not a need the baby has. Unsatisfied cravings cause no harm.
“Ghee and extra butter make the birth easier.”
There is no evidence for this. Healthy fats are part of a balanced diet, but large amounts add calories without benefit and can worsen heartburn.

soon: Cravings for clay, chalk, ice, raw rice, ash or other non-food items
Little appetite for more than a few days with weight loss
Extreme thirst with passing large amounts of urine
A history of an eating disorder, or anxiety about weight gain that is affecting how you eat
urgent: Unable to keep food or fluids down for 12 hours or more
Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Severe abdominal pain with vomiting

blocks.p: Eating in pregnancy is rarely just personal in Pakistani households. Relatives may urge you to eat more, push certain foods (desi ghee, panjeeri, almonds), or forbid others as “garam” or “thanda”. You may feel guilty if you can’t eat what is prepared for you. It is fine to explain that pregnancy changes your appetite and that your doctor has advised small, frequent, balanced meals. Equally, if you find yourself anxious about every bite, restricting food, or feeling out of control around eating, that is worth discussing with your doctor.

takeaway: Appetite changes in pregnancy are driven by hormones and your changing body. You don’t need to eat for two; you need to eat well, little and often. Enjoy cravings in moderation, but tell your doctor about cravings for non-food items like clay or ice, since they can signal iron deficiency.
prompt: What has your appetite been like lately, and what is one small, nourishing food you could keep within easy reach?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Preparing for the Transition to Motherhood
description: Becoming a mother is a transformation, not just an event. Researchers call it matrescence: a shift in identity, relationships, priorities and daily life as significant as adolescence. This guide explains what changes, the practical and emotional conversations worth having before birth, and how to prepare without trying to control everything.
glance: Matrescence is the term for the physical, emotional and social transition into motherhood. Like adolescence, it takes time.
The most useful preparation is often practical conversations about roles, help, money and rest, rather than buying things.
Mixed feelings about becoming a mother are common and do not predict how you will parent.
Planning who will support you in the first six weeks matters as much as planning the birth.

ul: **Your time:** a newborn feeds 8 to 12 times in 24 hours and needs care around the clock. Your days will be organised around the baby’s needs, especially in the first three months.
**Your body:** recovery from birth takes weeks to months, and if you breastfeed, your body continues to be closely linked to your baby’s.
**Your identity:** you remain who you were, and you also become someone new. Your priorities, values, ambitions and sense of self may shift in ways that are hard to predict.
**Your relationships:** with your husband, your mother, your mother-in-law and friends. New closeness and new tensions can both appear.
**Your role in the household:** in many Pakistani families, becoming a mother, especially of a first child, changes your status, the expectations placed on you and how much say you have.

blocks.h: The conversations worth having before birth

ol: **The first 40 days.** Where will you spend them, at your mother’s home or your in-laws’? Who will cook, clean and care for you? What does chilla mean in your family, and which customs do you want to follow?

**Night-time.** Who will help at night? How can your husband or others support you, even if you are breastfeeding, for example by changing nappies, burping and settling the baby, bringing water and taking a shift with the baby so you can sleep?
**Visitors.** How many and when? Who will manage them, so you can rest and feed in private?
**Household duties.** What will you stop doing for several weeks, and who will take it on?
**Money.** Hospital costs, baby needs, and any change in income if you take leave from work or studies.
**Feeding.** What you hope to do, and how your family can support it.
**Your own needs.** What helps you when you are stressed or tired? Tell your husband now, while you can think clearly.

blocks.p: A newborn needs much less than shops suggest: a safe place to sleep, clothes suitable for the season, nappies, a way to feed, a few blankets and a car seat if you travel by car. See the guide on preparing your home for a newborn. Spend more of your preparation energy on support, rest and learning the basics of newborn care.

ul: How breastfeeding works and what the first days look like (see the breastfeeding guide)
How often newborns feed, sleep and need changing
Safe sleep basics
Newborn danger signs that need urgent care (see the guide on building confidence as a first-time mother)
How you might feel emotionally in the first weeks, including baby blues
**Expect a learning curve.** Confidence in caring for a baby comes from doing it, not from feeling ready beforehand. Almost no one feels ready.
**Expect mixed feelings.** Love may arrive instantly or grow slowly. Both are normal.
**Lower your standards for the house** in advance. Decide now what “good enough” looks like.
**Plan for rest.** A recovering mother who rests heals better and copes better.
**Know where to turn** if you feel low or overwhelmed after birth.

myth: “Motherhood comes naturally, so you don’t need to learn anything.”
Caring for a baby is learned. Instinct helps, but skills such as feeding, settling and reading cues develop with practice and support.
“Once the baby arrives, your own needs no longer matter.”
Your recovery, rest, nutrition and mental health directly affect your ability to care for your baby. Meeting your needs is part of caring for your baby.

soon: You feel persistently low, anxious or numb about becoming a mother
You have a history of depression, anxiety or other mental health conditions and want to plan support for after birth
You have no one to help you after birth and need to explore options
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself or the baby
Feeling unable to keep yourself safe

blocks.p: Preparing for motherhood often brings up your own childhood, how you were mothered, and what you want to repeat or do differently. You may grieve your independence while also looking forward to your baby. If your pregnancy was unplanned, came after loss, or arrives at a difficult time, preparing may feel complicated. All of this is part of matrescence. Becoming a mother is not a single moment; it is a process that continues for months and years.

takeaway: The best preparation for motherhood is often a handful of honest conversations about support, rest, roles, visitors and money, plus learning a few essentials of newborn care. Expect a learning curve and mixed feelings. You do not have to feel ready to become a good mother; you will grow into it.
prompt: What would a well-supported first six weeks look like for you, and which conversation do you need to have to make it more likely?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide
NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Understanding Your Changing Body
description: Your body changes continuously from conception to about a year after birth, and each phase has its own logic. This guide maps the whole arc: what changes in pregnancy, what happens in the first days and weeks after birth, what settles over months, and what may stay. Knowing the timeline helps you set fair expectations and spot what needs attention.
glance: Pregnancy changes are mostly driven by hormones, a growing uterus, extra blood and fluid, and looser ligaments.
After birth, the uterus shrinks back over about six weeks, fluid is lost over the first weeks, and hormones drop sharply.
Many changes, such as abdominal muscle separation, pelvic floor strength and hair shedding, take months, not weeks.
Some changes are lasting. They are signs of what your body has done, not damage.

blocks.p: Think of the journey in four phases. Each has different priorities, and the timelines overlap.

ul: **Early weeks:** invisible but intense changes. Hormones rise, blood volume starts expanding, breasts change, digestion slows. You may feel very different while looking the same.
**Middle weeks:** visible change. The bump appears, skin may darken in places, hair often thickens, and ligaments loosen.
**Late weeks:** the body prepares for birth. The pelvis becomes more flexible, the cervix softens, breasts may leak colostrum, and fluid retention increases.

blocks.p: See the guide on physical changes during pregnancy for a system-by-system explanation.

blocks.h: Phase 2: The first two weeks after birth

ul: **Bleeding (lochia)** starts heavy and red, like a heavy period, and gradually lightens.
**The uterus contracts** to close blood vessels where the placenta was attached. This causes afterpains, which can be stronger when breastfeeding.
**Your belly** will still look around five or six months pregnant at first, because the uterus is still large and the stretched abdominal wall needs time.
**Fluid shifts:** you may sweat heavily at night and pass large amounts of urine as your body clears extra fluid. Swelling in the legs can briefly worsen before improving.
**Breasts** change from producing colostrum to producing more milk, usually around day 2 to 5, which can cause fullness and tenderness.
**The perineum or caesarean wound** begins healing.
**Hormones drop sharply** after the placenta is delivered, which affects mood (see the guide on baby blues).

blocks.h: Phase 3: Six weeks to six months

ul: **The uterus** is back to near its pre-pregnancy size by around six weeks.
**Bleeding** usually stops within about six weeks.
**Abdominal muscles** gradually draw back together, helped by appropriate exercise.
**Pelvic floor muscles** regain strength over months; leaking urine is common early on and usually improves with exercises.
**Hair shedding** often starts around two to four months after birth, as hairs that stayed in the growing phase during pregnancy fall out together.
**Periods** may return within weeks if you are not breastfeeding, or much later if you are.
**Weight** changes gradually; there is no fixed timeline.

blocks.h: Phase 4: Six months to a year and beyond

ul: **Hair** usually returns to its normal cycle by around a year after birth.
**Pigmentation** such as melasma and linea nigra often fades, though sun exposure can slow this.
**Joints and ligaments** gradually stabilise, sometimes more slowly while breastfeeding.
**Breast shape** may change after weaning, as milk-producing tissue reduces.
**Strength and fitness** can return progressively with a gradual exercise plan.
Stretch marks, which fade from red or purple to pale silver lines
A softer belly, or some remaining abdominal muscle separation
Changes in breast size and shape
Wider hips or ribcage
Sometimes a larger shoe size
A caesarean scar or perineal scar

blocks.p: These changes are evidence of growth, birth and feeding. Many women find that their relationship with them softens over time, especially when the pressure to “bounce back” is removed.

ul: Nutrition and rest that match the demands of each phase
Pelvic floor exercises in pregnancy and after birth
Gradual, appropriate movement rather than sudden intense exercise
Patience with timelines measured in months, not weeks
Clothes that fit your body now, not your body before or the body you hope to have

soon: Leaking urine or wind that is not improving several months after birth
A sensation of heaviness, dragging or a bulge in the vagina
A gap down the middle of your abdomen that is not improving, or that causes back pain
Hair loss that continues beyond a year, or is patchy
urgent: Heavy bleeding after birth, soaking a pad in an hour, or large clots
Fever, chills, or a wound that is red, hot, swollen or oozing
A painful, swollen calf, chest pain or sudden breathlessness

blocks.p: Comments like “You still look pregnant” or “When will you lose the weight?” are common and can sting. Understanding your body’s timeline gives you a reply, even if only to yourself: your body is still in the middle of a process that takes about a year.

takeaway: Your body changes in phases from conception to around a year after birth. Most changes resolve gradually over months, some take longer, and a few are lasting. Expect a long, gradual recovery and measure progress in months, not weeks.
prompt: Which phase are you in right now, and is there a change you have been judging too quickly?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Body Image During Pregnancy
description: Pregnancy can change how you feel about your body in many directions: pride, awe, discomfort, loss of control, or distress. This guide explains why body image shifts during pregnancy, how comments and social media affect it, and practical ways to build a steadier relationship with your changing body.
glance: Body image is how you see, think about and feel about your body. It can change even when your body is doing exactly what it should.
Comments from family and strangers are among the most common triggers of body image distress in pregnancy.
Focusing on what your body is doing, rather than how it looks, can help.
A history of an eating disorder makes pregnancy more complex. Tell your doctor so you can get support early.

ul: **Speed of change:** your body changes faster than your mental picture of it can update.
**Loss of control:** shape, weight, skin and appetite are no longer fully yours to manage.
**Visibility:** a pregnant body is commented on, touched and judged by others in a way most bodies are not.
**Cultural ideals:** expectations around fairness, slimness, and looking “neat” in front of guests can collide with the realities of pregnancy.
**Your history:** past comments about your weight or appearance, or a history of disordered eating, may resurface.
Feeling awkward in the “in-between” stage, before you clearly look pregnant
Loving the bump but disliking changes in your face, arms or thighs
Worry about stretch marks, skin darkening or weight gain
Feeling invisible, or feeling like your body now belongs to everyone
Distress at the scale at antenatal visits

blocks.p: Comments such as “You’ve become so big”, “Your face has spread, it must be a girl” or “You’ve gone dark” are common in Pakistani households and gatherings, and are often meant as harmless observations. They can still hurt.

ul: **Decide on a short reply in advance:** “The baby and I are healthy, that’s what matters”, “My doctor is happy with how things are going”, or simply “Shukriya” and a change of subject.
**Ask your husband or mother to step in** when certain relatives repeatedly comment.
**Remember what comments really measure:** the speaker’s habits and beliefs, not your health or worth.

ol: **Shift from appearance to function.** Notice what your body is doing: growing organs, pumping extra blood, preparing to feed.
**Wear clothes that fit now.** Squeezing into pre-pregnancy clothes keeps reminding you of change. See the guide on clothing and comfort.
**Curate social media.** Unfollow accounts that make you compare, and follow accounts that show real pregnant and postpartum bodies.
**Limit body checking.** Repeatedly checking mirrors, pinching skin or weighing yourself tends to increase distress rather than reduce it.
**Ask not to be told your weight** at appointments if numbers upset you. You can ask your doctor to tell you only if there is a concern.
**Move for how it feels,** not to control shape.
**Talk to someone** about what specifically bothers you. Naming it often reduces its power.

blocks.h: If you have a history of disordered eating

blocks.p: Pregnancy can trigger old patterns, such as restricting, bingeing, purging or over-exercising, or it can be a time when they ease. Either way, tell your doctor early. Restricting food in pregnancy affects your and your baby’s nutrition, and support during pregnancy and after birth makes a real difference.
