soon: Skipping meals, restricting food, making yourself sick, or exercising excessively to control weight
Body-related distress most days, or avoiding people because of how you look
Feeling low or anxious most of the time
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: It is possible to feel grateful for your pregnancy and still find the physical changes hard. Body image struggles are not vanity; they touch on identity, control, and how you are treated by others. They deserve care, not dismissal.

takeaway: Pregnancy changes your body faster than your mind can adjust, while inviting constant comments. Shift your attention to what your body is doing, dress for your body now, prepare responses to comments, and limit the comparisons and checking that feed distress. If body worries are affecting how you eat, tell your doctor.
prompt: What is one thing your body has done in this pregnancy that you have not given yourself credit for?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Accepting Weight Changes
description: Weight gain in pregnancy is necessary and expected, but it is often surrounded by anxiety and unhelpful comments. This guide explains where pregnancy weight actually goes, the recommended ranges based on your starting weight, why dieting in pregnancy isn’t advised, and what realistic weight change after birth looks like.
glance: Pregnancy weight includes your baby, placenta, amniotic fluid, extra blood and fluid, a larger uterus and breasts, and some fat stored for breastfeeding.
How much you are advised to gain depends on your pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI). There is no single right number.
Dieting to lose weight in pregnancy isn’t recommended. The focus is on balanced eating and regular activity.
Weight loss after birth is gradual. Many women take months to a year.

blocks.p: Only part of the weight gained in pregnancy is the baby. The rest is made up of:

ul: The placenta
Amniotic fluid
A larger uterus
Increased blood volume
Extra fluid in your tissues
Larger breasts
Fat stores, which provide energy for late pregnancy and breastfeeding

blocks.p: This is why most women lose a substantial amount of weight within the first weeks after birth, as the baby, placenta, fluid and blood volume are lost, while the rest comes off more gradually.

blocks.h: How much weight gain is recommended?

blocks.p: Widely used guidance from the US Institute of Medicine bases recommendations on pre-pregnancy BMI. For a single baby, the ranges are roughly:

ul: **Underweight (BMI below 18.5):** around 12.5 to 18 kg
**Healthy weight (BMI 18.5 to 24.9):** around 11.5 to 16 kg
**Overweight (BMI 25 to 29.9):** around 7 to 11.5 kg
**Obese (BMI 30 and above):** around 5 to 9 kg

blocks.p: Some guidance suggests lower BMI cut-offs for South Asian women, because health risks can appear at lower weights. Ranges differ for twins. Your doctor will tell you what applies to you, and different services weigh women at different frequencies.

blocks.h: Why dieting in pregnancy isn’t advised

blocks.p: Restricting calories in pregnancy can reduce the nutrients available to your baby and leave you tired and unwell. If you started pregnancy above a healthy weight, the usual focus is limiting excess gain through balanced eating and regular activity, not losing weight. Your doctor may refer you to a dietitian.

blocks.h: What healthy eating looks like for weight

ul: Regular meals with protein, vegetables, whole grains and some healthy fats
Watching portions of ghee, oil, fried foods, mithai, sugary drinks and white flour
Small, extra amounts only in the third trimester
Not “eating for two”
Daily activity, if your pregnancy is uncomplicated
**First weeks:** a noticeable drop as baby, placenta, fluid and extra blood are lost
**Following months:** gradual change, often slower than expected
**Breastfeeding** uses energy, and helps some women lose weight, but not all. Appetite also increases.
**Sleep loss and stress** affect appetite hormones, and can make weight loss harder

blocks.p: A gradual approach, with balanced meals and gradual exercise once you are recovered, works better than strict dieting, which can affect milk supply, energy and mood. Speak to your doctor before starting any significant diet while breastfeeding.

myth: “Breastfeeding guarantees weight loss.”
Breastfeeding uses energy, but appetite also rises, and many factors affect weight. Some women lose weight while breastfeeding; others do not until later.
“You should lose the baby weight within six weeks.”
There is no medical timeline like this. Many women take a year or more, and that is normal.
“Panjeeri and desi ghee are needed to recover.”
These foods are traditional and nourishing in moderate amounts, but they are very energy-dense. Large daily portions can lead to weight gain without extra benefit.

soon: Very rapid weight gain over a short period, especially with swelling
Losing weight in pregnancy, or being unable to eat enough
Anxiety about weight that is affecting how you eat
urgent: Sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet with headache or vision changes

blocks.p: Weight is one of the most commented-on aspects of pregnancy and postpartum life in Pakistan, with remarks running in both directions: “You’re not eating enough” and “You’ve gained too much”. It is fine to direct those conversations to what your doctor has said and leave them there. Your weight is a medical matter between you and your doctor, not a public measure of your success.

takeaway: Pregnancy weight gain is necessary and is made up mostly of your baby and the systems supporting it. Follow guidance based on your starting weight, focus on balanced eating and activity rather than dieting, and expect weight loss after birth to take months, not weeks.
prompt: Which comment about your weight has stayed with you most, and what would you say back if you could?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Skin, Hair and Appearance Changes
description: Skin and hair change noticeably in pregnancy and after birth: darker patches, a dark line on the belly, stretch marks, acne, thicker hair, and then hair shedding months after birth. This guide explains why each change happens, what you can and can’t influence, which products to check before using, and which changes need a doctor.
glance: Hormones stimulate pigment cells, causing darker nipples, a dark line on the belly (linea nigra) and facial patches (melasma). These usually fade after birth.
No cream has been proven to prevent stretch marks. Genetics play a big role.
Postpartum hair shedding usually starts two to four months after birth and settles within about a year.
Check with your doctor before using skin-lightening creams, retinoid products or chemical treatments.

blocks.p: **Why:** pregnancy hormones stimulate melanocytes, the cells that produce pigment. Women with darker skin tones often notice these changes more.

ul: **Linea nigra:** a dark line from the navel down to the pubic area.
**Darker nipples and areolas**, and sometimes darker skin in the armpits, inner thighs and genital area.
**Melasma (chloasma or “the mask of pregnancy”):** brownish patches on the cheeks, forehead, upper lip or nose.

blocks.p: **What helps:** sun exposure makes melasma darker. Use sun protection, shade, a wide dupatta or hat outdoors, and a broad-spectrum sunscreen. Most pigmentation fades over months after birth.

**Caution:** many skin-lightening creams sold in Pakistan have been found to contain mercury or strong steroids, which can harm you and, in pregnancy, potentially your baby. Avoid them, and ask your doctor before using any treatment for pigmentation in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

**Why:** when skin stretches faster than its supporting fibres can adapt, small tears form in the deeper layer. They often appear on the belly, breasts, hips and thighs. Genetics, the rate of weight gain and skin type all play a role.

**What helps:** moisturising may relieve itching and dryness, but no cream or oil has been reliably shown to prevent stretch marks. Gradual weight gain may help. Stretch marks fade from red or purple to paler, silvery lines over months.
**Why:** hormones increase oil production. Some women get acne for the first time; others find it improves.

**What helps:** wash gently twice a day, avoid harsh scrubs and do not pick. Many acne treatments are not recommended in pregnancy, especially retinoids (vitamin A derivatives found in some creams and pills). Ask your doctor before using anything.

ul: **Skin tags:** small, soft growths often on the neck or under the arms. Usually harmless.
**Spider veins and red palms:** caused by increased blood flow, and usually fade after birth.
**Itching:** mild itching from stretching skin is common, but intense itching, especially of palms and soles, needs checking for obstetric cholestasis.

**Itchy rash on the belly:** an itchy rash that starts in stretch marks (polymorphic eruption of pregnancy) can occur in late pregnancy. It is not harmful to the baby but can be very uncomfortable. Your doctor can advise.
**During pregnancy:** many hairs stay in the growing phase, so fewer fall out and hair often looks thicker and shinier. Some women notice more body or facial hair.

**After birth:** hormone levels drop and many hairs move into the resting phase together, then shed around two to four months later. This is called telogen effluvium. It can be alarming, with hair coming out in handfuls in the shower or on the pillow, but it is temporary, and hair usually returns to normal within about a year.

blocks.p: **What helps:** eat well, especially protein and iron, handle hair gently, avoid tight hairstyles, and consider a shorter cut during the shedding phase. Ask your doctor to check iron and thyroid levels if shedding seems excessive, lasts longer than a year, or comes with other symptoms.

blocks.h: Product safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding

ul: **Ask before using:** retinoid creams, skin-lightening creams, chemical peels, acne medication, and hair treatments.
**Hair dye:** there is limited evidence of harm, but many women choose to wait until after the first trimester. Use a well-ventilated area, and follow instructions.
**Mehndi:** natural henna is generally considered safe. Avoid “black henna”, which can contain a chemical called PPD that may cause severe skin reactions.
**Waxing and threading** are fine, though skin can be more sensitive.

soon: Intense itching, especially of the palms and soles
A rash that spreads, blisters, or is very itchy
A mole that changes in size, shape or colour, or bleeds
Hair loss that lasts beyond a year, or comes in patches
urgent: A rash with fever, or a rash that looks like bruising

blocks.p: Skin and hair are closely tied to identity, and changes can be painful, especially when relatives comment on darkening skin or hair loss. These changes are hormonal, not a result of anything you did, and most are temporary.

takeaway: Most skin and hair changes in pregnancy and after birth are driven by hormones and fade or settle within a year. Protect pigmented skin from the sun, avoid skin-lightening creams and retinoids, handle hair gently during postpartum shedding, and ask your doctor about any intense itching or unusual changes.
prompt: Which skin or hair change bothers you most, and does knowing it is likely temporary change how you feel about it?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Breast Changes and Body Awareness
description: Breasts are among the first parts of the body to change in pregnancy and continue changing through feeding and weaning. This guide explains what happens to breast tissue, why tenderness, leaking and colour changes occur, how to choose supportive bras, and why staying aware of lumps and changes still matters during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
glance: Breast tenderness and growth often begin in the first weeks of pregnancy as hormones develop milk-producing tissue.
Darker areolas, visible veins and small bumps on the areola (Montgomery’s glands) are normal changes.
Some women leak colostrum from the second trimester. Others do not leak at all; neither predicts milk supply.
A new lump in pregnancy or breastfeeding should still be checked by a doctor.

blocks.h: What happens to your breasts in pregnancy

ul: **Early weeks:** oestrogen and progesterone stimulate the milk ducts and glands to grow, so breasts may feel tender, heavy, tingling or sore. This often eases after the first trimester.
**Growth:** breasts may increase in size by one or more cup sizes over pregnancy.
**Darker areolas:** the areola (the skin around the nipple) becomes darker and larger, which may help a newborn see where to feed.
**Montgomery’s glands:** small bumps on the areola become more noticeable. They produce an oily substance that keeps the nipple and areola clean and moisturised.
**Visible veins:** increased blood flow makes veins more visible.

**Colostrum:** from the second trimester, the breasts begin producing colostrum, the first milk. Some women leak small amounts, often yellowish and sticky. Many do not, and this does not predict how much milk you will have.
**Stretch marks** may appear as breasts grow.
**Wear a well-fitting, supportive bra.** Soft, non-wired bras are often more comfortable. Get re-measured as you grow.
**A sleep bra** can help if breasts are heavy or tender at night.
**Breast pads** can absorb leaks.
**Wash with water;** soap can dry the skin of the nipples and areolas.
**Nursing bras** can be bought towards the end of pregnancy, when your size has mostly stabilised. Size may change again when milk comes in.
**Days 1 to 3:** the breasts produce small amounts of colostrum.
**Days 2 to 5:** milk “comes in”. Breasts may become fuller, warmer and heavier. Some women feel engorged (very full, hard and painful). See the breastfeeding guide for what helps.
**Weeks to months:** as supply adjusts to your baby’s needs, breasts usually feel softer, even though milk production continues.
**After weaning:** breasts may become smaller or softer than before pregnancy, as milk-producing tissue reduces.

blocks.p: Your breasts will still produce milk in the first days. Wearing a supportive bra, using cold compresses, and avoiding stimulating the breasts can help milk production slow down. Ask your doctor for advice if you are uncomfortable.

blocks.h: Breast awareness in pregnancy and breastfeeding

blocks.p: Breast changes are expected now, but this does not mean every lump is normal. Breast cancer during pregnancy and breastfeeding is uncommon, but it can be harder to notice because breasts are already changing. Get to know how your breasts look and feel, and see a doctor if you notice:

ul: A new lump or thickening that does not go away within a week or so, or that doesn’t change with feeding
Skin dimpling, puckering or redness that doesn’t settle
Changes in the nipple, such as it becoming pulled in, or a rash on the nipple
Blood-stained nipple discharge
A lump in the armpit

myth: “Small breasts won’t produce enough milk.”
Breast size mostly reflects fatty tissue, not the glandular tissue that makes milk. Women with small breasts can produce plenty of milk.
“Leaking colostrum in pregnancy means you will have lots of milk; not leaking means you will have too little.”
Leaking or not leaking in pregnancy does not predict supply after birth.
“Breastfeeding ruins your breasts.”
Pregnancy itself causes most changes to breast shape. Genetics, age and weight changes also matter.

soon: A new lump, skin changes, nipple changes or blood-stained discharge
Painful, cracked or bleeding nipples during breastfeeding
A hard, painful area of the breast that does not improve within a day
urgent: A red, hot, painful area of the breast with fever, chills or flu-like symptoms (possible mastitis needing treatment)

blocks.p: Breasts carry many meanings: sexuality, privacy, femininity, and now feeding. It is normal to feel protective, self-conscious, or ambivalent about changes, especially in households where privacy is limited.

takeaway: Breast changes in pregnancy and after birth are driven by hormones preparing your body to feed. Support your breasts with well-fitting bras, wash with water rather than soap, and expect changes to continue through feeding and weaning. Even with all these changes, a new lump or unusual change should still be checked.
prompt: How do you feel about the changes in your breasts, and is there something about feeding that you would like to understand better?

title: Clothing, Comfort and Personal Style
description: Clothes that fit your changing body make a real difference to comfort, confidence and practical life, from shalwar kameez that accommodate a bump to nursing-friendly kurtas and outfits that avoid pressing on a caesarean scar. This guide offers practical, budget-friendly guidance for each stage, for Pakistan’s climate and for social occasions.
glance: Dress for the body you have now, not the body you had before or hope to have later.
Elastic or drawstring waists, loose kurtas and breathable cotton work well throughout pregnancy.
For breastfeeding, front-opening or side-zip kurtas and a large dupatta give privacy and easy access.
After a caesarean, choose high, soft waistbands that sit above the scar, or loose clothes with no waistband pressure.

blocks.p: Tight clothes press on a sensitive bump, worsen heartburn, increase swelling and make it harder to breathe. Uncomfortable clothes also remind you of change all day. Clothes that fit can make you feel more like yourself.

ul: **Waistbands:** elastic or drawstring shalwar, trousers or pajamas you can loosen as you grow. Wear them under the bump or over it, whichever feels better.
**Kurtas and kameez:** A-line, flowing, or empire-waist styles leave room for the bump. Side slits help with movement.
**Fabric:** cotton, lawn and linen breathe well in summer. Layers help in winter. Pregnancy raises your body temperature and you may sweat more.
**Bras:** soft, supportive, non-wired bras, re-measured as you grow.
**Shoes:** low, wide, supportive shoes for balance and swelling. Avoid high heels in late pregnancy, when your centre of gravity changes.
**Budget:** many women adapt existing clothes by letting out seams, borrowing from relatives, or having a few kurtas stitched in a looser cut that will also work for breastfeeding.
**The first weeks:** your belly will still be rounded. Keep wearing loose maternity clothes. Soft, front-opening tops make feeding and skin-to-skin easier.
**After a caesarean:** choose high-waisted, soft shalwar or underwear that sits above the scar, or loose clothing without a tight waistband. Cotton underwear lets the skin breathe.
**After a vaginal birth:** loose, breathable underwear and clothes help with perineal comfort and maternity pads.
**Bleeding:** darker, washable clothing can help you feel less worried about leaks.
**Kurtas with front buttons, front zips, or hidden side zips** let you feed without lifting the whole garment.
**A large dupatta, shawl or chadar** can provide privacy when feeding in front of others.
**Two-layer approach:** a loose top over a vest or camisole that you pull down, so your belly stays covered.
**Nursing bras** that open with clips on each side.
**Breast pads** for leaks, especially in the first weeks.
**Choose fabrics that breathe,** because heavy embroidery and synthetic fabrics can be hot and scratchy.
**Choose a style you can feed in,** or bring a shawl and plan a quiet room.
**Comfortable shoes,** or flat shoes you can swap into.
**Avoid tight waistbands,** especially after a caesarean.
Keep a few comfortable outfits you like within easy reach.
Don’t buy too many postpartum clothes in advance, since your size will change.
Choose clothes you can wash easily, as leaks and spit-up are common.
Plan outfits for visitors so you aren’t changing in a rush.

soon: Skin irritation, rash or infection where clothes rub, especially near a wound
Swelling that clothing makes worse

blocks.p: Clothes are part of identity. It can be hard when favourite outfits no longer fit or when you feel pressure to look polished for guests. It is fine to prioritise comfort, and to choose a few pieces that make you feel like yourself.

takeaway: Comfortable, practical clothing supports your body and your confidence. Choose soft waistbands, breathable fabrics and feeding-friendly designs, avoid pressure on a caesarean scar, and dress for your body as it is now.
prompt: Which item of clothing makes you feel most comfortable and most like yourself, and how could you make wearing it easier?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Posture, Mobility and Physical Comfort
description: Pregnancy changes your posture, balance and how your joints move, and after birth the physical demands of lifting, feeding and carrying a baby can strain your back, neck and wrists. This guide explains the mechanics, and gives specific techniques for standing, sitting, lifting, getting out of bed, floor-level chores, feeding and carrying.
glance: Relaxin and progesterone loosen ligaments, and the bump shifts your centre of gravity, putting strain on the lower back and pelvis.
Small changes in how you sit, stand, lift and turn can reduce pain significantly.
Pelvic girdle pain is common and treatable. A physiotherapist can help.
After birth, feeding and carrying positions matter for your neck, back and wrists.

ul: **Looser ligaments:** relaxin helps the pelvis widen for birth, but it also makes joints less stable, especially in the pelvis and lower back.
**Forward shift:** as the bump grows, your weight moves forward. Many women compensate by arching the lower back and leaning back, which strains muscles.
**Stretched abdominal muscles:** the muscles that support the spine are stretched and weaker.
**Larger breasts:** extra weight on the chest can round the shoulders.
Stand tall, as if a string is pulling the top of your head upward.
Keep your weight evenly on both feet, with knees soft rather than locked.
Gently tuck your tailbone under rather than arching your lower back.
Wear low, supportive shoes.
Change position often; avoid standing still for long periods, such as at the stove.
Sit with your back supported, hips slightly higher than knees, and feet flat on the floor or a small stool.
Place a cushion or rolled towel behind your lower back.
Avoid crossing your legs.
If you sit on the floor for meals or chores, use a cushion or a low stool and lean against a wall. Avoid deep squats or twisting for long periods in late pregnancy if your pelvis is sore.

blocks.h: Getting in and out of bed (log rolling)

ol: Bend your knees and keep them together.
Roll onto your side as one unit, keeping shoulders and hips aligned.
Push yourself up with your arms while swinging your legs over the edge of the bed.
Reverse the process to lie down.

blocks.p: This technique is also very helpful after a caesarean.

ul: Avoid heavy lifting where possible, including buckets of water, gas cylinders, heavy pots, and toddlers.
When you must lift, bend your knees and keep your back straight, hold the object close to your body, and avoid twisting.
Break loads into smaller amounts.

blocks.p: Many household tasks in Pakistan, such as sweeping (jharoo), mopping (pocha), washing clothes and preparing vegetables, are done close to the floor.

ul: Use a long-handled broom or mop where possible.
Sit on a low stool rather than squatting for long periods.
Kneel on a cushion for tasks at floor level.
Take regular breaks and change position.
Ask others to take on heavier tasks in late pregnancy and after birth.

blocks.p: Pain at the front of the pubic bone, in the hips or buttocks, worse when walking, climbing stairs, standing on one leg or turning in bed. It is common and treatable.

ul: Keep knees together when moving.
Sit to dress.
Take stairs one at a time.
Avoid wide stances and heavy lifting.
Ask your doctor for a referral to a physiotherapist.

blocks.h: After birth: feeding, carrying and lifting

ul: **Feeding posture:** bring the baby to the breast rather than leaning forward. Use pillows to support your arms and the baby’s weight. Keep your shoulders relaxed and your back supported.
**Carrying:** hold the baby close to your body, and switch sides. A well-fitted carrier can spread the weight, with the baby high and close enough to kiss on the head.
**Lifting the baby:** bend your knees to pick up the baby from low surfaces.

**Wrists:** “mother’s wrist” (De Quervain’s tenosynovitis) is pain at the thumb side of the wrist from repeated lifting with the thumb outstretched. Lift with your palms facing up and thumbs close to your hand, and rest the wrist.

blocks.p: The two halves of the abdominal muscle can separate down the middle during pregnancy. It is common and often improves on its own in the months after birth. Avoid strain such as sitting straight up from lying (roll to your side instead), and start with gentle core and pelvic floor exercises. A physiotherapist can assess the gap and guide you.

soon: Pelvic or back pain that limits walking, sleeping or caring for your baby
Pain or a bulge down the middle of your abdomen that is not improving after birth
Wrist pain that makes holding your baby difficult
Numbness or tingling in the legs
urgent: Back pain with fever, burning when passing urine, or pain in your side (possible kidney infection)
Back pain with regular tightening, bleeding or fluid loss in pregnancy (possible labour)
Sudden weakness in the legs, or loss of bladder or bowel control

blocks.p: Pain affects mood, sleep and patience. It can also make you feel guilty if you can’t keep up with household tasks. Pain in pregnancy and after birth is a reason to adapt tasks and ask for help, not a sign of weakness.

takeaway: Posture changes in pregnancy are driven by looser ligaments and a shifting centre of gravity. Small adjustments to how you stand, sit, lift and turn can reduce pain, and physiotherapy is effective for pelvic and back pain. After birth, protect your back, neck and wrists while feeding and carrying.
prompt: Which daily movement causes you the most discomfort, and how could you change or share that task?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Feeling Attractive During Pregnancy
description: How attractive you feel in pregnancy can shift dramatically. Some women feel more feminine and confident; others feel unrecognisable or invisible. Desire also changes from trimester to trimester. This guide explains why, what is safe for intimacy in pregnancy, and how to stay connected to yourself and your husband.
glance: Feeling attractive is shaped by body changes, hormones, energy levels, comments from others and your own expectations.
Desire often dips in the first trimester, may rise in the second, and dips again in the third. All patterns are normal.
In an uncomplicated pregnancy, sex is generally considered safe. Your doctor may advise against it in some situations.
Connection doesn’t only mean sex; affection, conversation and care count.

ul: **Body changes:** weight, shape, skin and hair are all changing.
**Hormones:** can increase blood flow and sensitivity, or bring nausea and tiredness.
**Energy:** exhaustion makes it hard to feel desirable or interested.
**Comments and expectations:** remarks about your size or skin, or beliefs that pregnant women should not be seen as sexual, can affect how you see yourself.
**Your husband’s reactions:** some partners feel more attracted; some feel unsure or worried about hurting the baby.

blocks.h: How desire may change across pregnancy

ul: **First trimester:** nausea, tiredness and tender breasts often reduce interest.
**Second trimester:** many women feel better and some notice increased desire, partly due to increased blood flow to the pelvic area.
**Third trimester:** the bump, discomfort, tiredness and anxiety about birth often reduce interest again.

blocks.p: Any pattern is normal. Desire can change from week to week.

In an uncomplicated pregnancy, sex is generally considered safe. The baby is protected by the amniotic fluid, the uterus and the mucus plug sealing the cervix. Your doctor may advise avoiding sex if you have:

ul: Vaginal bleeding
A low-lying placenta (placenta praevia)
Waters that have broken
A risk of preterm labour, or a history of it
A weakened cervix

blocks.p: Mild cramping or tightening after sex can be normal. Bleeding, pain or fluid loss is not and needs checking. Positions that avoid pressure on the bump, such as side-lying, tend to be more comfortable later on.

blocks.h: Ways to feel more like yourself

ul: **Wear something you like,** whether a favourite colour, comfortable nightwear, or simple jewellery.
**Small rituals:** oiling your hair, a skincare routine, mehndi, or a long shower.
**Move your body** in a way that feels good.
**Limit comparison** with social media images.
**Notice what your body can do,** not just how it looks.
**Talk openly** about how you feel physically and emotionally. Many couples don’t discuss this, especially in households with little privacy.
**Affection without pressure:** holding hands, massage, sitting close, or time alone together.
**Address worries:** if either of you is anxious about harming the baby, ask your doctor together.
**Protect private time** where possible, even if it’s a short walk or a cup of tea alone.

myth: “Sex can hurt the baby.”
In an uncomplicated pregnancy, the baby is well protected. Ask your doctor if you have specific concerns.
“A pregnant woman shouldn’t care about looking attractive.”
Wanting to feel attractive is normal and healthy at any stage of life.

soon: Pain during sex
Feeling persistently low about your appearance or relationship
Feeling pressured into sex you don’t want
urgent: Bleeding, severe pain, or fluid loss after sex
Feeling unsafe with your partner

blocks.p: Feeling attractive is about more than looks. It’s also about feeling seen, valued and connected. If you feel invisible or that your body only matters as a vessel for the baby, it’s worth talking about. You remain a woman with your own needs, not just a mother-to-be.

takeaway: How attractive you feel and how much desire you have can change throughout pregnancy, and all patterns are normal. Sex is generally safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy unless your doctor advises otherwise. Small rituals, honest conversation and affection can help you feel connected to yourself and your husband.
prompt: When did you last feel most like yourself, and what was happening at that moment?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Rebuilding Body Confidence After Birth
description: Rebuilding confidence in your body after birth is a gradual process, not a race to “bounce back”. This guide explains realistic recovery timelines, how to approach the belly, scars, stretch marks and breasts with patience, the truth about abdominal binding, and practical steps to feel strong and at home in your body again.
glance: Most women take months to a year to feel physically recovered after birth. There is no single timeline.
Rebuilding strength starts with the pelvic floor and deep core, not crunches or diets.
Abdominal binders can support comfort after birth, but they don’t flatten the belly permanently.
Confidence often returns through strength and function, not through returning to your old shape.

ul: Your body has grown and birthed a baby, and in the first year it is still recovering and often feeding.
Social media often shows edited or atypical bodies.
Comments about your body after birth are common in Pakistan, including “When will your stomach go?” and comparisons with other relatives.
Focusing on appearance can distract from rest, recovery and real strength.
**First six weeks:** the uterus shrinks, bleeding settles, and wounds heal. Your belly will still look rounded. Focus on rest, feeding and gentle walking.
**Six weeks to three months:** gradual return to everyday activities, pelvic floor and core work, and longer walks.
**Three to six months:** building strength, returning to more vigorous exercise if recovered.
**Six months to a year:** continued progress in strength, weight, hair and skin.

blocks.p: The stretched skin and abdominal muscles take time to recover. Your belly may look soft or rounded for months.

ul: **Start with the deep core:** gentle breathing and pelvic floor exercises, gently drawing in the lower belly as you breathe out.
**Build gradually:** move to exercises like pelvic tilts, side-lying leg lifts and bridges, then more challenging exercises.
**Avoid early crunches and sit-ups** if you have abdominal separation; they can increase pressure on the gap.
**See a physiotherapist** if you have a noticeable gap, doming or bulging in the middle of your belly when you sit up.

blocks.p: Binding the belly after birth is a common tradition in Pakistan.

ul: **It can help comfort**, especially after a caesarean or with back pain.
**It doesn’t shrink the uterus faster** or flatten the belly permanently.
**Avoid binding very tightly**, as this can increase pressure on the pelvic floor and make breathing uncomfortable.
After a caesarean, ask your doctor before using a binder.
**Caesarean scar:** once fully healed (usually after around six weeks, as advised by your doctor), gentle scar massage can help reduce tightness and numbness. The area may feel numb for months.
**Perineal scar:** gentle massage once healed may help. Pain during sex or ongoing pain should be checked.
**Stretch marks:** fade from red or purple to silvery lines over months. Moisturising can help with dryness.

blocks.p: Breasts may change size and shape during feeding and after weaning. A well-fitting bra improves comfort and confidence.

ol: Wear clothes that fit your body now.
Choose movement that makes you feel strong and capable.
Celebrate progress in strength, such as carrying the baby without pain or walking further.
Limit comparison with others and social media.
Prepare a response to comments, such as “My body is still recovering.”
Be patient with timelines measured in months, not weeks.

soon: Leaking urine or wind that is not improving
A sensation of heaviness or bulging in the vagina
A gap or bulge in the middle of your abdomen
Pain during sex
Persistent low mood about your body
urgent: Wound redness, swelling, heat or oozing with fever

blocks.p: Rebuilding body confidence is often about acceptance as much as change. You may grieve your previous body while also feeling proud of what it has done. Both can be true.

takeaway: Rebuilding body confidence after birth is gradual, and focusing on strength and function is more useful than chasing a pre-pregnancy shape. Start with the pelvic floor and deep core, be careful with binding, care for scars once healed, and give yourself months, not weeks.
prompt: What would feeling strong in your body look like for you, and what is one small step toward it this week?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Understanding Postpartum Body Changes
description: Your body continues changing for months after birth, well beyond the first six weeks: belly, skin, hair, breasts, weight, periods, bladder and sexual health. This guide explains what to expect, what’s normal, what usually improves with time and exercise, and what’s worth seeing a doctor or physiotherapist about.
glance: Hair shedding typically starts two to four months after birth and settles by around a year.
Periods may return within weeks if not breastfeeding, or much later if breastfeeding. You can ovulate before your first period.
Leaking urine is common after birth but isn’t something you have to live with. Pelvic floor exercises help.
Vaginal dryness is common while breastfeeding, because oestrogen is low.

blocks.p: The uterus returns to its usual size by about six weeks, but the abdominal wall and skin take longer. A soft, rounded belly is normal for months. Abdominal muscle separation (diastasis recti) is common and often improves over the first year, especially with appropriate exercise.

Weight changes gradually and varies widely. Breastfeeding, sleep, stress, appetite and activity all play a part. A gradual, balanced approach works better than strict dieting, especially while breastfeeding.

In pregnancy, hairs stay in the growing phase longer. After birth, many of them enter the resting phase together and shed two to four months later. This can look dramatic but is usually temporary, settling by about a year after birth. See the guide on skin, hair and appearance changes.
Pigmentation (melasma, linea nigra) usually fades gradually. Stretch marks fade to silvery lines. Acne may flare or settle as hormones change.
Breasts change throughout feeding, often feeling softer once supply settles. After weaning, they may become smaller or change shape.

ul: **If you are not breastfeeding:** periods may return within around six to eight weeks, sometimes sooner.
**If you are breastfeeding:** periods may not return for months, especially if you breastfeed exclusively, day and night.

**You can ovulate before your first period,** so you can become pregnant before you notice your period has returned. Discuss contraception with your doctor before resuming sex if you don’t want to become pregnant.
**First periods** can be heavier, lighter or more irregular than before.
**Leaking urine** when you cough, sneeze, laugh or lift is common after birth, especially after a vaginal birth. Pelvic floor exercises help significantly.
**Urgency** (a sudden need to pass urine) can also occur.
**Leaking wind or stool** is less common, but needs checking, especially after a severe tear.
**Constipation and haemorrhoids** are common in the early weeks.

ol: Sit, stand or lie comfortably.
Squeeze and lift the muscles you would use to stop passing urine and to hold in wind, at the same time.
Hold for a few seconds while breathing normally, then fully relax.
Do a set of slow holds and a set of quick squeezes, several times a day.
Build up gradually. It can take weeks to months to notice improvement.

blocks.p: Don’t practise by stopping urine flow regularly, since that can interfere with emptying the bladder.

ul: **Vaginal dryness** is common while breastfeeding because oestrogen is low. A water-based lubricant can help.
**Pain during sex** is common at first, especially after a tear or episiotomy. It often improves, but persistent pain should be checked.
**Desire** often returns slowly, affected by tiredness, hormones, body confidence and emotional connection.

blocks.p: Ligaments can remain looser for months, especially while breastfeeding. Build strength gradually and avoid high-impact exercise until you are ready.

soon: Leaking urine or wind that is not improving after a few months of pelvic floor exercises
A sensation of heaviness, dragging, or a bulge in the vagina (possible prolapse)
Leaking stool, or being unable to control wind
Pain during sex that persists
Very heavy or prolonged periods
Hair loss beyond a year or in patches
urgent: Heavy bleeding, soaking a pad in an hour
Fever with abdominal pain or foul-smelling discharge

blocks.p: Many of these changes, such as leaking, pain during sex or hair loss, are hard to talk about, especially with family. They are common and often treatable. A doctor, midwife or physiotherapist can help.

takeaway: Your body continues changing for a year or more after birth. Expect hair shedding, gradual changes in your belly and weight, and periods that return on their own timeline. Leaking, pain during sex and heaviness in the vagina are common but treatable, and worth discussing with a professional.
prompt: Which change have you been hesitant to mention to a doctor, and what would make it easier to bring up?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Understanding Pregnancy Anxiety
description: Some worry in pregnancy is natural; your brain is adjusting to the responsibility of protecting a baby. But anxiety can become constant, physical and exhausting. This guide explains how anxiety works in the body, the specific worries common in pregnancy, how to tell everyday worry from an anxiety disorder, and practical techniques that help.
glance: Anxiety is your body’s threat system switching on. It causes real physical symptoms such as a racing heart, tight chest, nausea and poor sleep.
Common pregnancy worries include miscarriage, scans, the baby’s health, labour, money and coping after birth.
Everyday stress does not harm your baby. Severe, long-lasting anxiety is worth treating for your own wellbeing.
Talking therapies such as CBT are effective, and help is available during pregnancy.

blocks.p: When your brain detects a possible threat, it triggers the stress response: adrenaline and cortisol prepare your body to fight or run. Your heart beats faster, breathing quickens, muscles tense, digestion slows and your mind scans for danger. This is useful in a real emergency. In anxiety, the system switches on in response to “what if” thoughts and stays on.

In pregnancy, some anxiety symptoms overlap with normal pregnancy changes, such as a faster heart rate, breathlessness and poor sleep. This can create a loop: you notice a symptom, worry it means something is wrong, and the worry makes the symptom stronger.

ul: Miscarriage, especially in the first trimester or after a previous loss
Scan results and tests
Whether the baby is moving enough
Labour and birth
Being a good mother
Money, work and housing
Family reactions, including pressure about the baby’s sex
Your own health, or health conditions you already have

blocks.h: Everyday worry or an anxiety disorder?

blocks.p: Everyday worry tends to be linked to specific events, comes and goes, and can be eased by reassurance or information. Anxiety may need professional support when:

ul: You worry most of the day, on most days, for weeks
The worry is hard to control, even after reassurance
You have physical symptoms such as a racing heart, trembling, nausea or breathlessness that come on suddenly (panic attacks)
You avoid things, such as scans, appointments or going out, because of fear
You spend a lot of time checking, seeking reassurance or searching online
Sleep, eating, work or relationships are affected

blocks.p: Specific conditions include generalised anxiety, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and tokophobia (severe fear of childbirth). All are treatable.

ol: **Slow your breathing.** Breathe in through your nose for about four counts and out through your mouth for about six. A longer out-breath activates the body’s calming response.
**Ground yourself.** Name five things you can see, four you can feel, three you can hear, two you can smell and one you can taste.
**Schedule “worry time.”** Write worries down during the day and set a 15-minute window to think about them. When worries arise at other times, note them and postpone them.
**Separate the solvable from the unsolvable.** For solvable worries, plan one next step. For worries you can’t control, practise noticing and letting go.
**Limit online searching.** Search engines and forums tend to show the most frightening cases. Write questions down and ask your doctor.
**Plan for scan anxiety.** Bring someone with you, ask questions, and plan something calming afterward.
**Move your body.** Walking, stretching and prenatal yoga can reduce anxiety.
**Talk about it.** Share worries with someone who will listen without dismissing them.

ul: **Talking therapies**, such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), help you understand and change patterns of anxious thinking and behaviour.
**Support groups** for pregnant women or mothers.
**Medication** may be considered by a doctor for some women. The decision weighs benefits and risks for you and your baby. Do not stop any medication you already take without advice.

myth: “Stress and anxiety will harm the baby.”
Everyday stress is not known to harm a baby. Severe, prolonged anxiety is worth treating, mainly because it affects your wellbeing, sleep and daily life.
“If you’re anxious, you’ll be a bad mother.”
Anxiety is common and treatable, and has nothing to do with how much you love your baby or your ability to care for them.

soon: Worry most days for two weeks or more
Panic attacks
Avoiding appointments or scans because of fear
Anxiety affecting sleep, eating or daily life
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself
Panic symptoms with chest pain or breathlessness that doesn’t settle (get checked to rule out a physical cause)

blocks.p: In Pakistan, anxiety is sometimes dismissed as “tension” or “weak nerves”, or attributed to nazar. It is a real health condition that responds to treatment. Seeking help is not weakness; it is a way of caring for yourself and your baby.

takeaway: Anxiety in pregnancy is common and is caused by the brain’s threat system working overtime. Use breathing, grounding and worry time to calm your body, limit online searching, and talk to your doctor if worry is constant, hard to control, or affecting daily life. Effective help is available.
prompt: What worry has been taking up the most space in your mind, and is there one small step you could take toward it?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Managing Overthinking and Worry
description: Overthinking is the mental loop of replaying, predicting and analysing that feels productive but leaves you more tired and anxious. Pregnancy and early motherhood bring endless decisions and unknowns, making overthinking very common. This guide explains why the mind does this, the difference between problem-solving and rumination, and specific techniques to break the loop.
glance: Overthinking often feels like problem-solving but rarely leads to action.
Night-time worry feels bigger because tiredness and darkness amplify threat.
Repeated reassurance seeking and online searching give short-term relief but strengthen worry in the long run.
Techniques such as worry postponement, writing things down and sorting worries can break the loop.

ul: **Uncertainty:** pregnancy and parenthood bring many unknowns, and the brain tries to fill the gaps by predicting outcomes.
**Responsibility:** caring for a baby raises the stakes of every decision.
**Information overload:** advice from family, doctors, social media and the internet often conflicts.
**Tiredness:** sleep deprivation reduces the brain’s ability to regulate emotions and filter thoughts.
**Personality and history:** people who have experienced anxiety, perfectionism or difficult events may be more prone to overthinking.
**Problem-solving** focuses on a specific problem, generates options, and leads to a decision or action.
**Rumination** replays events or questions (“Why did I...?”, “What if...?”) without reaching a conclusion.

blocks.p: A useful test: after five minutes of thinking, ask yourself, “Am I closer to a decision or an action?” If not, you are probably ruminating.

ul: **What-if spirals:** one worry leads to another, each more frightening.
**Reassurance seeking:** asking others repeatedly whether something is OK. Relief is brief, and the worry returns.
**Online searching:** looking up symptoms or worries often leads to frightening, rare outcomes.
**Mind reading:** assuming what others think of you or your parenting.
**Catastrophising:** jumping to the worst possible outcome.

blocks.p: At night, you are tired, the house is quiet, and there’s nothing to distract you. Problems feel bigger and harder to solve. A useful rule is not to make decisions or draw conclusions in the middle of the night. Write the thought down and look at it again in the morning.

ol: **Write it down.** Getting thoughts out of your head onto paper or a phone note reduces their hold.
**Sort worries into three groups:** things you can act on now, things to ask a professional, and things outside your control.
**Postpone worry.** Set a daily 15-minute “worry time”. When a worry arises at other times, note it and save it for later.
**Ask the “most likely” question.** For each worry, consider the worst outcome, the best outcome, and the most likely outcome.
**Label thoughts.** Say to yourself, “I’m having the thought that...” This creates distance from the thought.
**Limit searching.** Choose one or two trusted sources, such as your doctor or a reputable health website.
**Shift attention.** Engage your senses or body with a walk, a shower, a call to a friend, or a simple task.
**Make decisions “good enough”.** Many parenting decisions have several reasonable answers. Choose one and adjust as you go.

soon: Overthinking is taking up hours each day
You feel unable to make decisions
Anxiety, low mood or sleep problems persist for two weeks or more
You have repeated unwanted, distressing thoughts that you can’t shake (see the guide on postpartum anxiety)
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Overthinking is often a sign of how much you care. But caring doesn’t require constant worrying. Learning to step out of the loop frees up energy for rest, connection and enjoying your baby.

takeaway: Overthinking feels like problem-solving but often just increases anxiety. Notice when you’re ruminating, write worries down, sort them, postpone them, and limit searching and reassurance seeking. Make decisions good enough rather than perfect.
prompt: What question has your mind been circling, and which of the three groups (act now, ask a professional, outside your control) does it belong to?

title: Mood Swings and Emotional Sensitivity
description: Mood swings in pregnancy and after birth can feel sudden and confusing: laughing one moment, crying the next, snapping at someone you love. This guide explains the biological and practical drivers, the times when mood swings are most likely, how to steady yourself, and the signs that mood changes may be part of a larger problem.
glance: Hormones, sleep loss, hunger and stress all affect mood regulation.
Mood swings are common in the first trimester, late pregnancy, and in the first week after birth.
Irritability is as common as tearfulness, and often gets less attention.
Very high moods, racing thoughts and little need for sleep after birth can signal a serious condition that needs urgent help.

ul: **Hormones:** rapid rises in oestrogen and progesterone in pregnancy, and a sharp fall after birth, affect brain chemicals that regulate mood.
**Sleep loss:** tiredness reduces the brain’s ability to manage emotions.
**Hunger:** low blood sugar can cause irritability, anxiety and tearfulness.
**Physical discomfort:** nausea, pain or heartburn wear down patience.
**Stress:** big changes, family tensions and uncertainty increase emotional reactivity.
**First trimester:** hormones rise quickly, combined with nausea and tiredness.
**Third trimester:** discomfort, poor sleep and anxiety about birth.
**Days 3 to 5 after birth:** hormones drop sharply, milk comes in, sleep is broken, and baby blues often begin.
**Before your first periods return:** some women notice mood changes as their cycle restarts.

blocks.h: What mood swings can feel like

ul: Crying easily, sometimes without knowing why
Irritability or anger, often directed at those closest to you
Feeling overwhelmed by small things
Rapid shifts between happiness and sadness
Sensitivity to criticism or comments

ol: **Eat regularly.** Keep snacks with protein nearby, such as nuts, yoghurt, eggs or chana.
**Rest when possible.** Even short rests can help.
**Notice patterns.** Track when mood swings occur. Are they linked to hunger, tiredness, certain people or times of day?
**Pause before reacting.** Take a breath, step away, or say “I need a minute.”
**Name the feeling.** Labelling emotions (“I’m feeling overwhelmed”) can reduce their intensity.
**Explain to your husband** that mood swings are partly hormonal, and agree on how he can support you, for example by giving you space or bringing food.
**Move your body.** A short walk or stretching can reset mood.
**Reduce triggers where possible,** such as limiting time with people who criticise you when you are tired.

blocks.h: When mood changes may be something more

ul: **Depression:** persistent low mood, loss of interest, hopelessness lasting two weeks or more.
**Anxiety:** constant worry, panic attacks.

**Bipolar disorder:** periods of very high mood, energy, or irritability, racing thoughts, little need for sleep, and impulsive behaviour, alternating with depression. Women with bipolar disorder have a higher risk of severe mood episodes after birth and need a plan with their doctor.

**Postpartum psychosis:** a rare but serious condition, usually starting in the first weeks after birth, with confusion, high mood, paranoia, hallucinations or strange beliefs. This is a medical emergency.

soon: Low mood, irritability or anxiety most days for two weeks or more
Mood swings that cause frequent conflict or affect your ability to care for yourself or your baby
A personal or family history of bipolar disorder or postpartum psychosis
urgent: Very high mood, racing thoughts, feeling you don’t need sleep, or behaving unusually
Seeing or hearing things others don’t, or beliefs that seem strange to others
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby

blocks.p: Mood swings can leave you feeling guilty or ashamed, especially if you snap at people you love. Understanding the biological drivers can reduce self-blame. Apologising, repairing and explaining are part of any relationship.

takeaway: Mood swings in pregnancy and after birth are common and driven by hormones, sleep, hunger and stress. Eat regularly, rest, notice patterns and pause before reacting. Low mood or anxiety lasting two weeks needs a conversation with your doctor, and very high moods or confusion after birth need urgent help.
prompt: When do your mood swings tend to happen, and what is one thing that seems to help?

title: Emotional Overwhelm During Pregnancy
description: Emotional overwhelm is the feeling that there is simply too much: too many tasks, decisions, feelings and expectations at once. In pregnancy, it often builds from appointments, work, household duties, family expectations and physical exhaustion. This guide explains what overwhelm is, how it differs from anxiety and depression, and gives a step-by-step approach to reducing it.
glance: Overwhelm happens when demands exceed your current capacity. In pregnancy, capacity is lower because of tiredness and physical change.
It often shows up as freezing, irritability, tearfulness or shutting down.
The fastest relief usually comes from reducing demands, not trying harder.
Overwhelm that doesn’t lift, or comes with low mood or panic, may need professional support.

blocks.h: Why overwhelm is common in pregnancy

ul: **Lower capacity:** fatigue, nausea, poor sleep and physical discomfort reduce your energy and patience.
**More demands:** appointments, tests, work, household duties, preparing for the baby, and family events.
**Decisions:** hospital choice, doctor, birth preferences, what to buy, where to stay after birth.
**Emotional load:** worries about the baby, birth and the future.
**Expectations:** pressure to keep up with housework, hosting, or work as before.
Not knowing where to start
Freezing, procrastinating or scrolling
Snapping at people, or crying unexpectedly
Feeling numb, or shutting down
Physical tension, headaches, or difficulty sleeping

blocks.h: How it differs from anxiety and depression

ul: **Overwhelm** is usually linked to load and often eases when demands reduce.
**Anxiety** involves persistent worry or fear, even when tasks are under control.
**Depression** involves persistent low mood and loss of interest, even when life is calmer.

blocks.p: They can overlap, and prolonged overwhelm can lead to anxiety or depression.

ol: **Stop and breathe.** Take a few slow breaths with a longer out-breath to calm your body before trying to plan.
**Empty your head.** Write down everything on your mind: tasks, worries, decisions.
**Sort the list** into must do this week, can wait, someone else can do, and can drop.
**Choose one next step.** Not the whole project, just the next action, such as calling the hospital or asking your sister to help with shopping.
**Delegate specifically.** Ask clearly: “Could you cook dinner on Tuesdays and Thursdays?” or “Could you take me to my appointment on the 15th?”
**Drop or lower standards.** Decide what is “good enough” for housework, hosting and preparations.
**Protect rest.** Schedule rest as you would an appointment.
**Review weekly.** Check what is working and adjust.

blocks.p: Pregnancy is a valid reason to decline extra responsibilities, including hosting, attending every event or taking on new work. You can say, “I’d love to, but I need to rest right now,” or ask your husband to help explain.

soon: Overwhelm most days for two weeks or more
Low mood, loss of interest or hopelessness
Panic attacks
Difficulty eating, sleeping or functioning
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Many women feel guilty when they can’t manage everything, especially if they compare themselves to mothers or relatives who seemed to cope. But capacity in pregnancy is genuinely lower, and needing support is not failure.

takeaway: Overwhelm is a sign that demands exceed your current capacity. Empty your head, sort tasks, choose one next step, delegate specifically and drop what you can. If overwhelm persists or comes with low mood or panic, talk to your doctor.
prompt: If you could drop or hand over one responsibility for the rest of your pregnancy, what would it be?

title: Coping With Fear of Childbirth
description: Fear of childbirth ranges from ordinary nervousness to tokophobia, an intense fear that affects sleep, daily life and decisions about birth. This guide explains where the fear comes from, how fear affects labour, how to work through specific fears, and the support available, including discussing birth options with your doctor.
glance: Some fear of birth is common. Severe fear (tokophobia) affects a significant minority of women and is treatable.
Fear can be about pain, losing control, harm to the baby, medical procedures, being judged, or past trauma.
Information, planning and support can reduce fear considerably.
If fear is intense, talk to your doctor early about support and birth options.

blocks.h: Where fear of childbirth comes from

ul: **Unknowns:** not knowing what labour will feel like or how it will go.
**Stories:** frightening birth stories from relatives, friends or media.
**Pain:** fear of pain, and uncertainty about pain relief.
**Loss of control:** fear of not being able to cope, or of decisions being made without you.
**Past experience:** a previous difficult or traumatic birth (secondary tokophobia).
**Past trauma:** sexual abuse or medical trauma can make vaginal examinations and birth especially frightening.
**Anxiety:** a general tendency to anxiety.

blocks.p: Labour relies partly on oxytocin, the hormone that drives contractions. Fear triggers adrenaline, which can slow labour in its early stages and increase tension and pain perception. This is sometimes called the fear-tension-pain cycle. This doesn’t mean fear will cause problems, but it shows why feeling informed, supported and calm can help.

ul: **Fear of pain:** learn about pain relief options available at your hospital. In Pakistan, availability of epidurals and other options varies widely between hospitals, so ask in advance. Learn non-medical techniques such as breathing, movement, warmth and massage.
**Fear of losing control:** learn about the stages of labour (see the guide on preparing emotionally for labour), write birth preferences, and choose a birth companion who can speak for you.
**Fear of tearing:** ask your doctor about techniques that may reduce severe tearing, and what care is available if a tear happens.
**Fear of something happening to the baby:** learn how babies are monitored in labour, and ask your doctor about your specific risks.
**Fear of a caesarean:** learn what happens and why it might be recommended (see the guide on managing fear and expectations around delivery).
**Fear of being judged or treated badly:** ask your hospital about its policies on companions, privacy and consent.

ol: Write down your fears specifically. Vague fear is harder to address than specific fear.
Ask your doctor about each fear at an antenatal appointment.
Visit the hospital, if possible, to see the labour ward.
Learn breathing and relaxation techniques and practise them regularly (see the breathing guide).
Choose a calm, supportive birth companion.
Limit frightening birth stories. You can say, “I’d rather not hear that right now.”

blocks.p: Signs include intense fear that affects sleep or daily life, avoiding pregnancy because of fear, nightmares or panic about birth, or requesting a caesarean mainly to avoid labour. Tokophobia is recognised and treatable. Talking therapy can help, and your doctor can discuss birth options, including the benefits and risks of different approaches.

soon: Fear that affects sleep, eating or daily life
Panic attacks or nightmares about birth
A previous traumatic birth or past trauma that makes you dread birth
You want to discuss a caesarean because of fear
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: In some families, fear of birth is dismissed: “Every woman goes through it.” Fear is not weakness. It is a normal response to an intense, unpredictable experience, and it deserves to be addressed.

takeaway: Fear of childbirth is common, and severe fear is treatable. Name your specific fears, gather information, learn coping techniques, choose a supportive companion and talk to your doctor early if fear is intense.
prompt: What is the specific moment of birth that you fear most, and what information or support might change how you feel about it?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Managing Uncertainty and Loss of Control
description: Pregnancy and early motherhood are full of things you can’t control: the due date, how labour goes, the baby’s sleep, your body’s changes, and family decisions. This guide explains why uncertainty is so stressful, how to focus energy where you have influence, and how to make plans flexible enough to survive reality.
glance: Humans are wired to dislike uncertainty, so not knowing can feel worse than knowing bad news.
Pregnancy involves many uncontrollable elements, including the due date: only a small minority of babies arrive on it.
Focusing on what you can influence reduces helplessness.
Flexible plans (Plan A, Plan B, Plan C) reduce disappointment.

blocks.p: The brain tries to predict what will happen so it can prepare. When it can’t, it often fills the gap with worst-case scenarios. People who find uncertainty especially difficult may experience more anxiety and overthinking.

blocks.h: Things you can’t fully control in pregnancy and motherhood

ul: When labour starts
How labour progresses
Whether interventions are needed
Your baby’s temperament, sleep and feeding patterns
How your body changes and recovers
Some family decisions, especially in joint families

blocks.p: Draw two circles. In the inner circle, write what you can influence: your preparation, questions you ask, who supports you, how you respond, rest, and nutrition. In the outer circle, write what you can’t control: the due date, how labour unfolds, others’ opinions. Focus energy on the inner circle, and practise accepting the outer.

ol: **Make flexible plans.** For birth, write Plan A (your preferences), Plan B (if things change) and Plan C (if an emergency happens).
**Ask questions.** Information reduces uncertainty. Ask your doctor about likely scenarios.
**Tell people your due month,** not your due date, to reduce pressure.
**Practise acceptance statements:** “I’ve prepared what I can. The rest will unfold.”
**Focus on today.** Ask, “What do I need to do today?”
**Notice control-seeking behaviour,** such as over-researching, over-planning, or checking, which can increase anxiety.
**Lean on faith or meaning,** if that helps you. Many women find comfort in prayer, tawakkul (trust in God) or other spiritual practices.

blocks.p: In many Pakistani households, decisions about birth, feeding and childcare may involve elders. You may feel a loss of control. It helps to identify which decisions are most important to you, discuss them with your husband in advance, and agree on how to present them to the family. See the guide on managing family expectations.

soon: Uncertainty is causing constant worry, checking or reassurance seeking
You feel unable to make decisions
Anxiety affects sleep or daily life
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Losing control can bring frustration, fear and grief. Acceptance doesn’t mean giving up; it means directing energy where it matters.

takeaway: Pregnancy and motherhood involve real uncertainty. Focus on what you can influence, make flexible plans, ask questions and practise accepting what is outside your control. Seek help if uncertainty is causing constant anxiety.
prompt: What is one thing in your circle of influence that you could act on this week?

title: Feeling Lonely During Pregnancy
description: Loneliness in pregnancy and early motherhood is common, even in busy households. You may be surrounded by people but feel unseen, or far from your own family after marriage, or missing your husband if he works abroad. This guide explains why loneliness happens, its effects, and practical ways to build connection that fits your life.
glance: Loneliness is about feeling disconnected, not just being alone. You can feel lonely in a full house.
It often comes from life changes: moving after marriage, friends at different life stages, a husband working away, or being at home more.
Small, regular connections can reduce loneliness over time.
Persistent loneliness can lead to low mood and is worth addressing.

ul: **Moving after marriage:** many women live in a new city or household, far from parents, siblings and friends.
**Husband away:** working long hours or abroad, especially in the Gulf, can leave you managing alone.
**Friends at different stages:** friends who aren’t pregnant or don’t have children may not understand.
**Being at home more:** pregnancy and early motherhood can limit outings.
**Feeling unseen:** in a busy household, people may focus on the baby or on household duties, not on how you feel.
**Not feeling able to share:** worries about being judged as ungrateful or weak.

blocks.p: Loneliness can increase stress, worsen sleep and raise the risk of low mood and anxiety. It is a signal that you need connection, just as hunger signals the need for food.

ol: **Identify one or two people** who make you feel understood, and schedule regular contact, such as a weekly call with your sister or a friend.
**Use voice notes and video calls** with family and friends far away.
**Connect with other mothers** through antenatal classes, mother-and-baby groups, online communities, or neighbours with young children.
**Share honestly with one person.** Saying “I feel lonely” can open a door.
**Plan small outings,** such as a walk, a visit to a relative or a park.
**Create shared moments at home,** such as tea with your mother-in-law or a short walk with your husband.
**If your husband is away,** schedule regular calls and share small moments, such as photos and updates.

blocks.p: If loneliness comes with persistent low mood, loss of interest, hopelessness or withdrawal from people, it may be depression. Talk to your doctor.

soon: Loneliness most days for weeks
Low mood, hopelessness or loss of interest
Feeling unable to talk to anyone
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Loneliness can carry shame, especially in a culture that values family closeness. It’s not a failure; it’s a sign that your needs for connection have changed with your life. Reaching out is a strength.

takeaway: Loneliness is common in pregnancy and early motherhood, even in busy households. Identify a few people who understand you, schedule regular contact, connect with other mothers, and share honestly. If loneliness comes with persistent low mood, seek help.
prompt: Who is one person you could reach out to this week, and what would you like to share with them?

title: Building Emotional Resilience
description: Emotional resilience isn’t about being tough or never struggling. It’s your capacity to bend under pressure and recover, and it is built from resources and skills that can be strengthened. This guide explains what resilience is made of, why it naturally dips in pregnancy and early motherhood, how to spot when yours is running low, and specific, evidence-informed practices, from self-compassion to reframing, that help you recover more easily.
glance: Resilience is not a fixed trait. It rises and falls with sleep, support, health and stress.
Its building blocks include rest, connection, a sense of meaning, flexible thinking, self-compassion and practical problem-solving.
Research on self-compassion suggests it is linked with lower anxiety and depression and with coping better under stress.
Asking for help is part of resilience, not the opposite of it.

blocks.p: Psychologists describe resilience as the ability to adapt well in the face of stress and adversity. It isn’t the absence of distress: resilient people still feel sadness, fear and frustration. The difference is that they can recover, find support and keep functioning. Importantly, resilience depends partly on what’s around you, such as people, resources and safety, not only on what’s inside you.

ul: **Physical foundations:** sleep, food, movement and health. These are the base layer, and when they’re depleted, everything else is harder.
**Connection:** relationships where you feel understood and supported. This is one of the strongest protective factors.
**Meaning:** faith, values, or a sense that what you’re doing matters.
**Flexible thinking:** being able to see a situation from more than one angle, rather than locking into the worst interpretation.
**Self-compassion:** treating yourself with the kindness you’d offer a friend.
**Practical skills:** breaking problems into steps, asking for help, and managing emotions.

blocks.h: Why resilience dips in pregnancy and early motherhood

ul: Sleep loss and physical recovery deplete the base layer.
Hormonal shifts affect emotional regulation.
Old sources of support, such as work, friends or free time, may be less available.
Demands are constant and new.

blocks.p: A dip in resilience during this period is expected. It means your resources are stretched, not that you’re weak.

blocks.h: Signs your resilience is running low

ul: Small problems feel overwhelming
You snap or cry more easily than usual
You feel you can’t recover between difficult moments
You’re withdrawing from people
You’re relying more on unhelpful coping, like endless scrolling or skipping meals

blocks.p: **1. Protect the base layer**

ul: One protected block of sleep each day
Regular meals and water
A short walk or time in daylight

blocks.p: **2. Strengthen connection**

ul: A regular call or visit with someone who lifts you
Telling one person honestly how you are
Connecting with other mothers at the same stage

blocks.p: **3. Practise self-compassion**
When you’re struggling, try three steps:

ol: **Notice:** “This is really hard right now.”
**Remember you’re not alone:** “Many mothers feel this way.”
**Offer kindness:** “What do I need right now?” or a kind phrase, with a hand on your heart if it helps.

blocks.p: **4. Reframe gently**
Reframing doesn’t mean pretending things are fine. It means looking for other true angles:

ul: “I’m failing” → “I’m learning something difficult with very little sleep.”
“I should be coping better” → “This is a hard season, and I’m getting through it.”
Ask: “What would I say to my sister if she were in this situation?”

blocks.p: **5. Focus on what you can influence**
Sort worries into what you can act on and what you can’t. Take one small step on something in your control. See the guide on managing uncertainty.
**6. Notice small wins**
At the end of each day, note one thing that went well or that you handled. This trains attention toward evidence of coping, which stress tends to hide.
**7. Draw on meaning and faith**
For many Pakistani women, prayer, dhikr, tawakkul (trust in God) and community practices are sources of strength. Use what feels meaningful to you.
**8. Ask for help early**
Asking for help before you’re overwhelmed is a resilience skill. It stops a hard day from becoming a hard month.

ul: Expect setbacks. A bad day doesn’t erase progress.
Repair if needed: apologise, reconnect, rest.
Ask what you can learn: “What would make tomorrow a little easier?”

soon: Feeling unable to cope most days for two weeks or more
Persistent low mood, anxiety or hopelessness
Relying heavily on coping that’s making things worse
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: “Be strong” is a common message to women in Pakistan. But real strength includes rest, honesty and asking for help. Resilience isn’t about carrying everything alone; it’s about having what you need to carry it.

takeaway: Resilience is built from rest, connection, meaning, flexible thinking, self-compassion and practical skills. It naturally dips when you’re depleted. Protect your base layer, stay connected, speak to yourself kindly, reframe gently, notice small wins and ask for help early.
prompt: What has helped you recover from a hard time in the past, and how could a small version of it help you now?

title: Understanding Baby Blues
description: The baby blues are a short spell of tearfulness, mood swings, irritability and anxiety that a large proportion of new mothers experience in the first days after birth. This guide explains the hormonal and physical reasons they happen, the typical timeline, what they feel like from the inside, what genuinely helps in a Pakistani household full of visitors, and the clear differences between the blues, postpartum depression, postpartum anxiety and the rare emergency of postpartum psychosis.
glance: The baby blues are very common and are considered a normal reaction to the enormous changes of the first week, not an illness.
They usually begin around day two to five, often peak around day four or five, and ease on their own within about two weeks.
They’re linked to the sudden drop in pregnancy hormones after the placenta is delivered, plus exhaustion, pain, milk coming in and the emotional weight of new motherhood.
Low mood lasting beyond two weeks, or feelings that are severe, need a doctor. Confusion, very high mood or strange beliefs need emergency care.

ul: **A steep hormone fall:** during pregnancy, the placenta produces very high levels of oestrogen and progesterone. Within days of delivering the placenta, these levels drop sharply. Both hormones influence brain chemicals involved in mood, so the drop can make emotions swing.
**Milk coming in:** around days two to five, milk production increases. Breasts may be full and sore, and this often coincides with the emotional dip.
**Exhaustion:** labour may have lasted many hours, and newborns feed day and night from the start.
**Pain and recovery:** stitches, a caesarean wound, afterpains and bleeding.
**Emotional processing:** the birth itself, the shock of responsibility, and the gap between what you imagined and what’s happening.
**Social pressure:** a stream of visitors, advice and expectations at exactly the moment you’re most tired.
Crying suddenly, sometimes without being able to say why, sometimes at something small
Feeling happy and loving one moment, then flat or overwhelmed the next
Feeling irritable or snapping at people you love
Anxiety about the baby, feeding, or whether you’re doing things right
Feeling fragile, sensitive to comments, or easily hurt
Feeling unexpectedly lonely, even with people around
Trouble sleeping, even when someone else is watching the baby

blocks.p: Importantly, with the blues you usually still have moments of enjoyment, warmth or laughter, and the feelings come in waves rather than staying heavy all the time.

ul: **Days 1 to 2:** many mothers feel relief, excitement or numbness after birth.
**Days 2 to 5:** the blues often appear and may peak around day four or five, around the time milk comes in.
**Up to day 14:** feelings gradually settle as hormones stabilise and you recover.

ol: **Expect it.** Knowing the blues are common and temporary can take away some of the fear.
**Rest in real blocks.** Ask someone to take the baby between feeds so you can sleep for a few hours.
**Eat and drink regularly,** with water at every feed. Hunger and dehydration make mood swings worse.
**Limit visitors.** The first week is often when relatives arrive in large numbers. Ask your husband or mother to keep visits short and to send people away kindly if you’re resting.
**Let yourself cry.** Tears are a release, not a sign that something terrible is happening.
**Say how you feel** to one person who will listen without telling you to “be strong” or “be grateful”.
**Get daylight.** Sit by a window or in a courtyard for a few minutes each day.
**Get help with feeding** if pain or worry about milk is adding to your distress.

blocks.p: In some families, crying after birth is put down to nazar (the evil eye), weakness or ingratitude. The baby blues are a well-recognised biological and emotional response to birth. You can say, “The doctor told me this is very common in the first week and passes,” and ask for practical support instead.

ul: Take over cooking, cleaning and hosting.
Hold the baby so the mother can sleep.
Bring food and water without being asked.
Listen without criticism or comparison.
Keep track of whether she’s improving over the first two weeks.

blocks.h: Baby blues, depression, anxiety or psychosis?

ul: **Baby blues:** start in the first week, come in waves, include moments of enjoyment, ease within about two weeks.

**Postpartum depression:** lasts longer than two weeks, or is heavier: persistent low mood, emptiness, loss of interest, hopelessness, guilt, difficulty functioning. It can begin at any time in the first year. See the guide on postpartum depression.
**Postpartum anxiety:** constant worry, panic attacks, intrusive frightening thoughts, inability to rest. See the guide on postpartum anxiety.

**Postpartum psychosis:** rare but serious, usually starting within the first two weeks. Signs include confusion, very high or rapidly changing mood, not sleeping, racing thoughts, paranoia, hallucinations or strange beliefs. This is a medical emergency. Women with bipolar disorder, or a personal or family history of postpartum psychosis, have a higher risk and should plan with their doctor before birth.

soon: Low mood, tearfulness or anxiety that is still present after two weeks
Feelings that are heavy all the time, with few or no moments of enjoyment
Being unable to sleep even when someone else is caring for the baby
Feeling unable to cope with your baby or daily tasks
urgent: Confusion, very high mood, racing thoughts, not sleeping for days, or behaving out of character
Seeing or hearing things others don’t, or beliefs that seem strange or frightening to others
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby

blocks.p: Many mothers feel ashamed of crying when they “should” be happy, especially with family celebrating around them. The blues don’t mean you’re ungrateful or weak, and they don’t mean you love your baby less. They are one of the most common experiences of the first week after birth.
