takeaway: The baby blues are common, usually begin around days two to five and pass within about two weeks. They’re driven by a sharp hormone drop, exhaustion and the intensity of new motherhood. Rest, food, fewer visitors and someone to listen help. If low mood lasts beyond two weeks see a doctor, and treat confusion or strange beliefs as an emergency.
prompt: Who in your family could you ask to watch for how you’re feeling over the first two weeks, and what would you want them to do?

title: Postpartum Depression Awareness
description: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a common, treatable condition that can begin at any time in the first year after birth, sometimes starting during pregnancy. It is not a weakness or a lack of love for your baby. This guide explains symptoms, causes, how it differs from the baby blues, and the support and treatments available, including in Pakistan.
glance: PPD is more than feeling sad. It can include emptiness, exhaustion, irritability, guilt, anxiety and loss of interest.
It can start any time in the first year, not only in the first weeks.
Risk factors include previous depression, lack of support, stressful life events, a difficult birth and relationship problems.
Treatment works. Talking therapies, support and, where needed, medication can help.

ul: Persistent low mood, sadness or emptiness
Loss of interest or pleasure in things
Feeling hopeless, worthless or guilty
Exhaustion that doesn’t improve with rest
Difficulty sleeping, even when the baby is sleeping
Changes in appetite
Difficulty concentrating or making decisions
Irritability or anger
Feeling disconnected from your baby, or unable to bond
Withdrawing from people
Thoughts of self-harm or that others would be better off without you

blocks.p: The baby blues start within the first week and ease within two weeks. PPD lasts longer, is more severe, or starts later.
There is no single cause. Contributing factors include:

ul: A history of depression or anxiety, including during pregnancy
Lack of support from husband or family
Stressful life events, money worries or relationship problems
A difficult or traumatic birth
A baby who is unwell, premature or in the NICU
Feeding difficulties
Pressure about the baby’s sex, or conflict with in-laws
Sleep deprivation

blocks.p: Research in Pakistan has found that perinatal depression is common. The WHO-endorsed Thinking Healthy programme, developed and tested in Pakistan and delivered by Lady Health Workers, shows that structured psychological support helps mothers recover.

ul: **Talking therapies:** CBT and other therapies help change patterns of negative thinking and behaviour.
**Support groups:** connecting with other mothers who have experienced PPD.
**Medication:** a doctor may recommend medication, and many treatments can be used while breastfeeding. Discuss options with your doctor.
**Practical support:** help with sleep, household tasks and childcare.

ol: Tell someone how you feel: your husband, mother, a friend or your doctor.
Make an appointment with your doctor or gynaecologist and describe your symptoms.
Accept help with practical tasks.
Rest when you can.
Eat regularly.
Get some daylight and gentle movement.

ul: Listen without judgement.
Take over practical tasks.
Help her sleep.
Encourage her to see a doctor, and go with her.
Avoid blaming her or attributing her symptoms to weakness or nazar.

myth: “PPD means you don’t love your baby.”
PPD is an illness that affects mood and can make bonding harder, but it doesn’t reflect your love.
“It will go away on its own.”
Some mild cases improve, but many need treatment, and early help leads to faster recovery.

soon: Low mood, loss of interest or hopelessness lasting two weeks or more
Difficulty caring for yourself or your baby
Feeling disconnected from your baby
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
Feeling that your family would be better off without you
Seeing or hearing things others don’t, or confusion

blocks.p: Many mothers hide PPD because they fear being judged, or that their baby might be taken away. Seeking help is about getting support. Healthcare professionals aim to help you recover and care for your baby.

takeaway: PPD is common, can start any time in the first year, and is treatable. If you have persistent low mood, loss of interest, hopelessness or difficulty coping, tell someone and see your doctor. Treat thoughts of harming yourself or your baby as an emergency.
prompt: What would you want your family to understand about how you feel right now?

title: Postpartum Anxiety Awareness
description: Postpartum anxiety can feel like constant worry, a racing heart, checking the baby repeatedly, being unable to sleep even when the baby sleeps, or frightening unwanted thoughts. It is common and treatable. This guide explains its forms, including postpartum OCD and birth trauma, and why intrusive thoughts don’t mean you will act on them.
glance: Postpartum anxiety is common, but it is often missed because it can look like ordinary new-parent worry.
It can include generalised worry, panic attacks, postpartum OCD and post-traumatic stress after birth.
Unwanted, intrusive thoughts of harm coming to the baby are very common in new parents and don’t mean you want to act on them.
Treatment, especially talking therapy, is effective.

ul: Constant worry, often about the baby’s health or safety
Racing thoughts
Difficulty sleeping, even when the baby is asleep
Feeling on edge, restless or irritable
Physical symptoms: racing heart, tight chest, nausea, dizziness
Checking the baby repeatedly, such as checking breathing
Avoiding certain activities, like bathing the baby, out of fear

blocks.p: Sudden waves of intense fear with physical symptoms: racing heart, breathlessness, chest tightness, trembling, sweating, dizziness, or a sense of doom. Panic attacks are frightening but not dangerous. Slow breathing and grounding can help. If you have chest pain or breathlessness, get checked to rule out physical causes.

Many new parents experience sudden, unwanted thoughts or images of harm coming to their baby, such as dropping the baby or the baby being hurt. These thoughts are distressing precisely because they go against what you want. They are very common and do not mean you will act on them.

Postpartum OCD occurs when intrusive thoughts are frequent and distressing, and lead to behaviours to reduce anxiety, such as repeated checking, avoiding being alone with the baby, or repeated cleaning. It is treatable with talking therapy, especially CBT.
A difficult or frightening birth can lead to post-traumatic stress, with flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance of reminders, feeling numb, and being on edge. Talk to your doctor; treatment helps.

ol: **Slow breathing:** breathe out for longer than you breathe in.
**Grounding:** name what you can see, hear and feel.
**Label thoughts:** “I’m having an intrusive thought; it doesn’t mean I want this.”
**Limit checking:** gradually reduce repeated checks.
**Share responsibility:** take turns watching the baby so you can rest.
**Talk to someone:** sharing intrusive thoughts with a professional can bring relief.

soon: Worry or anxiety most days for two weeks or more
Panic attacks
Intrusive thoughts that are frequent and distressing
Repeated checking, cleaning or avoidance
Flashbacks or nightmares about the birth
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself
Thoughts of harming your baby that you feel you might act on, or that don’t feel distressing
Confusion, hallucinations or strange beliefs

blocks.p: Many mothers keep intrusive thoughts secret, fearing they will be judged. Health professionals understand that these thoughts are common in anxiety and OCD, and are trained to help.

takeaway: Postpartum anxiety is common and treatable. It can include constant worry, panic, intrusive thoughts and trauma symptoms. Intrusive thoughts don’t mean you will act on them. Talk to your doctor if anxiety affects your daily life.
prompt: What would help you feel safe enough to share your worries with someone?

title: Emotional Exhaustion and Burnout
description: Emotional exhaustion and burnout go beyond tiredness. They come from months of constant demands, an invisible mental load and almost no recovery time. This guide explains the recognised signs of parental burnout, why it builds up, how it differs from depression, and practical ways to reduce the load and restore your energy rather than simply pushing harder.
glance: Researchers describe parental burnout as four things together: exhaustion, emotional distance from your child, loss of fulfilment, and a painful contrast with the parent you used to be.
The “mental load” of planning, remembering and anticipating is often invisible, and often falls almost entirely on mothers.
Burnout is caused by demands persistently outweighing resources. Recovery comes from rebalancing that, not from more willpower.
Burnout and depression overlap. If symptoms persist for weeks or you feel hopeless, see a professional.

blocks.p: Burnout is not a single bad day or a hard week. It is the result of a long period in which what is asked of you exceeds the resources you have to meet it, whether those resources are sleep, help, money, time, health or emotional support. The body’s stress response, designed for short emergencies, stays switched on, and over time energy, patience and pleasure drain away.
Parental burnout has been studied in many countries, and researchers describe four features that tend to appear together:

ul: **Exhaustion:** feeling physically and emotionally drained by parenting, often waking already tired.
**Emotional distance:** going through the motions of care, feeding, changing and settling, while feeling detached or on autopilot.
**Loss of fulfilment:** no longer finding meaning or enjoyment in time with your child.
**Contrast:** feeling you are no longer the mother you were or wanted to be, which brings guilt and shame.

blocks.h: Why it builds up in early motherhood

ul: **Round-the-clock demand:** a young baby’s needs don’t stop at night or on weekends.
**Little recovery time:** breaks, sleep and time alone are scarce.
**Physical depletion:** recovering from birth, breastfeeding and broken sleep.

**The mental load:** remembering vaccine dates, tracking feeds and nappies, noticing when supplies run out, knowing which relative is visiting, anticipating what the baby needs next. This cognitive work is constant and usually invisible to others.
**Multiple roles:** in many Pakistani households, mothers also manage cooking, cleaning, hosting and caring for elders, often while being expected to keep up appearances.
**Perfectionism and comparison:** trying to meet every expectation, from family and from social media.
**Low recognition:** care work is often unseen and unthanked.
**Ordinary tiredness** improves with a good night’s sleep or a day off.
**Burnout** is closely tied to the role of parenting and the load it carries. It often improves when demands fall and support rises, but it doesn’t lift after one rest.
**Depression** affects every area of life, not only parenting, and includes persistent low mood, hopelessness and loss of interest even when demands are lighter.

blocks.p: They often overlap, and prolonged burnout can lead to depression, so persistent symptoms deserve a professional conversation.

ol: For three days, write down every task and every thing you keep track of, including the invisible ones: “noticed we’re low on nappies”, “remembered the BCG follow-up”, “planned what to cook for guests”.
Show the list to your husband. Many partners genuinely don’t realise how much is being carried.

Agree on whole areas of responsibility to hand over, not single tasks. “Please help with the baby” is vague. “You own nappies and wipes: noticing when they’re low and buying them” is a transfer of responsibility.
Agree that the person who owns an area does it their way, without being supervised. Otherwise the mental load stays with you.

ul: **Lower standards on purpose:** decide what “good enough” looks like for cooking, cleaning and hosting for the next few months.
**Cut optional obligations:** not every gathering needs attending, and not every guest needs a full meal.
**Simplify meals:** repeat a small set of easy meals, cook in batches, or accept help with cooking.
**Use systems:** a shared list on your phone, a weekly plan for the baby’s appointments, or a basket of supplies in each room where you feed.
**Protected rest:** a regular block of sleep each night or a daily nap while someone else watches the baby.
**Time off duty:** even 30 minutes a day when you are fully off, not “listening out” for the baby.
**Restorative activities:** what refills you is personal. It could be a walk, prayer, a call with a friend, reading or time in a garden.
**Connection:** talking honestly with someone who doesn’t judge.
**Recognition:** ask for it. Saying “I need you to notice how much I’m doing” is reasonable.

soon: Exhaustion and emotional distance most days for several weeks
Feeling hopeless, worthless, or that nothing will improve
You are snapping or shouting far more than you want to and can’t stop
Physical symptoms such as frequent headaches, illness or disturbed sleep that don’t settle
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming your baby
Feeling that you can’t keep your baby safe

blocks.p: Burnout often comes with shame, because it can feel like a failure to love your baby enough. It isn’t. Burnout happens to parents who care deeply and have been running on empty for too long. The answer is not to try harder; it is to carry less and to be supported more.

takeaway: Burnout is what happens when demands outweigh resources for too long. Make the mental load visible, hand over whole areas of responsibility, lower standards on purpose, and protect real rest and time off duty. If exhaustion and detachment persist, or hope disappears, speak to a professional.
prompt: If you wrote down everything you keep track of in a day, which item would you most like someone else to own completely?

title: Feeling Disconnected or Unlike Yourself
description: Many mothers say they feel “not like myself”: foggy, flat, distant from their own life, or unrecognisable in the mirror and in their own reactions. This guide explains the real causes, from sleep loss and pregnancy-related brain changes to identity shifts, depression and trauma. It also explains how to tell normal adjustment from symptoms that need help, and practical ways to reconnect with yourself.
glance: Feeling unlike yourself is very common in pregnancy and the first year, and is often driven by sleep loss, hormones and the scale of change in your life.
Brain imaging studies have found that pregnancy is associated with changes in brain structure, thought to support caregiving.
Persistent numbness, emptiness, or feeling as if you are watching yourself from outside can be symptoms of depression, anxiety or trauma, and are treatable.
Reconnecting usually happens through small, regular contact with the things that make you you, not a single big change.

blocks.h: What “not feeling like myself” can mean

blocks.p: Mothers describe this in different ways:

ul: **Foggy:** forgetting words, losing things, struggling to concentrate or follow conversations.
**Flat:** less able to feel excitement or pleasure, even about good things.
**Distant:** as if life is happening behind glass, or you are going through the motions.
**Unrecognisable:** reacting with irritation or tears in ways that surprise you, or not recognising your body or priorities.
**Lost:** unsure who you are now beyond being a mother.
**Sleep loss:** broken sleep impairs memory, concentration and emotional regulation. Many “not myself” feelings improve noticeably with even a few nights of better sleep.

**Hormonal shifts:** the large changes in pregnancy and after birth affect mood and thinking. Thyroid problems after birth can also cause fatigue, low mood and brain fog, and are diagnosed with a blood test.

**Brain adaptation:** research has found that pregnancy is associated with structural changes in areas of the brain linked to social understanding, thought to help mothers read and respond to their baby. Your attention is being redirected, which can make other things feel less vivid.
**Identity change:** your roles, routines, relationships and priorities have shifted. This transition, sometimes called matrescence, takes time to settle.
**Loss of the familiar:** less time for friends, work, study, hobbies, and the small habits that made you feel like you.
**Depression and anxiety:** numbness, emptiness and loss of pleasure are key symptoms.
**Trauma:** after a frightening birth, some women feel detached, numb or unreal as a way the mind protects itself.
**Usually adjustment:** fogginess and tiredness that come and go, moments when you feel like yourself, improvement on better-rested days, and feelings that gradually ease over weeks.

**Worth checking:** feeling numb or empty most of the time, no pleasure in anything for two weeks or more, feeling persistently unreal or detached (depersonalisation), flashbacks or nightmares about the birth, or no improvement even when you get rest.

ol: **Rest first.** Before drawing conclusions about who you have become, try to get a few better nights of sleep, with help.
**Keep one thread of your old life.** A favourite type of music, a short daily read, a recipe you love, a call with an old friend. Small and regular matters more than big and rare.
**Use your body.** A walk outside, stretching, or a shower can bring you back into the present.
**Talk to someone who knew you before.** Friends and siblings who know your history can reflect your continuity back to you.
**Write it down.** Try: “Before the baby I was... Now I am... What I want to keep is...”
**Look after the basics.** Food, water, daylight and medical checks such as haemoglobin and thyroid if you feel very tired.
**Give it time.** Many women describe gradually feeling like a new version of themselves over the first year, someone who includes their old self rather than replacing it.

soon: Numbness, emptiness or loss of pleasure for two weeks or more
Feeling detached from yourself or your surroundings most of the time
Flashbacks, nightmares or strong avoidance related to the birth
Extreme tiredness with feeling cold, constipation, weight changes or hair loss (ask about thyroid tests)
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself
Seeing or hearing things others don’t, confusion, or beliefs others find strange

blocks.p: Feeling like a stranger to yourself can be frightening, and it can bring guilt, as if you should be happier. It is often a sign of a very large transition, not of something broken. If it lasts or deepens, it may be a treatable symptom, and asking for help is a way of getting yourself back.

takeaway: Feeling unlike yourself is common and has real causes: sleep loss, hormones, brain adaptation, identity change, and sometimes depression or trauma. Rest, keep small threads of your old life, and connect with people who know you. Persistent numbness or detachment deserves a professional conversation.
prompt: What is one small thing that made you feel like yourself before you became pregnant, and how could you bring a version of it into this week?

title: Asking for Emotional Support
description: Asking for emotional support, being listened to and understood rather than given advice, can feel harder than asking for practical help. Many women worry about being a burden, seeming ungrateful or being talked about. This guide explains why reaching out is hard, how to choose who to ask, what to say, and what to do if the first person you ask doesn’t respond well.
glance: Emotional support means being heard, understood and comforted. It is different from advice or solutions.
Common barriers include fear of being a burden, being judged as ungrateful or weak, and worry about privacy in the family.
Telling people what kind of support you need makes it far easier for them to help.
If no one around you can listen well, a professional, a helpline or a mothers’ group can.

ul: **Fear of burdening others,** especially if everyone around you seems busy.
**Fear of seeming ungrateful,** particularly after a longed-for pregnancy, or when others have struggled to conceive.
**“Log kya kahenge”:** worry about what people will say, or that your feelings will be repeated to others in the family.
**Being dismissed before:** if past attempts were met with “Everyone goes through this” or “Be strong”, it’s harder to try again.
**Not knowing what you need:** sometimes you only know that you feel bad.
**Cultural messages** that a good woman or mother copes quietly.

blocks.p: Feeling understood has real effects on the body and mind. It reduces stress, eases loneliness, and protects against depression and anxiety. Women who feel emotionally supported in pregnancy and after birth tend to cope better with the challenges of early motherhood.
Think about the people in your life and notice:

ul: Who listens without rushing to advise, criticise or compare?
Who keeps things private?
Who has been kind when you struggled before?
Who makes you feel calmer after talking to them?

blocks.p: That might be your husband, your mother, a sister, a cousin, a friend from school or university, a neighbour, or another mother you’ve met. It doesn’t have to be the person who is closest in the family hierarchy.
Being clear about what you need helps the other person respond well:

ul: “I don’t need advice right now. I just need you to listen.”
“Can I tell you something without you worrying or telling anyone else?”
“I’ve been feeling low and I wanted someone to know.”
“I’m not okay today. Can you sit with me for a bit?”
“When I tell you how I feel, it helps if you say you understand, even if you don’t have a solution.”

blocks.p: Choose a calm moment rather than the middle of a stressful one. Start with how you feel (“I’ve been feeling overwhelmed and lonely”), then what would help (“It would help if we could talk for 15 minutes after the baby sleeps, without phones”). Many husbands want to help but don’t know how; specific requests make it possible.

blocks.h: If the response isn’t what you hoped

blocks.p: Sometimes people respond with advice, minimising (“It’s nothing”) or their own stories. It can help to redirect gently: “I know you mean well. Right now I just need you to listen.” If someone is consistently unsupportive, it’s okay to turn to someone else. One poor response doesn’t mean no one will understand.

blocks.h: If you have no one to ask

ul: Your gynaecologist, GP or Lady Health Visitor can listen and connect you with support.
A counsellor or psychologist offers a private, confidential space.
Online mothers’ groups and communities can be supportive, though choose moderated, respectful ones.

soon: You feel you have no one to talk to
Low mood, anxiety or loneliness persist for two weeks or more
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Reaching out can feel exposing, especially if you’ve always been the strong one. But most people are glad to be trusted. Asking for support teaches the people around you how to care for you, and it models something important for your child: that feelings can be shared.

takeaway: Emotional support is about being heard, not fixed. Choose someone who listens and keeps things private, tell them exactly what you need, and redirect gently if they jump to advice. If no one around you can provide this, a professional or mothers’ group can.
prompt: Who is one person who has made you feel calmer after talking to them, and what would you like to tell them?

title: When to Seek Professional Mental Health Support
description: It can be hard to know when struggles in pregnancy or early motherhood have moved beyond what self-care and family support can manage. This guide sets out clear thresholds for seeking help, explains the different types of professionals and what each does, describes what happens at an appointment, and addresses common barriers in Pakistan, including stigma, cost, family resistance and fear.
glance: Seek professional help if symptoms last two weeks or more, are getting worse, or are affecting your ability to function.
Seek urgent help for thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, or for confusion, hallucinations or very unusual beliefs.
Your gynaecologist, GP or Lady Health Visitor can be a first step and can refer you.
Perinatal mental health conditions are common and treatable, and early help means faster recovery.

blocks.p: **Self-care and support may be enough when:**

ul: Feelings come and go and improve with rest, food, connection and time
You can still enjoy things some of the time
You’re managing daily life, even if it’s hard

blocks.p: **Book an appointment with a professional when:**

ul: Low mood, anxiety, irritability or numbness last most days for two weeks or more
You’ve lost interest or pleasure in most things
You can’t sleep even when given the chance
You have panic attacks
Intrusive thoughts are frequent and distressing, or you’re checking, cleaning or avoiding things to manage anxiety
You have flashbacks or nightmares about the birth
It’s hard to look after yourself or your baby
You have a history of mental health conditions and feel symptoms returning

blocks.p: **Get urgent help now when:**

ul: You have thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life
You have thoughts of harming your baby that frighten you, or that don’t feel distressing
You or others notice confusion, very high mood, racing thoughts, little need for sleep, seeing or hearing things others don’t, or strong unusual beliefs (possible postpartum psychosis)
**Gynaecologist or GP:** can listen, screen for depression and anxiety, check for physical causes such as anaemia or thyroid problems, and refer you onward.

**Lady Health Visitors and Lady Health Workers:** in many communities they offer home visits, support and referrals. Some have been trained in psychological support programmes such as Thinking Healthy.
**Clinical psychologists and counsellors:** provide talking therapies such as CBT, which teaches practical skills for managing thoughts, feelings and behaviour.

**Psychiatrists:** medical doctors who diagnose and treat mental health conditions, including with medication when appropriate. They can advise on options that are compatible with pregnancy or breastfeeding.
**Online therapy:** many Pakistani psychologists offer sessions by video or phone, which can be more private and easier to arrange around a baby.
**Hospital psychiatry or psychology departments:** many teaching and public hospitals offer services at lower cost.
You’ll be asked about mood, sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, worries, and thoughts of self-harm. Being honest helps them help you.
You may complete a short questionnaire, such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, which is widely used to screen for depression around pregnancy and birth.
They’ll ask about support at home, the birth, feeding and your history.
Together you’ll discuss options, which might include talking therapy, practical support, follow-up, or medication.

blocks.p: It can help to write down your symptoms and how long they’ve lasted before you go, and to bring someone you trust.

blocks.h: Common barriers and how to approach them

ul: **“It’s just tension” or “It’s nazar”:** mental health conditions involve real changes in the brain and body. They respond to treatment just as physical conditions do.
**Fear of being judged:** professionals see perinatal depression and anxiety often and are trained to respond without judgement.
**Fear your baby will be taken away:** asking for help is about getting support. Health professionals aim to help mothers recover while caring for their babies.
**Family resistance:** ask your doctor to explain to your husband or family, or bring a supportive relative with you.
**Cost and access:** ask about hospital services, community programmes, or sliding-scale fees with private psychologists.
**Privacy at home:** online sessions can be done during a walk, at a relative’s house, or when the household is quieter.

soon: Symptoms that have lasted two weeks or more
Symptoms getting worse, or affecting your ability to care for yourself or your baby
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
Confusion, hallucinations, very high mood or strange beliefs
Feeling unable to keep yourself or your baby safe

blocks.p: Deciding to seek help can feel like admitting defeat. It is the opposite: it is taking your wellbeing seriously so you can be present for yourself and your baby. Many women say they wish they had asked sooner.

takeaway: If symptoms last two weeks or more, worsen or affect daily life, book an appointment with your gynaecologist, GP or a mental health professional. Treat thoughts of harm, confusion or hallucinations as an emergency. Perinatal mental health conditions are common and treatable.
prompt: What is one concrete step, such as writing down your symptoms or booking an appointment, that you could take in the next few days?

title: Preparing Emotionally for Labour
description: Feeling emotionally prepared for labour starts with understanding what labour actually involves. This guide explains each stage, what contractions feel like and why, how hormones shape labour, when to go to hospital, and coping techniques you can practise now, along with how to prepare your mind for an experience you can’t fully predict.
glance: Labour usually has a long early (latent) phase, an active phase, a pushing stage, and delivery of the placenta.
Oxytocin drives contractions, and endorphins help with pain. Fear and adrenaline can slow early labour.
Movement, upright positions, breathing, warmth, massage and a calm companion help many women cope.
Ask your hospital in advance about birth companions and pain relief, since policies vary widely.

blocks.p: **Early (latent) labour:** the cervix softens, thins and begins to open to about 4 cm. Contractions may be irregular, mild to moderate, and feel like period pain or backache. This phase can last hours or even days, especially with a first baby. It’s usually best spent at home if your pregnancy is uncomplicated, resting, eating lightly, drinking, walking and keeping calm.

**Active labour:** the cervix opens from around 4 cm to 10 cm. Contractions become regular, stronger, longer and closer together, often every three to five minutes. You’ll need to focus fully during contractions. This is usually when you’re in hospital.

**Second stage (pushing):** once the cervix is fully open, you’ll feel an urge to push, often with pressure in your bottom. This can last minutes to a few hours. Upright positions can use gravity to help.
**Third stage (placenta):** after the baby is born, the uterus contracts to deliver the placenta. You may be offered an injection to help this stage and reduce bleeding.

blocks.h: What contractions feel like and why

blocks.p: Each contraction is the uterus muscle tightening, pulling the cervix open and pushing the baby down. They build, peak and fade, like a wave. Most women find there is a break between contractions; using that break to rest and breathe is a key coping skill.

ul: **Oxytocin** drives contractions and is released more easily when you feel safe, calm and private.
**Endorphins** are natural pain-relieving hormones that build as labour progresses.
**Adrenaline** is released when you feel frightened or disturbed. In early labour it can slow contractions. Near the end, a surge of adrenaline can give energy for pushing.

blocks.p: This is why a calm environment, a trusted companion, dim light and privacy can genuinely help.
Follow your hospital’s advice. Common guidance:

ul: Regular contractions about every five minutes, lasting about a minute, for at least an hour (first babies)
Your waters break
Any bleeding
Reduced baby movements
Constant severe pain
You feel you need to push
You’re worried, or you have a high-risk pregnancy and were told to come earlier

ol: **Breathing:** slow breaths in through your nose and longer breaths out through your mouth during contractions. Practise daily.
**Movement and positions:** walking, swaying, leaning on a bed or wall, kneeling, using a birth ball, sitting backwards on a chair.
**Warmth:** a warm shower or a warm compress on your lower back.
**Massage and counter-pressure:** firm pressure on your lower back or hips during contractions.
**Focus:** a word, prayer, dhikr or counting to keep your mind steady.
**Rest between contractions:** relax your shoulders, jaw and hands.

blocks.p: The WHO recommends that women have a companion of their choice during labour. In Pakistan, many hospitals limit who can be present in labour rooms, so ask in advance whether a female relative, your mother, or your husband can stay. Brief your companion on your preferences and how to help you.

ul: **Expect intensity.** Labour is hard work. Expecting that helps.
**Expect the unexpected.** Labour rarely follows a script. Flexibility reduces disappointment.
**Focus on one contraction at a time.**
**Know your options** for pain relief and interventions.
**Plan for after:** many women feel a mix of relief, exhaustion, joy and shock.

soon: You feel very frightened about labour (see the guide on fear of childbirth)
You have questions about your pain relief options
urgent: Bleeding, green or brown fluid, reduced movements, or constant severe pain
Regular contractions before 37 weeks

blocks.p: Many women feel nervous and excited at once. Learning about labour can reduce fear and help you feel more in control.

takeaway: Labour unfolds in stages, driven by hormones that work best when you feel safe and calm. Learn the stages, practise breathing and movement, ask your hospital about companions and pain relief, and approach labour one contraction at a time.
prompt: Which coping technique would you like to practise this week?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Understanding Birth Preferences
description: Birth preferences, often called a birth plan, help you learn your options before labour and communicate what matters to you when you may be tired, in pain or not able to speak up. This guide walks through each decision worth considering, explains which practices are recommended by the WHO for healthy births, how to ask about interventions using the BRAIN questions, what to ask your hospital in advance, and how to write a one-page plan that stays flexible.
glance: A birth plan is a set of preferences, not a contract. Some things may need to change for safety, and that’s part of the plan.
WHO recommendations for healthy births include a companion of choice, freedom to move, delayed cord clamping, immediate skin-to-skin and breastfeeding within the first hour.
The WHO advises against routine episiotomy. It’s reasonable to ask your doctor about their approach.
Newborns need no prelacteal feeds such as ghutti, honey, sugar water or plain water. Colostrum is enough.

ul: **You learn your options** before you need to choose under pressure.
**You can discuss them with your doctor** during pregnancy, so you know what’s realistic at your hospital.
**Your companion knows what you want** and can speak for you.
**Feeling informed and involved** in decisions is linked to a more positive birth experience, even when things don’t go to plan.
**Companion:** who you want with you, and a backup if the hospital limits who can enter.
**Movement and positions:** walking, kneeling, leaning forward, using a birth ball, rather than lying on your back throughout.
**Pain relief:** epidural, injected pain relief, or non-medical methods such as breathing, warmth, massage and movement. Ask which are available at your hospital and at what hours.
**Eating and drinking:** light snacks and fluids in early labour if your pregnancy is low-risk and your doctor agrees.
**Monitoring:** whether intermittent monitoring is possible if you’re low risk, or continuous monitoring is needed.
**Privacy and environment:** dim lights, fewer interruptions, a dupatta or covering, female staff where possible.
**Vaginal examinations:** you can ask that they’re kept to what is needed, and that you’re told before each one.
**Pushing:** pushing with your body’s urges, and in positions that feel right, unless there’s a reason not to.
**Perineal care:** ask about techniques that may reduce severe tears, such as warm compresses and a slow, controlled birth of the head.
**Episiotomy:** the WHO advises against routine episiotomy. You can ask that it’s only done if there’s a clear need, and that you’re told first.
**Assisted delivery or caesarean:** what you’d want to know and who you’d want with you if one becomes necessary.
**Delayed cord clamping:** the WHO recommends waiting at least one minute before clamping the cord in healthy babies, which allows more blood to pass to the baby.
**Immediate skin-to-skin:** the baby placed on your bare chest, dried and covered, which helps regulate temperature, heart rate and blood sugar.
**Breastfeeding within the first hour:** recommended by the WHO.
**No prelacteal feeds:** no ghutti, honey, sugar water or water. Honey can cause infant botulism and shouldn’t be given before one year.
**Who holds the baby first,** and whether routine checks can wait until after the first feed.
**After a caesarean:** whether skin-to-skin in theatre or recovery is possible, and whether your companion can hold the baby skin-to-skin if you can’t.

blocks.p: When something is proposed, you or your companion can ask:

ul: **Benefits:** What are the benefits for me and the baby?
**Risks:** What are the risks?
**Alternatives:** Are there other options?
**Intuition:** What does my gut tell me?
**Nothing:** What happens if we wait or don’t do it now?

blocks.p: In a true emergency, there may be no time, and quick action is part of keeping you safe. In many situations there is time for a short conversation.

blocks.h: Questions to ask your hospital in advance

ol: Who can be with me during labour and birth?
Which pain relief options are available, and at all hours?
Can I move around and choose positions?
What is your approach to episiotomy?
How often do you recommend caesareans, and for what reasons?
Do you support delayed cord clamping, skin-to-skin and breastfeeding in the first hour?
Will my baby stay with me after birth?

blocks.p: In some private settings in Pakistan, caesarean rates are high. Asking these questions helps you understand a hospital’s approach before you choose it.

ul: Use short bullet points under headings: labour, birth, after birth, if things change.
Lead with your top three priorities.
Include medical information: blood group, allergies, conditions.
Add a short “if things change” section, such as “If I need a caesarean, I’d like my husband or mother with me and skin-to-skin as soon as possible.”
Discuss it with your doctor at an antenatal appointment, and bring copies to the hospital.

soon: You have a medical condition that may affect your birth options
Your hospital’s policies don’t match what matters most to you and you’d like to discuss alternatives
urgent: Bleeding, reduced baby movements, severe pain, or fluid leaking before labour

blocks.p: Preparing preferences can feel empowering. It can also stir up worry about what might go wrong. A flexible plan protects you from feeling you’ve failed if things change. What matters most is that you’re safe, respected and involved.

takeaway: Birth preferences help you learn options, talk with your doctor and guide your companion. Consider movement, pain relief, episiotomy, delayed cord clamping, skin-to-skin and breastfeeding in the first hour, ask your hospital key questions in advance, use BRAIN for decisions, and keep a section for when things change.
prompt: What are the three things that matter most to you about your birth, and has your doctor heard them yet?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Managing Fear and Expectations Around Delivery
description: Births don’t always go to plan, and fear of what might go wrong is common. This guide explains the interventions you may hear about, including induction, monitoring, assisted delivery, episiotomy and emergency caesarean, why they are recommended, what they involve, and how to keep realistic expectations while still feeling involved in decisions.
glance: Interventions are used when the benefits outweigh the risks for you or your baby.
Common interventions include induction, continuous monitoring, assisted delivery (vacuum or forceps), episiotomy and caesarean.
You have the right to ask questions and give consent, except in rare emergencies.
Feeling disappointed or upset after an unexpected birth is common and deserves support.

blocks.p: **What it is:** starting labour artificially, using methods such as medication to soften the cervix, breaking the waters, or a drip to stimulate contractions.
**Why:** going well past your due date, waters breaking without labour starting, high blood pressure, diabetes, or concerns about the baby’s growth.
**What to expect:** induction can take time, sometimes days, and contractions may feel more intense.
**What it is:** checking the baby’s heartbeat, either intermittently with a handheld device or continuously with a belt monitor.
**Why:** continuous monitoring is often recommended if there are risk factors, induction, or epidural.
**What it is:** using a vacuum cup or forceps to help the baby out during pushing.
**Why:** the baby is distressed, pushing is not progressing, or you are exhausted.
**What to expect:** you’ll usually have pain relief. There may be bruising or swelling on the baby’s head, which usually resolves.
**What it is:** a cut to the perineum to widen the vaginal opening.
**Why:** sometimes used in assisted deliveries or when the baby needs to be born quickly. The WHO advises against routine episiotomy.
**What to expect:** stitches, and recovery similar to a tear.
**What it is:** an operation to deliver the baby through a cut in the abdomen and uterus.
**Why:** planned for reasons such as placenta praevia, breech position, or previous caesarean, or done as an emergency for concerns like the baby’s heart rate or labour not progressing.
**What to expect:** usually spinal anaesthesia so you’re awake. Recovery takes longer than a vaginal birth (see the guide on caesarean recovery).
In some private settings in Pakistan, caesarean rates are high. It’s reasonable to ask your doctor why a caesarean is recommended and what the alternatives are.
You have the right to ask questions and understand what’s proposed, except in emergencies where action is needed immediately. Your companion can help ask questions.

ul: Prepare for different scenarios (Plan A, B, C).
Focus on what matters most: safety, respect, and involvement in decisions.
Remember that interventions are tools to keep you and your baby safe.

soon: You have questions about interventions your doctor has recommended
urgent: Bleeding, reduced movements, severe pain or fluid loss

blocks.p: Many women feel disappointed or traumatised after unexpected interventions. These feelings are valid and can be discussed with a doctor or counsellor. See the guide on expectations versus reality.

takeaway: Interventions are sometimes needed for safety. Learn what they involve, ask questions, and prepare for different scenarios. Feelings about an unexpected birth deserve support.
prompt: Which intervention would you like to understand better?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide

title: Building Your Birth Support System
description: The support around you shapes how labour feels, how well you recover and how you cope with a newborn. This guide helps you plan support in four layers: a birth companion, a practical team for hospital logistics, a postpartum team for the first 40 days and nights, and a professional team. It includes specific roles, the conversations to have now, and what to do if support is thin.
glance: Continuous support from a companion during labour is associated with better birth experiences, and the WHO recommends a companion of choice.
Practical logistics in Pakistan often include transport at night, blood donors, hospital deposits and someone to manage visitors.
The first six weeks need a named plan for nights, meals, housework and your rest, not just “family will help”.
Choose a paediatrician and know how to reach your gynaecologist or a Lady Health Visitor before the baby arrives.

blocks.p: A good birth companion stays with you, keeps you calm, helps you move and breathe, brings water, massages your back, and speaks up for your preferences when you can’t.

ul: **Who:** your husband, your mother, a sister, a cousin or a close friend. Choose the person who makes you feel calmest, not necessarily the most senior relative.
**Check the rules:** many hospitals in Pakistan allow only a female relative, or no one, in the labour room. Ask at an antenatal visit and plan around the answer.
**Brief them:** share your birth preferences, what helps you when you’re in pain or frightened, and which decisions matter most to you.
**Teach them:** counter-pressure on the lower back, slow breathing with you, reminding you to rest between contractions, and offering sips of water.
**Give them a script:** “She’d like to know the reasons and options before any intervention, unless it’s an emergency.”

ol: **Transport:** a main driver and two backups, with phone numbers saved. Agree who is reachable at night.
**Blood:** many hospitals ask families to arrange donors or replace blood used. Know your blood group, and list two or three relatives or friends with compatible groups who have agreed to be on call.
**Money and documents:** who will carry cash, a card, CNICs, your antenatal card and reports.
**Older children:** who will look after them during labour and the hospital stay.
**Messaging:** one person who shares news with the wider family, so your phone stays quiet.
**Hospital food:** who will bring meals for you and your companion.

blocks.h: Layer 3: the postpartum team (the first 40 days)

blocks.p: “Family will help” is not a plan. Write down specific names next to specific tasks:

ul: **Where you’ll stay:** at your mother’s house, your in-laws’, or your own home, and for how long.
**Nights:** who will help between midnight and 6 a.m. Even if you breastfeed, someone else can change nappies, burp, settle the baby, bring you water and take the baby for a stretch so you can sleep.
**Meals:** who cooks, and what you’ll eat (see the guide on postpartum nutrition).
**Housework and laundry:** who takes over, especially floor-level and heavy tasks.
**Visitors:** who decides when people visit, how long they stay, and who reminds them to wash their hands.
**Your rest:** who protects a daily block of sleep for you.
**Your emotional wellbeing:** who will check in on how you’re feeling, not just how the baby is.
**Gynaecologist or midwife:** for postnatal checks. The WHO recommends postnatal contacts in the first 24 hours, around day three, between days 7 and 14, and around six weeks.
**Paediatrician:** choose one before birth, and know their clinic hours and what to do out of hours.
**Breastfeeding support:** a lactation specialist, a trained nurse or midwife, or an experienced Lady Health Visitor.
**Lady Health Worker or Visitor:** in many areas they can provide home visits and referrals.
**Mental health:** know who you’d contact if you felt low or anxious after birth.

blocks.p: Keep these numbers in one note on your phone and on paper by the bed.

ul: Start conversations in the second trimester, not in the last week.
Be specific: “Could you stay with us for the first two weeks and help at night?” is easier to say yes to than “Will you help?”
Spread tasks among several people so no one person burns out.
Discuss differences in expectations early, for example around chilla customs or visitors.
Write the plan down and share it with your husband and helpers.

blocks.p: If your husband works abroad, you live far from family, or relationships are strained:

ul: Ask whether a relative could stay for even a week or two.
Consider paid help for housework, even part-time, if it’s affordable, so that family help can go to you and the baby.
Build a small circle of neighbours or friends who could bring a meal or sit with you.
Ask your doctor or Lady Health Visitor about community support and home visits.
Plan regular video calls with family and friends for emotional support.

soon: You have no one to help at home after birth
Family conflict is making planning for support difficult
You feel anxious or low about how you’ll cope
urgent: Emergency symptoms in pregnancy or after birth: bleeding, severe headache, breathing difficulty, or thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Planning support can bring up difficult feelings: that you shouldn’t need help, worry about owing people, or sadness about who isn’t there. Needing support after birth is not a weakness. It is how women have recovered across cultures and generations, and the chilla tradition itself reflects that understanding.

takeaway: Plan support in four layers: a briefed birth companion, a practical team for logistics and blood donors, a named postpartum team for nights, meals and visitors, and your professional contacts. Be specific, spread the load, write it down and start early.
prompt: Who could take responsibility for your nights in the first two weeks, and when could you ask them?
sources: NHS — Your pregnancy and baby guide
NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Preparing Your Home for a Newborn
description: Preparing your home for a newborn is less about buying things and more about creating a safe, practical space for sleeping, feeding, changing and recovering. This guide covers a realistic essentials list, safe sleep setup and why it matters, temperature and the danger of gas heaters, mosquito protection, hygiene, car and motorbike safety, a recovery corner for you, and the traditional practices that are worth avoiding.
glance: Safe sleep: baby on their back, on a firm, flat surface, with nothing else in the sleep space, in your room for the first six months.
Never leave a gas heater or charcoal angeethi burning in a closed room while anyone sleeps. Carbon monoxide has no smell and can kill.
Use a car seat for every car journey. Carrying a newborn on a motorbike is very risky.
Avoid surma or kajal on babies’ eyes, and avoid putting oil, ghee, ash or other substances on the umbilical cord.

ul: **A safe sleep space:** a cot, crib, Moses basket or a firm, flat surface with a fitted sheet
**Clothes for the season:** soft vests, front-opening tops, caps, socks, and a few light blankets
**Nappies:** disposable or cloth, plus soft cloths or cotton wool and clean water for cleaning
**Feeding supplies:** breast pads, a pillow for support; or bottles, teats, a way to sterilise and formula if you plan to use it
**A thermometer**
**A car seat** if you travel by car
**A baby carrier or pram** if useful for your lifestyle

blocks.p: Many families receive clothes and blankets as gifts. Buy the basics and wait to see what you actually need.
Following safe sleep guidance lowers the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) and suffocation.

ul: **On the back** for every sleep, including naps. Babies placed on their tummy or side are at higher risk.
**Firm, flat mattress** that fits the cot without gaps. Avoid soft mattresses, gaddas, pillows or cushions for the baby.
**Clear space:** no pillows, quilts, bumpers, soft toys or loose blankets. If you use a blanket, tuck it firmly no higher than the baby’s shoulders, with feet near the bottom of the cot.
**Room-share** for the first six months, with the baby in their own sleep space near your bed.
**Never sleep with your baby on a sofa, armchair or floor cushion.**

**Bed-sharing** is common in Pakistan and carries higher risks, especially if anyone in the bed smokes, has taken alcohol or medicine that causes drowsiness, if the baby was premature or small, or if you’re extremely tired. If you do bed-share, put the baby on their back on a firm surface, away from pillows and quilts, not between two adults, and never with older children or pets in the bed.
**No smoking** in the home or near the baby.
Babies can overheat and can get cold. Dress them in roughly one more layer than you’re comfortable in, and check the back of the neck or chest: it should feel warm, not hot and sweaty.
Keep the baby’s head uncovered while sleeping indoors.
**Summer:** use fans, keep rooms shaded, and keep the baby out of direct sun.

**Winter:** gas heaters and charcoal angeethis produce carbon monoxide. Never leave them burning in a closed room while anyone sleeps. Keep a window slightly open when they’re on, and turn them off before sleeping. Headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or drowsiness when a heater is on are warning signs: get everyone into fresh air and seek help.

blocks.p: Use mosquito nets over cots and beds, especially in areas and seasons where dengue or malaria occur. Ask your doctor before using any repellent on a young baby.

ul: Set up a handwashing point with soap near where visitors arrive or where the baby is.
Ask visitors to wash hands, avoid kissing the baby’s face, and stay away when unwell.
Wash baby clothes separately at first if possible, and dry them fully.
Use a properly fitted, rear-facing car seat for every car journey, even short ones. Holding a baby in your lap in a car is not safe in a crash.
Carrying a newborn on a motorbike is very risky. Use a car, rickshaw or other transport when possible.

blocks.p: Plan a space where you can feed, rest and recover: a comfortable bed or chair with back support, pillows, water, snacks, a phone charger, maternity pads and a bin. In a shared home, a curtain or screen can give privacy.

ul: **Surma or kajal on the eyes:** some products contain lead, and applying anything to a newborn’s eyes can cause infection.
**Substances on the umbilical cord:** follow your health provider’s advice. Avoid oil, ghee, ash, turmeric, surma or other substances.
**Tight swaddling with straight legs:** can affect hip development. Leave room for the hips and knees to bend.
**Ghutti, honey, water or sugar water** for young babies.
**Baby walkers** later on, which are linked to falls and injuries.

soon: Questions about safe sleep, bed-sharing or car seats
Uncertainty about whether your home is too hot or cold for the baby
urgent: Headache, dizziness, nausea or drowsiness in anyone when a heater is on: get to fresh air and seek help
Your baby has difficulty breathing, is unusually sleepy, floppy or hard to wake, or has a fever

blocks.p: Preparing the home can be exciting, and it can also become a source of pressure to buy everything. Safety and a calm space for you and your baby matter far more than having the latest products.

takeaway: Focus on safety and practicality: a clear, flat sleep space with the baby on their back in your room, safe heating with ventilation, mosquito nets, handwashing, a car seat, and a recovery corner for you. Avoid surma, cord substances, tight leg swaddling and prelacteal feeds.
prompt: Looking around your home, what is the one safety change you’d most like to make before the baby arrives?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Preparing Mentally for Life With a Baby
description: Mental preparation for life with a baby works best when it is grounded in what the first weeks are really like: how often a newborn feeds, how sleep actually works, how much time care takes, and what happens to your mind and relationships. This guide gives a realistic picture of a day and night with a newborn, explains why it’s so demanding, and suggests concrete ways to prepare your mindset.
glance: Newborns typically feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, and a feed can take 20 to 45 minutes or more early on.
Newborns sleep a lot in total, often 14 to 17 hours, but in short stretches across day and night.
The first six weeks are about feeding, recovering and learning. Little else gets done, and that is normal.
The most useful mental preparation is lowering expectations of yourself and agreeing on roles before birth.

blocks.h: What a 24 hours with a newborn often looks like

ul: **Feeding:** around every two to three hours, counted from the start of one feed to the start of the next. That means a feed can begin before you feel you’ve recovered from the last one. Some feeds will be closer together, especially in the evenings (cluster feeding).
**Nappies:** by around day five to six, a baby who is feeding well usually has at least six heavy wet nappies a day, plus several dirty ones. Each change takes a few minutes.
**Burping and settling:** after many feeds, your baby will need help to settle, which can take minutes or much longer.
**Sleep:** newborns sleep in short stretches, often one to three hours, and their sleep doesn’t follow day and night at first.
**Your own needs:** eating, drinking, using the toilet, showering and resting all have to fit into the gaps.

blocks.p: Put together, the work of caring for a newborn can fill most of the day and a good part of the night. It’s not that you’re doing something wrong; it’s simply the job.

ul: **No breaks:** caring for a newborn is continuous, unlike most work.
**Sleep loss:** broken sleep affects mood, memory and patience.
**Recovery:** you’re healing from birth at the same time.
**Learning curve:** everything is new, so even small tasks take thought.
**Responsibility:** knowing a tiny person depends on you can feel heavy.
**Emotional swings:** hormones shift dramatically in the first weeks.

blocks.h: What changes in your mind and life

ul: **Time:** you’ll measure days in feeds rather than hours.
**Attention:** your brain becomes tuned to the baby’s sounds and needs, which can make it harder to focus on other things.
**Relationships:** your marriage, your relationship with your mother and mother-in-law, and friendships shift as roles change.
**Identity:** you may feel both deeply connected to your baby and unsure who you are.
**Freedom:** going out, sleeping in, or doing things on impulse become much harder for a while.

ol: **Expect the first six weeks to be about survival.** Feeding, resting, recovering and getting to know your baby are the goals. Anything else is a bonus.
**Expect to feel unsure.** Confidence comes from repetition. Nobody knows their baby on day one.
**Expect mixed emotions.** Joy, love, boredom, frustration, tenderness, resentment and fear can all appear in the same day.
**Expect your body to need care.** Plan for rest, food and help.
**Expect things to improve.** Many parents find that around six to twelve weeks, feeding becomes easier, the baby becomes more responsive, and patterns begin to form.

blocks.h: Agree on roles before the birth

ul: Who does what at night?
Who handles cooking and housework?
How will your husband support you when he’s home, and when he’s at work?
How will you both get some rest?
How will you decide on visitors?
What will you each do if one of you is struggling?

blocks.p: Decide now what “good enough” looks like:

ul: Simple meals, repeated often
A tidy-enough house, not a spotless one
Fewer guests, shorter visits
Unanswered messages are fine
Asking for help is normal

soon: You feel very anxious, low or numb about becoming a mother
You have a history of depression or anxiety and want to plan support after birth
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Imagining life with a baby can bring a mix of excitement and dread. You might worry you’ll lose yourself, or that you won’t be good at it. These thoughts are common. Preparing realistically doesn’t make it less joyful; it often makes the joy easier to notice, because you’re not fighting reality.

takeaway: A newborn feeds 8 to 12 times a day and sleeps in short stretches, so the first six weeks are about feeding, recovery and learning. Prepare by understanding the realities, agreeing on roles with your husband, lowering standards on purpose and expecting things to ease over the first few months.
prompt: Looking at a typical newborn day, which part do you think will be hardest for you, and who could help with it?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Setting Realistic Expectations of Motherhood
description: Expectations of motherhood are shaped by family stories, dramas, social media and the mothers around you, and many of them set women up for guilt and disappointment. This guide takes the most common expectations one by one, explains what reality usually looks like and why, and helps you build expectations before birth that are both hopeful and realistic.
glance: Love for your baby may arrive instantly or grow over weeks and months. Both are normal.
Breastfeeding is natural, but it is also a skill that mother and baby learn together, often with help.
Newborns cannot follow a schedule, and frequent night waking is normal for months.
Recovery after birth takes months, and needing help is the norm, not a sign of failure.

blocks.p: When reality falls short of what we expected, we often blame ourselves rather than the expectation. Mothers who expected instant love, easy breastfeeding or a quick recovery are more likely to feel they’ve failed when these don’t happen. Realistic expectations don’t take away hope; they protect you from unnecessary guilt.

myth: “I’ll feel overwhelming love the moment I see my baby.”

Some mothers do. Many feel shock, exhaustion, relief or numbness first, especially after a long or difficult labour. Love often deepens over days, weeks and months as you care for your baby and get to know them.
“Breastfeeding comes naturally.”
The instinct is natural, but latching, positioning and building supply are learned skills. Soreness, worries about supply and the need for help in the first weeks are common.
“A good baby sleeps through the night.”

Newborns wake to feed because their stomachs are small and they grow quickly. Frequent night waking is biologically normal for months and says nothing about how “good” your baby is or how well you’re parenting.
“I’ll get back to normal in 40 days.”
The chilla period is a valuable time of rest, but full physical recovery, especially of the pelvic floor, abdominal muscles and energy levels, often takes many months.
“I’ll know what my baby needs.”
Reading cues is learned. In the first weeks, much of parenting is trying things and seeing what works.
“If I’m not happy, I’m ungrateful.”
Gratitude and difficulty can exist together. Feeling overwhelmed doesn’t cancel your love.
“My husband will naturally know how to help.”
Most partners need to be told what’s helpful. Clear, specific requests work better than hoping.
“Everything will go back to how it was, plus a baby.”
Your relationships, priorities and routines will change. Many of these changes are positive, but they take adjustment.

ol: **Talk to honest mothers.** Ask a sister, cousin or friend who had a baby recently what surprised them.
**Expect a learning curve** in feeding, settling and reading cues.
**Expect tiredness** that lasts months, not days.
**Expect mixed feelings** about the baby, your body and your new life.
**Expect to need help,** and plan for it.
**Expect to make mistakes,** and to recover from them. Babies need care and repair, not perfection.

blocks.p: Realistic expectations don’t mean expecting the worst. They mean expecting a wide range of experiences: joy and exhaustion, confidence and doubt. Many mothers find motherhood more meaningful than they expected, even when it’s harder than they imagined.

soon: You feel very anxious or low when you think about motherhood
You have strong fears that you won’t be a good mother
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: In Pakistani culture, motherhood is often idealised. Mothers are praised for sacrifice and endurance, which can make it hard to admit struggle. Building realistic expectations is a way of protecting yourself from guilt and allowing yourself to ask for help.

takeaway: Many common expectations of motherhood, from instant love to a baby who sleeps through the night, set mothers up for guilt. Expect a learning curve, months of tiredness, mixed feelings and the need for help, and hold that realism alongside hope.
prompt: Which expectation about motherhood do you think you’d judge yourself most harshly for not meeting?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Understanding Expectations Versus Reality
description: When birth, feeding, bonding or early motherhood turn out differently from what you hoped, the gap can bring disappointment, grief, guilt or anger, sometimes alongside gratitude. This guide explains why the gap hurts so much, how to process it step by step, how a birth debrief works, and how to tell normal disappointment from birth trauma or depression.
glance: Feeling disappointed about your birth or early motherhood is common, and doesn’t mean you’re ungrateful for your baby.
Grief for what you hoped for is a valid response, even when everyone is healthy.
Asking your doctor to go through what happened (a birth debrief) can answer questions and reduce self-blame.
Flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance or persistent distress may be signs of birth trauma, which is treatable.

ul: **Expectations carry hopes:** a planned vaginal birth, exclusive breastfeeding, or instant bonding may have meant something important to you.
**Loss of control:** unexpected interventions or decisions made quickly can leave you feeling powerless.
**Self-blame:** many women wonder if they did something wrong. Most birth outcomes are not caused by anything the mother did.
**Dismissal by others:** “At least the baby is healthy” is meant kindly, but it can make your feelings seem unimportant.
**Cultural comments:** remarks such as “You didn’t have a real birth” after a caesarean, or “Your milk isn’t enough”, can deepen the hurt.
An emergency caesarean when you hoped for a vaginal birth, or the reverse
A long, painful labour, or interventions you didn’t want
Not having your chosen companion with you
Separation from your baby, for example a NICU stay
Breastfeeding difficulties or needing to use formula
Not feeling an instant bond
Feeling low or anxious when you expected to be happy

blocks.h: Processing the gap step by step

ol: **Name what you hoped for.** Write it down or say it to someone.
**Name what happened.** Write the story of your birth or early weeks as you remember it.
**Name what you feel.** Disappointment, sadness, anger, guilt, relief, gratitude. Mixed feelings are normal.
**Separate facts from blame.** Ask, “What was in my control? What wasn’t?”
**Get answers.** Ask your doctor for a birth debrief.
**Talk to someone who listens.** Your husband, a friend, or a counsellor.
**Focus forward.** What can you influence now, for example feeding support, bonding time or rest?

blocks.p: A birth debrief is a conversation with your doctor or midwife, after birth, to go through your notes and what happened. You can ask:

ul: Why was a particular decision made?
Could anything have been done differently?
What does this mean for my recovery?
What does this mean for future pregnancies?

blocks.p: Many women find that understanding what happened reduces self-blame and helps them move forward.

ul: **Disappointment** usually eases over weeks, especially with support and understanding.

**Birth trauma** may involve flashbacks, nightmares, intense distress when reminded of the birth, avoiding anything related to it, feeling numb, irritability, or being constantly on edge. These may be signs of post-traumatic stress, which responds well to treatment.

soon: Distress about your birth that doesn’t ease over several weeks
Flashbacks, nightmares or avoiding reminders of the birth
Persistent low mood, guilt or anxiety
Fear of future pregnancies that affects your life or relationship
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: You can be deeply grateful for your baby and still grieve the experience you hoped for. Both feelings are true. Giving yourself permission to feel disappointment is part of healing, and it often makes room for more joy over time.

takeaway: The gap between what you hoped for and what happened is common and can be painful. Name what you hoped for, what happened and how you feel, separate facts from blame, ask for a birth debrief, and seek support if distress persists or includes trauma symptoms.
prompt: What part of your experience would you most like to understand better, and who could help you get those answers?

title: Building Confidence as a First-Time Mother
description: Confidence as a first-time mother doesn’t come from feeling ready. It comes from doing things repeatedly until they feel familiar. This guide teaches the core newborn care skills, including holding, reading feeding cues, burping, nappy changing, cord care, bathing, temperature, jaundice and settling, and gives a clear list of newborn danger signs that need urgent care.
glance: Confidence follows competence, and competence follows repetition. Expect the first two weeks to feel clumsy.
Crying is a late hunger cue. Watch for earlier cues like stirring, rooting and hand-sucking.
Keep the umbilical cord clean and dry and follow your health provider’s advice. Avoid putting oil, ghee, ash or surma on it.
Know the newborn danger signs. If you see one, seek care immediately.

ul: Support your baby’s head and neck, since newborns can’t hold their heads up.
Common holds: cradle (head in the crook of your elbow), upright against your shoulder, and the “football” hold under your arm.
Move slowly and talk to your baby; newborns startle easily.
Never shake a baby, even in play.
**Early cues:** stirring, opening mouth, turning head side to side, rooting (searching with the mouth), sucking on hands or lips.
**Mid cues:** stretching, more movement, fussing.
**Late cues:** crying, agitated movements.

blocks.p: Feeding at early cues is easier, because a crying baby can find it hard to latch. See the breastfeeding guide for more.

Hold your baby upright against your shoulder, or sit them on your lap supporting their chin, and gently pat or rub their back. Not every feed produces a burp; if nothing comes after a few minutes, it’s fine to stop.

ul: Clean girls from front to back to reduce infection risk.
Use water and soft cloth or cotton wool in the early weeks.
Let the skin dry before putting on a new nappy.
Nappy rash: change frequently, give some nappy-free time, and ask your doctor or pharmacist about barrier creams.
**First days:** dark, sticky meconium.
**Around days three to four:** greenish transitional stools.
**By day five:** yellow, seedy stools in breastfed babies.
**Wet nappies:** increasing daily, to at least six heavy wet nappies by around day five.
Keep the stump clean and dry, and fold the nappy below it.
It usually falls off within about one to two weeks.
Follow your health provider’s advice on cord care. Avoid applying oil, ghee, ash, surma, turmeric or other substances.
See a doctor if there is redness spreading onto the skin, swelling, pus, a bad smell or bleeding.
Sponge baths until the cord falls off and the area heals.
Use warm, not hot, water; test with your elbow.
Never leave your baby alone in water, even for a moment.
Daily bathing isn’t necessary.
Avoid putting oil or water in your baby’s nose, ears or eyes.
Newborns lose heat easily but can also overheat.
Dress your baby in one more layer than you’re wearing.
Feel the back of the neck or chest to check temperature.
A thermometer is useful to have at home.

blocks.p: Yellowing of the skin and eyes is common in the first week, caused by a build-up of bilirubin. Frequent feeding helps. Jaundice that appears in the first 24 hours, is spreading or deepening, or comes with a very sleepy baby who isn’t feeding well needs urgent assessment.

ul: Swaddling (with legs free to bend), rocking, shushing, and holding close often help.
See the guide on understanding your baby’s crying.

blocks.p: Seek care immediately if your baby:

ul: Is not feeding well or refuses feeds
Has a fever or feels unusually cold
Is breathing fast, struggling to breathe, or has the chest pulling in with each breath
Has yellow skin in the first 24 hours, or yellow palms and soles
Is very sleepy, floppy or difficult to wake
Has a seizure or abnormal movements
Has a bulging soft spot on the head
Has repeated vomiting, especially green vomit
Has redness spreading from the umbilical cord

soon: Concerns about feeding, weight gain or nappies
Persistent nappy rash
Questions about your baby’s development
urgent: Any newborn danger sign listed above

blocks.p: Almost every first-time mother feels unsure at first. Others may offer advice, and some may take over. It’s okay to say, “I’d like to try myself.” Each nappy, feed and bath builds your confidence.

takeaway: Confidence comes from repetition. Learn the basics of holding, feeding cues, burping, nappies, cord care and bathing, and know the newborn danger signs. Trust yourself to learn, and ask for help when you need it.
prompt: Which newborn care task makes you most nervous, and how could you practise it with support?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Understanding the Fourth Trimester
description: The “fourth trimester” is the first three months after birth, when your body recovers, your hormones reset, your baby adjusts to life outside the womb and your family reorganises around a new person. This guide explains what happens to both mother and baby in these weeks, how it connects with the chilla tradition, which postnatal checks to expect, and how to make these months as supported as possible.
glance: The fourth trimester is roughly the first 12 weeks after birth. It is a period of major physical, hormonal and emotional change for the mother, not just the baby.
Newborns are adjusting to a world very different from the womb, which is why they want to be held, fed often and kept close.
The WHO recommends postnatal contacts within 24 hours of birth, around day three, between days 7 and 14, and around six weeks.
The chilla tradition of rest and care has real value. Some associated customs are worth questioning.

blocks.h: Why it’s called the fourth trimester

blocks.p: The term recognises that birth is not the end of the pregnancy process. Your body takes months to recover. Your baby, born with an immature nervous system and digestion, still needs womb-like closeness, warmth and frequent feeding. Viewing these months as a continuation of pregnancy helps families treat them with the same care.

ul: **Weeks 0 to 2:** the uterus contracts rapidly, bleeding is heaviest, milk comes in, hormones drop sharply, and wounds begin healing. Emotions can be intense, and the baby blues are common.
**Weeks 2 to 6:** bleeding lightens and usually stops, the uterus returns close to its usual size, wounds heal, and feeding often becomes more settled. Tiredness is often at its peak.
**Weeks 6 to 12:** energy gradually improves, many women feel more confident with their baby, and you may begin gradually returning to activities. Hair shedding may begin around this time.
**Newborns are adjusting** from a warm, dark, fluid-filled, constantly rocking environment, where they were never hungry, to a bright, still, noisy world.
**Their sleep is disorganised:** they don’t yet distinguish day from night.
**Their digestion is immature:** wind, spitting up and grunting are common.
**Crying often increases** from around two weeks, peaks around six to eight weeks, then gradually declines.
**They want closeness:** being held, hearing your voice and heartbeat, and skin-to-skin contact help regulate their temperature, heart rate and stress.

blocks.p: The traditional 40-day rest period reflects a deep understanding that new mothers need protection, food and care. What tends to help:

ul: Rest and being freed from household duties
Nourishing food prepared by others
Family members caring for the baby so the mother can sleep
Warmth and comfort

blocks.p: Customs worth questioning:

ul: **Not bathing for days:** showering is safe after birth and helps hygiene and wound healing. Follow your doctor’s advice about caesarean wounds.
**Restricting water:** breastfeeding mothers need to drink to thirst. Restricting fluids can cause dehydration and constipation.
**Avoiding fruit and vegetables as “thanda” (cold):** these provide fibre, vitamins and fluids that help recovery and prevent constipation.
**Very heavy diets of ghee, panjeeri and sweets:** nourishing in moderation, but large amounts can cause weight gain and indigestion without extra benefit.
**Staying in bed all the time:** some gentle movement from early on reduces the risk of blood clots.
**Isolation from support:** if chilla means being cut off from your own mother or friends, think about how to keep connected.

blocks.p: The WHO recommends at least four postnatal contacts. At these, health professionals typically check:

ul: **For you:** bleeding, blood pressure, temperature, wound or perineum healing, breasts and feeding, bladder and bowel, mood, and contraception plans.
**For your baby:** feeding, weight, jaundice, cord, breathing, temperature, and vaccinations such as BCG, polio and hepatitis B at birth, as part of Pakistan’s vaccination schedule.

blocks.p: If your hospital doesn’t arrange follow-up, ask your gynaecologist and paediatrician when they want to see you, and ask whether a Lady Health Visitor can visit.

ol: **Lower expectations of yourself.** Feeding, resting and recovering are your main tasks.
**Protect sleep** with help at night and naps during the day.
**Eat and drink regularly.**
**Limit visitors** in the early weeks.
**Hold your baby close.** Contact helps your baby settle, and can help you feel connected.
**Get some daylight** every day.
**Know the warning signs** for you and your baby.

soon: Bleeding that doesn’t lighten over the first weeks, or that returns after it had stopped
Pain, redness or discharge from your wound or stitches
Low mood, anxiety or numbness that lasts beyond two weeks
Feeding difficulties or concerns about your baby’s weight
urgent: Heavy bleeding, soaking a pad in an hour or passing large clots
Fever, chills, or foul-smelling discharge
Severe headache, vision changes, or high blood pressure readings
Chest pain, breathlessness, or a painful, swollen calf
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, confusion, or hallucinations
Any newborn danger sign (see the guide on building confidence as a first-time mother)

blocks.p: The fourth trimester can feel like a blur of love, exhaustion and adjustment. Many mothers feel the world moves on while they’re still recovering. Recognising this period as part of the journey, not something to rush through, gives you permission to rest and receive care.

takeaway: The fourth trimester is the first three months after birth, a time of major recovery for you and adjustment for your baby. Use the best of chilla traditions, such as rest, nourishing food and care, but shower, drink to thirst, eat fruit and vegetables and move gently. Attend postnatal checks and know the warning signs.
prompt: Which chilla customs feel supportive to you, and which would you like to adapt?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: The Emotional Experience of the First Few Weeks
description: The first few weeks after birth can bring a flood of emotions: euphoria, relief, tenderness, fear, boredom, resentment, grief and love, sometimes in the same hour.
