This guide explains why emotions are so intense, the typical emotional arc of the first six weeks, how to process your birth experience, handle visitors, and know when feelings may need more support.
glance: Intense, mixed emotions in the first weeks are normal and driven by hormones, sleep loss, recovery and huge life change.
Many mothers feel a high after birth, a dip around days three to five, and a period of tiredness and adjustment in weeks two to six.
Feeling “touched out”, bored or resentful sometimes doesn’t mean you don’t love your baby.
Processing your birth story can help, especially if it was difficult.

ul: **Hormones:** a sharp drop in oestrogen and progesterone after birth, alongside oxytocin and prolactin linked to feeding and bonding.
**Sleep loss:** emotions become harder to regulate.
**Physical recovery:** pain, bleeding, and healing wounds.
**The weight of responsibility:** realising a baby depends on you.
**Identity shift:** becoming a mother changes how you see yourself.
**Relationships:** new dynamics with your husband and family.
**The first day or two:** relief, euphoria, shock or numbness. Some mothers feel a rush of love; others feel mostly exhausted.
**Days three to five:** a dip as hormones fall and milk comes in. Crying, mood swings and anxiety are common (the baby blues).
**Weeks two to six:** tiredness peaks, the novelty fades, visitors drop off, and the reality of daily care sets in. Many women feel isolated or overwhelmed, but also more confident with practice.
**Love and tenderness,** sometimes overwhelming
**Anxiety** about your baby’s health and safety
**Boredom** with the repetitive nature of care
**Resentment** toward your husband if he can sleep or go out
**Grief** for your old life, or for the birth you hoped for
**Feeling “touched out”:** wanting no one to touch you after hours of feeding and holding
**Guilt** about not feeling the “right” emotions

blocks.p: All of these are common and don’t mean you’re a bad mother.

Your birth is a major life event, and your mind may replay it. Talking or writing about it can help you make sense of it. Ask your doctor to go through what happened if you have questions. If your birth was frightening, or you have flashbacks or nightmares, see the guide on expectations versus reality and postpartum anxiety.
In Pakistan, visitors arrive quickly after a birth to offer congratulations. While well-meant, many visitors can be exhausting, interrupt feeding and rest, and expose a newborn to infections.

ul: Decide in advance how many visitors and when.
Ask your husband or mother to manage them.
Keep visits short.
Ask visitors to wash their hands and avoid kissing the baby.
Excuse yourself to feed or rest.

blocks.p: See the guide on setting boundaries with relatives and visitors.

ol: Rest whenever possible.
Eat and drink regularly.
Talk about your feelings.
Get daylight and fresh air.
Accept help with practical tasks.
Spend quiet time with your baby, away from visitors.

soon: Low mood, anxiety or numbness lasting more than two weeks
Feeling unable to cope
Flashbacks or nightmares about the birth
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
Confusion, hallucinations or very high mood

blocks.p: Many mothers feel they should only be grateful and happy. Giving yourself permission to feel the full range of emotions reduces guilt and makes it easier to notice when you need support.

takeaway: The first weeks bring intense, mixed emotions driven by hormones, sleep loss, recovery and change. Expect highs, dips and tiredness, process your birth story, limit visitors, and seek help if low mood lasts beyond two weeks.
prompt: What emotion has surprised you most since your baby arrived?

title: Understanding Postpartum Physical Recovery
description: Physical recovery after birth involves your uterus, bleeding, breasts, perineum or caesarean wound, bladder, bowel and circulation. This guide explains what happens in each part of your body in the first six weeks, what is normal, how to care for yourself, and which symptoms need urgent attention, including the warning signs of postpartum haemorrhage, infection, pre-eclampsia and blood clots.
glance: Bleeding after birth (lochia) is normal and usually lasts up to about six weeks, changing from red to pink-brown to yellow-white.
Afterpains, cramps as the uterus shrinks, are common and often stronger during breastfeeding.
Constipation and haemorrhoids are common. Fluids, fibre and not straining help.
Heavy bleeding, fever, severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness or a painful swollen calf need urgent care.

blocks.p: After birth, the lining of the uterus sheds, and the place where the placenta was attached heals. This causes bleeding, called lochia.

ul: **Days 1 to 3 or 4:** bright or dark red, heavier than a period, with small clots possible.
**Up to around two weeks:** pinkish or brownish, lighter.
**Up to around six weeks:** yellowish or whitish discharge, gradually stopping.

blocks.p: Bleeding may briefly increase when you stand up after resting, after feeding, or after more activity. Use maternity pads, not tampons or menstrual cups, until bleeding stops, to reduce infection risk.

Immediately after birth, the uterus is around the size of a large grapefruit and can be felt near your navel. It contracts to close blood vessels at the placental site and shrinks back into the pelvis over about two weeks, returning to near its usual size by around six weeks.
**Afterpains** are cramps as the uterus contracts. They are often stronger:

ul: During breastfeeding, because oxytocin released during feeding causes the uterus to contract
After second and later babies

blocks.p: They usually ease within a few days. Ask your doctor what pain relief is safe while breastfeeding.
Colostrum is produced first, then milk comes in around days two to five, often causing fullness or engorgement. See the breastfeeding guide.
See the guides on recovery after vaginal birth and recovery after a caesarean.

ul: **Difficulty passing urine** in the first hours or days can happen due to swelling, pain or anaesthesia. Pouring warm water over the area while you pass urine can help.
**Leaking** when you cough, sneeze or laugh is common, especially after a vaginal birth. Pelvic floor exercises help.
**Signs of infection:** burning, frequency, urgency, cloudy or smelly urine, or fever.

**The first bowel movement** can feel frightening, especially with stitches. Support your stitches with a clean pad held gently against the perineum, or a pillow against a caesarean wound, and avoid straining.

**Constipation** is common, caused by hormones, pain medication, iron supplements, low fluids and less movement. Drink plenty, eat fibre such as fruit, vegetables, whole wheat atta and daal, and walk gently.
**Haemorrhoids** may appear or worsen. Cool compresses and avoiding constipation help.

blocks.p: Night sweats and passing lots of urine in the first weeks are your body’s way of removing extra fluid from pregnancy. Swelling in the legs can briefly worsen before improving.
The risk of blood clots is higher after birth, especially after a caesarean. Gentle walking, staying hydrated, and moving your feet and legs when resting reduce the risk.

Pre-eclampsia can develop after birth, usually in the first days but sometimes up to six weeks later. Watch for severe headache, vision changes, pain under the ribs, or sudden swelling of the face and hands.

Around six weeks after birth, your doctor may check your recovery, blood pressure, wound or perineum, mood, contraception plans, and any concerns about bladder, bowel or sex. It’s a good time to ask questions.

soon: Bleeding that suddenly becomes heavier or red again after it had lightened
Burning or stinging when passing urine
Constipation for more than three days, or severe haemorrhoid pain
Leaking urine that doesn’t improve, or any leaking of stool
Pain or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina
urgent: Heavy bleeding: soaking a pad in an hour, or passing clots larger than a plum
Fever, chills, or foul-smelling discharge
Severe abdominal pain
Severe headache, vision changes, or pain under the ribs
Chest pain, breathlessness, or coughing up blood
A painful, swollen, warm calf
Fainting or feeling faint

blocks.p: Many women are surprised by how much physical recovery is involved after birth, and how little attention it gets once the baby arrives. Your recovery matters. Caring for your body is part of caring for your baby.

takeaway: Physical recovery involves bleeding, afterpains, wound healing, bladder and bowel changes, fluid shifts and circulation. Use pads, drink fluids, eat fibre, move gently and attend your postnatal checks. Know the urgent warning signs and act on them immediately.
prompt: Which part of your physical recovery would you like to understand better?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Rest and Recovery After Delivery
description: Rest after birth is how your body heals. In the first weeks it is repairing a wound inside the uterus where the placenta was attached, mending muscles and skin, rebuilding lost blood and resetting hormones, while also producing milk. This guide explains what rest does, how much movement is helpful, a realistic week-by-week picture, and how to protect rest in a household where you may feel pressure to get back to work.
glance: Where the placenta separated, it leaves a wound inside the uterus that takes several weeks to heal. Bleeding (lochia) comes from this healing site.
Rest supports wound healing, rebuilding blood after birth, milk production and emotional recovery.
Too little movement raises the risk of blood clots, which is higher after birth. Short, frequent walks help.
Real rest means being freed from household duties and hosting, not only lying down.

blocks.h: What your body is doing while you rest

ul: **Healing the placental site:** the uterus contracts to close blood vessels, then the lining regrows over the area. Overexertion in the early weeks can make bleeding heavier.
**Repairing tissue:** perineal tears, an episiotomy or a caesarean incision need energy and protein to heal.

**Rebuilding blood:** everyone loses some blood at birth. If you lost a lot, or were anaemic in pregnancy, you may feel breathless, dizzy and exhausted, and your body needs iron, protein and rest to recover.
**Producing milk:** milk production uses energy and fluids. Exhaustion and dehydration make feeding harder.
**Adjusting hormones:** sleep and rest make it easier to cope with emotional swings.

blocks.p: Rest doesn’t mean staying completely still. After birth, the blood clots more readily to protect you from bleeding, and long periods of immobility increase the risk of a clot in the legs.

ul: **From the first day:** short walks to the bathroom and around the room, and moving your ankles and feet while resting.
**First two weeks:** mostly resting, with short, gentle walks several times a day.
**Weeks two to six:** gradually longer walks and light activities, while still avoiding heavy lifting, floor-level chores and strenuous work.
**Listen to your bleeding:** if it gets heavier or turns red again after activity, it’s a sign to slow down.
**Week 1:** feeding, sleeping, eating, and short walks. Someone else does the cooking, cleaning and visitors.
**Week 2:** still mostly resting. You might do small tasks sitting down, like folding baby clothes.
**Weeks 3 to 4:** light tasks such as preparing a simple snack, short walks outside. Still no heavy lifting or mopping.
**Weeks 5 to 6:** gradually more activity, guided by how you feel and your doctor’s advice.

blocks.p: Some families use a “5-5-5” guide: five days in the bed, five days on the bed, five days around the bed. It’s a popular framework rather than a medical rule, but it captures the idea of a gradual return.

blocks.h: What rest looks like in practice

ul: Feeding lying down when it’s safe and comfortable
Sleeping when someone else is caring for the baby, not doing chores
Meals and drinks brought to you
Short visits, or none, in the first week or two
A quiet room, dim light and a fan or heater set safely
No hosting or serving guests

blocks.h: Protecting rest in a busy household

ol: **Agree in advance** who takes over cooking, cleaning, laundry and caring for older children.
**Name a visitor manager,** your husband or mother, who sets visiting times and politely ends visits.
**Use clear language:** “The doctor has advised me to rest for six weeks so I heal properly.”
**Ask for a daily protected sleep,** for example three to four hours when someone else takes the baby between feeds.
**Accept imperfection** in the house.

blocks.p: If you had heavy bleeding, a caesarean, a severe tear, pre-eclampsia, or a baby in the NICU, you may need longer rest and more help. Ask your doctor how long to avoid lifting and strenuous activity.

soon: Exhaustion that doesn’t improve despite rest, or breathlessness and dizziness (possible anaemia)
Bleeding that gets heavier with activity and doesn’t settle with rest
You feel pressured to resume heavy duties and can’t get enough rest
urgent: A painful, swollen, warm calf, chest pain, or sudden breathlessness
Heavy bleeding, soaking a pad in an hour
Fever or chills

blocks.p: Many women feel guilty resting, especially in joint families where others are working, or when they’re used to managing the household. Rest in the first six weeks is not indulgence; it’s the foundation of recovery, and it allows you to care for your baby for months and years to come.

takeaway: Rest after birth lets your body heal the placental site, repair tissues, rebuild blood and make milk. Balance rest with short, frequent walks to reduce clot risk, increase activity gradually over six weeks, and protect your rest with clear plans for household help and visitors.
prompt: Which household task would most help your recovery if someone else took it over for the next month?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Navigating Recovery After a C-Section
description: A caesarean section is major abdominal surgery, and recovery takes longer than after a vaginal birth. This guide explains what happens in the first hours and days, how to manage pain and wind, move safely, care for your wound, return to activities, and the warning signs of infection or blood clots. It also covers the emotional side of an unplanned caesarean and planning future pregnancies.
glance: Most women stay in hospital for a few days after a caesarean. Full recovery often takes six weeks or more.
Getting up and walking early, with support, reduces the risk of blood clots and helps wind pain.
Support your wound with a pillow when you cough, laugh or sneeze. Avoid lifting anything heavier than your baby for around six weeks.
The WHO recommends waiting at least 24 months after a birth before trying for another pregnancy.

ul: You’ll usually have had a spinal or epidural anaesthetic, so your legs will be numb for a few hours.
You may have a urinary catheter, removed within the first day.
You may have a drip.
Skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding can usually begin soon after surgery, with help.
**Pain:** you’ll be offered pain relief. Take it regularly as advised, since controlled pain makes moving, feeding and breathing easier.
**Getting up:** you’ll usually be encouraged to sit up and walk within the first day, with support.
**Wind pain:** trapped wind can cause cramping and even pain in the shoulder tip. Walking, gentle movement and peppermint tea may help.
**Eating and drinking:** you’ll usually start with fluids and progress to food.
**Bleeding:** lochia occurs as after a vaginal birth.
**Getting out of bed:** bend your knees, roll onto your side, push up with your arms and swing your legs over the side. Reverse to lie down.
**Coughing, laughing or sneezing:** hold a pillow firmly against your wound.
**Feeding positions:** use pillows to protect your wound. The “football” hold or side-lying positions avoid pressure on your abdomen.
**Lifting:** avoid lifting anything heavier than your baby for around six weeks, including toddlers, buckets and heavy shopping.
Keep the wound clean and dry. Follow your doctor’s advice on dressings and when to shower.
Pat the area dry after washing.
Wear loose clothing and high-waisted underwear that doesn’t rub the wound.
Numbness around the scar is common and may last for months.
Once healed, gentle scar massage may help reduce tightness, if your doctor agrees.
**Walking:** start with short walks and gradually increase.
**Housework:** avoid heavy tasks, including mopping, sweeping and lifting heavy items, for around six weeks.
**Driving:** usually not for several weeks. You should be able to wear a seatbelt comfortably and brake suddenly without pain.
**Exercise:** gentle exercises, such as pelvic floor and deep breathing, can begin early. More strenuous exercise usually waits until after six weeks, with your doctor’s advice.
**Sex:** when you feel ready and bleeding has stopped. Discuss contraception first.
The WHO recommends waiting at least 24 months after a birth before trying for another pregnancy, which allows your body and scar to heal.
Many women can have a vaginal birth after a caesarean (VBAC). Discuss your options with your doctor in your next pregnancy.

soon: Wound pain that is getting worse rather than better
Redness around the wound, or a small amount of discharge
Burning when passing urine
Low mood or distress about the birth
urgent: The wound becomes red, hot, swollen, or leaks pus or foul-smelling fluid, or opens
Fever or chills
Heavy bleeding
Severe abdominal pain
A painful, swollen calf, chest pain or breathlessness

blocks.p: Some women feel disappointed or traumatised after an unplanned caesarean, or hear comments such as “You didn’t have a real birth.” A caesarean is a real birth, and recovery from major surgery while caring for a newborn is demanding. If you feel distressed, talk to your doctor. A birth debrief may help.

takeaway: Caesarean recovery takes six weeks or more. Walk early, take pain relief as advised, support your wound, avoid heavy lifting, care for your wound, and know the warning signs of infection and blood clots. A caesarean is a real birth, and your feelings about it deserve support.
prompt: What kind of help would make caesarean recovery easier for you?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Navigating Recovery After Vaginal Birth
description: Recovery after a vaginal birth centres on the perineum, the area between the vagina and the anus, which stretches during birth and may bruise, swell, tear or be cut. This guide explains tear types, how to keep stitches clean using water, how to manage pain, swelling and the first bowel movement, a realistic healing timeline, how to rebuild pelvic floor strength, and when pain or leaking needs specialist help.
glance: Most women have some swelling or tearing. Tears are graded from first degree (skin only) to fourth degree (involving the anal sphincter and lining).
Rinsing with water after using the toilet, patting dry and changing pads every few hours helps prevent infection.
Cold packs, lying on your side and preventing constipation make the first weeks more comfortable.
Pain during sex, leaking urine, wind or stool, or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina are common but treatable, so don’t stay silent about them.

ul: **First degree:** a small tear in the skin of the perineum. Often heals without stitches and is usually sore for a few days.
**Second degree:** a tear through skin and muscle, usually repaired with stitches. This is the most common type requiring stitches.
**Third degree:** a tear extending into the muscle around the anus (the anal sphincter).
**Fourth degree:** a tear extending through the anal sphincter into the lining of the bowel.
**Episiotomy:** a cut made by the doctor or midwife to widen the opening. It is repaired with stitches, and recovery is similar to a second-degree tear.

blocks.p: Third and fourth-degree tears are less common, are usually repaired in an operating theatre, and need follow-up, often with a physiotherapist, to protect bowel control. If you’re not sure what kind of tear you had, ask.

ol: After using the toilet, rinse the area with clean, lukewarm water using a lota, shattaf or squeeze bottle. This is gentler than wiping.
Pat dry from front to back with a clean, soft cloth or tissue.
Change pads at least every four hours, and more often if they’re heavy.
Wash your hands before and after changing pads.
Wear loose, breathable cotton underwear and avoid tight shalwar.
Shower daily. Showering is safe and helps hygiene.
Avoid tampons and menstrual cups until bleeding has stopped and you’ve been checked.

ul: **Cold:** a cold pack or ice wrapped in a clean cloth, applied for 10 to 20 minutes at a time in the first 24 to 72 hours, can reduce swelling.

**Positions:** lie on your side to rest and feed. When sitting, a soft cushion or folded towel can help. Some women find a ring cushion helpful; others find it increases pressure, so use what feels comfortable.
**Passing urine:** pour warm water over the area as you pass urine to reduce stinging, or lean forward slightly.
**Pain relief:** ask your doctor or pharmacist what’s safe while breastfeeding.
**Rest:** standing or sitting for long periods increases swelling and discomfort in the first weeks.

blocks.p: Many women feel anxious about this, especially with stitches.

ol: Drink plenty of fluids and eat fibre-rich foods from the first day: fruit, vegetables, daal, whole wheat atta and soaked dried fruits.
Go when you feel the urge; don’t hold it in.
Use a small stool under your feet on a Western toilet so your knees are higher than your hips.
Hold a clean pad gently against your stitches for support.
Breathe out slowly rather than holding your breath and straining.
Ask your doctor about stool softeners if you’re constipated, especially after a third or fourth-degree tear.

ul: **First week:** soreness, swelling and bruising are at their worst. Stitches may feel tight or itchy as they heal.
**One to three weeks:** stitches usually dissolve, and pain gradually reduces. You may notice small bits of stitch on pads.
**Three to six weeks:** most women feel considerably better. Some tenderness may remain.
**Months:** scar tissue softens, and pelvic floor strength continues to improve with exercises.

blocks.p: The pelvic floor muscles support your bladder, uterus and bowel and help control urine, wind and stool. They’re stretched during pregnancy and birth.

ul: Start gentle pelvic floor squeezes as soon as you feel comfortable, even with stitches. They improve blood flow and healing.
Build up to regular sets of slow holds and quick squeezes (see the guide on understanding postpartum body changes).
Expect improvement over weeks to months.
If you had a third or fourth-degree tear, ask for a referral to a pelvic health physiotherapist if available.
Many couples wait until bleeding has stopped and the perineum has healed, often around six weeks. For many Muslim couples, the nifas period also guides timing.
Low oestrogen during breastfeeding can cause dryness. A water-based lubricant can help.
Some discomfort at first is common. Persistent or severe pain is not something to endure, so ask your doctor.
Discuss contraception before resuming sex.

soon: Pain that gets worse rather than better after the first week
Stitches that seem to have come apart, or a wound that isn’t healing
Leaking urine or wind that isn’t improving after several weeks
A feeling of heaviness, dragging or a bulge in the vagina
Pain during sex that persists
urgent: Fever or chills
Foul-smelling discharge from the vagina or stitches
Severe or increasing pain, redness or swelling of the perineum
Heavy bleeding, soaking a pad in an hour
Being unable to control your bowels, or leaking stool

blocks.p: Perineal pain and changes can affect how you sit, move, feel about your body and feel about intimacy. These topics can be hard to discuss, especially with family. They are common, and most are treatable. A doctor or physiotherapist can help you recover fully.

takeaway: Perineal recovery takes weeks to months. Rinse with water, pat dry, change pads often, use cold packs and side-lying for pain, prevent constipation and support your stitches during bowel movements. Start gentle pelvic floor exercises early, and ask for help with persistent pain, leaking or heaviness.
prompt: Which part of your recovery have you found hardest to talk about, and who could you raise it with?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Gentle Movement and Returning to Everyday Activities
description: Movement after birth helps recovery, mood and strength, but returning too quickly can strain healing tissues and the pelvic floor. This guide explains a gradual, phase-by-phase return to activity, how to tell if you’re doing too much, how to adapt household chores, how to check for abdominal muscle separation, and when to return to more vigorous exercise.
glance: Gentle walking, deep breathing and pelvic floor exercises can usually start in the first days after birth.
Increase activity gradually. Heavier bleeding, pain or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina are signs to slow down.
High-impact activities, such as running or jumping, are generally not advised until at least 12 weeks after birth, and only once you’re ready.
Floor-level and heavy chores such as mopping, washing clothes by hand and lifting water buckets should return gradually.

ul: Improves circulation and reduces the risk of blood clots
Helps with constipation and wind
Supports mood and reduces stress
Rebuilds strength for lifting and carrying your baby
Helps the pelvic floor and abdominal muscles recover
**Walking:** short walks around the house, gradually increasing.
**Breathing:** deep breaths into your belly and ribs, with a gentle drawing in of the lower belly as you breathe out.
**Pelvic floor exercises:** gentle squeezes and lifts, as comfortable.
**Ankle and foot movements** while resting.
**Longer walks:** gradually increase distance and pace.
**Gentle stretches** for the neck, shoulders and back.
**Core activation:** pelvic tilts, gentle bridges and side-lying leg lifts, if comfortable.
**Light household tasks:** sitting tasks, folding laundry, preparing simple food.
**Strength building:** gradually progress core and pelvic floor exercises, add squats and lunges using body weight.
**Low-impact activities:** brisk walking, stationary cycling, swimming once bleeding has stopped and wounds have healed.
**Most household tasks**, with good posture and gradual return to heavier ones.
**Higher-impact activities** such as running or jumping, if you have no symptoms such as leaking, heaviness or pain, and ideally after a pelvic floor and core check.
Bleeding becomes heavier or turns red again
Pain in your wound, perineum or pelvis
A feeling of heaviness, dragging or a bulge in the vagina
Leaking urine
Doming or bulging along the middle of your abdomen
Extreme tiredness

ol: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat.
Place your fingertips just above your navel, pointing toward your feet.
Lift your head slightly and feel for a gap between the muscles.
Repeat below the navel.

blocks.p: A gap of a few fingers wide, or doming, may suggest diastasis recti. A physiotherapist can guide you.

ul: Use long-handled brooms and mops.
Sit on a low stool for floor-level tasks.
Avoid lifting heavy buckets or gas cylinders.
Ask for help with heavy tasks for at least six weeks.

soon: Leaking urine or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina
Pain in your wound, perineum or pelvis with activity
A gap or bulge in the middle of your abdomen
urgent: Heavy bleeding, soaking a pad in an hour
Chest pain, breathlessness or a painful, swollen calf

blocks.p: Some women feel pressure to get moving quickly to “bounce back”; others feel anxious about moving at all. A gradual approach builds strength safely.

takeaway: Start with walking, breathing and pelvic floor exercises, increase activity gradually, watch for signs of overdoing it, and wait until at least 12 weeks for high-impact exercise.
prompt: What kind of movement would feel good for your body this week?

title: Postpartum Nutrition and Hydration
description: Nutrition and hydration after birth support healing, energy, mood and milk production. This guide explains what your body needs in the first months, how to make traditional postpartum foods work for you, how much to drink, which nutrients matter most (including iron and vitamin D), common myths, and how to eat well when you have no time.
glance: Healing, rebuilding blood and breastfeeding increase your need for protein, iron, calcium, fluids and energy.
Drink to thirst, with a glass of water at every feed. Pale yellow urine is a good sign you’re drinking enough.
Traditional foods such as panjeeri, harira and yakhni can be nourishing, but large amounts of ghee and sugar add calories without extra benefit.
No single food has been proven to increase milk supply. Frequent, effective feeding is what drives supply.

blocks.h: What your body needs after birth

ul: **Protein:** for tissue repair, from daal, chickpeas, eggs, yoghurt, milk, chicken, fish and meat.
**Iron:** to rebuild blood, from red meat, liver (in moderation), daal, chickpeas, beans and leafy greens, with vitamin C to improve absorption.
**Calcium:** for bones, from milk, yoghurt, paneer, and leafy greens.
**Vitamin D:** from sunlight and some foods. Deficiency is common in Pakistan, especially among women who spend most time indoors. Ask your doctor whether testing or supplements are right for you.
**Fibre:** to prevent constipation, from fruit, vegetables, whole wheat atta, daal and soaked dried fruits.
**Fluids:** for hydration and milk production.
**Energy:** breastfeeding uses extra energy, usually a few hundred extra calories a day.
**Panjeeri, gond ke laddu:** made with whole wheat, nuts, seeds, ghee and sugar. Nourishing in small amounts, but very energy-dense.
**Harira, doodh with haldi:** warm, comforting drinks.
**Yakhni (broth):** hydrating and nourishing.
**Dates and dried fruits:** provide energy and fibre.

blocks.p: Enjoy them as part of a balanced diet, rather than as replacements for meals.

ul: Keep a glass of water by your feeding spot.
Drink to thirst.
Check urine colour: pale yellow is a good sign.
In hot weather, drink more.
Limit caffeine to moderate amounts.

myth: “Avoid fruit and vegetables because they are ’thanda’ (cold).”
Fruit and vegetables provide fibre, vitamins and fluids that help recovery.
“Drinking less water is better after birth.”
Restricting fluids can cause dehydration and constipation.
“Certain foods will increase milk supply.”
No single food has been proven to increase milk supply. Frequent, effective milk removal is key.

ul: Keep snacks within reach: nuts, dates, fruit, yoghurt, boiled eggs.
Ask family to prepare simple meals.
Cook in batches.

soon: Extreme tiredness, breathlessness or dizziness
Constipation lasting several days
Poor appetite or weight loss
urgent: Signs of dehydration: very dark urine, dizziness, confusion

blocks.p: Food is often central to family care after birth. Balancing tradition with nutrition can help you feel cared for and nourished.

takeaway: Prioritise protein, iron, calcium, vitamin D, fibre and fluids. Enjoy traditional foods in moderation, drink to thirst and keep easy snacks nearby.
prompt: What is one nourishing snack you could keep within reach this week?

title: Sleep Deprivation and Rest Strategies
description: Sleep deprivation is one of the hardest parts of early motherhood, and one of the least discussed. This guide explains why newborns wake so often and why that is biologically normal, what broken sleep does to your body and mind, specific strategies for sharing nights and protecting a core block of sleep, how to stay safe when you’re exhausted, and how to recognise when poor sleep is a sign of something else.
glance: Newborns wake often because their stomachs are tiny, they grow fast, their sleep cycles are short, and they don’t yet know day from night.
Fragmented sleep is harder on the brain than short sleep. Protecting one unbroken block of three to four hours makes a real difference.
Even if you breastfeed, others can help at night by changing, burping and settling the baby and bringing you water.
Never fall asleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair. This carries a high risk of sudden infant death.

ul: **Tiny stomachs:** a newborn’s stomach holds only a small amount, and breast milk digests quickly, so frequent feeds are needed.
**Rapid growth:** babies grow faster in the first months than at any other time after birth.
**Short sleep cycles:** newborn cycles last around 40 to 60 minutes, compared with about 90 minutes in adults, so there are more chances to wake.

**Lots of active sleep:** newborns spend a large share of sleep in light, active sleep, when they twitch, grunt, smile and make noises. Many parents pick them up thinking they’re awake, when they would have settled on their own.
**No body clock yet:** the rhythm that makes us sleep at night develops over the first few months. Daylight, darkness and routines help it develop.

blocks.p: Night waking is not a sign of a “bad” baby, a hungry baby, or something you’re doing wrong. It protects babies by keeping them feeding and responsive.

blocks.h: What sleep deprivation does to you

ul: **Fragmented sleep** (waking repeatedly) affects how rested you feel more than total hours alone, because you rarely reach deeper, restorative sleep stages.
**Mood:** you may feel more irritable, tearful, anxious or low.
**Thinking:** concentration, memory and decision-making all suffer, which is why you might forget words or misplace things.
**Physical effects:** headaches, increased appetite for sugary food, lower immunity, and slower healing.
**Safety:** slower reaction times make driving and handling hot drinks or the stove riskier.

ol: **Share the night.** Even if you’re breastfeeding, someone else can change nappies, burp and settle the baby after a feed, and bring the baby to you. Some families take shifts: one adult covers 9 p.m. to 1 a.m., another covers 1 a.m. to 5 a.m.

**Protect a core block.** Aim for one stretch of three to four hours of unbroken sleep in 24 hours. For example, go to bed right after the evening feed while someone else takes the baby until the next feed, bringing the baby to you only when it’s needed.
**Sleep at the right time.** If the baby has a longer stretch early in the night, go to bed then rather than staying up.
**Nap strategically.** A 20 to 30 minute nap can refresh you without leaving you groggy. Longer naps can help too, if you have the chance.

**Make nights boring for the baby.** Keep lights dim, voices quiet and interaction minimal. Change nappies only when needed (a heavy or dirty nappy). Bright light and play at night can wake the baby more fully.
**Make days bright.** Get daylight, open curtains, and talk and play with your baby during the day. This helps the baby’s body clock develop.
**Reduce what you’re asked to do.** Sleep-deprived mothers shouldn’t also be cooking for guests or doing heavy household work.
**Limit caffeine later in the day,** so it doesn’t stop you sleeping when you get the chance.

blocks.p: Some breastfeeding mothers express milk so someone else can give one night feed. This can help, but in the early weeks, skipping feeds can affect supply and cause engorgement. If you want to try it, it’s usually easier once breastfeeding is established, and you may need to express at around the time of the skipped feed. Ask a breastfeeding supporter for guidance.

ul: **Never fall asleep with your baby on a sofa, armchair or floor cushion.** This carries a much higher risk of sudden infant death and suffocation.
If you think you might fall asleep while feeding at night, feed in bed rather than on a sofa, and move pillows and blankets away from the baby before you start.
Put the baby back in their own safe sleep space on their back after feeding when you can.
Ask someone to stay awake with you during a night feed if you’re extremely tired.
Avoid driving when you’re severely sleep-deprived.

blocks.h: When poor sleep may be something else

ul: You can’t sleep even when the baby is asleep and someone else is caring for them
You lie awake with racing thoughts or worries
You wake early and can’t get back to sleep, with low mood
You feel you don’t need sleep, have lots of energy and racing thoughts (this needs urgent assessment)

blocks.p: These can be signs of postpartum anxiety, depression, or, rarely, postpartum psychosis.

soon: You can’t sleep even when given the chance
Low mood or anxiety most days for two weeks or more
Extreme exhaustion with breathlessness or dizziness (ask about anaemia)
urgent: Little or no sleep with very high energy, racing thoughts, confusion or strange beliefs
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby

blocks.p: Sleep deprivation can make everything feel harder: small problems seem huge, and patience runs out. It can strain your marriage, especially if you feel you’re the only one waking. Asking for help with nights is not a weakness; it is one of the most effective ways to protect your health and mood.

takeaway: Frequent night waking is biologically normal for newborns. Share the night, protect one core block of sleep, keep nights dim and days bright, and never fall asleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair. If you can’t sleep even when given the chance, talk to your doctor.
prompt: What would one protected block of three to four hours of sleep look like in your household, and who could make it possible?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Personal Hygiene and Self-Care After Birth
description: Hygiene after birth supports healing, comfort and confidence, and it’s an area where traditional customs and medical advice sometimes conflict. This guide explains how to manage postpartum bleeding, care for stitches or a caesarean wound, bathe and wash hair safely, care for your breasts and nipples, maintain oral health, and use handwashing to protect your newborn, along with which beliefs are worth reconsidering.
glance: Showering and washing your hair after birth are safe and help prevent infection. Use warm water.
Use maternity pads, not tampons or menstrual cups, until bleeding has stopped.
Rinse the perineum with water after using the toilet, and pat dry from front to back.
Wash your hands before feeding or holding your baby, and after nappy changes and using the toilet.

blocks.p: In some families, new mothers are told not to bathe or wash their hair for days or weeks after birth, for fear of catching cold or causing illness. There is no evidence that bathing causes harm, and good hygiene reduces the risk of infection.

ul: Showering is safe from the first day, once you can stand steadily. Ask someone to stay nearby the first time, in case you feel faint.
Use warm, not very hot, water.
Dry yourself and your hair well, and dress warmly in cold weather.
Sitting in a bath tub isn’t common in Pakistani homes. If you use one, ask your doctor when it’s safe, especially with stitches or a caesarean wound.
Use maternity pads, which are larger and more absorbent than regular pads.
Change them every four hours, or more often when bleeding is heavy.
Wash hands before and after changing pads.
Avoid tampons and menstrual cups until bleeding has stopped and your doctor confirms you’ve healed, because they increase the risk of infection.
Dispose of pads hygienically: wrap them in paper or a bag.
Wear dark, comfortable underwear and keep spare pads and underwear in your bag when you go out.
Rinse with clean, lukewarm water after using the toilet, using a lota, shattaf or squeeze bottle.
Pat dry gently from front to back.
Wear loose cotton underwear.
Watch for signs of infection: increasing pain, redness, swelling, pus or a bad smell.
Follow your doctor’s advice about dressings and when you can shower.
Let water run over the wound in the shower rather than scrubbing.
Pat dry gently with a clean towel.
Wear loose clothing and high-waisted underwear that doesn’t rub.
Check the wound daily for redness, swelling, heat, pus or opening.
Wash breasts with water during your daily shower. Soap isn’t needed on the nipples and can dry the skin.
The Montgomery’s glands on the areola produce oils that keep nipples clean and moisturised.
After feeding, let nipples air-dry. A little expressed breast milk on sore nipples can help.
Change breast pads regularly to keep skin dry.
Wear a clean, supportive bra.

blocks.p: Pregnancy can make gums swollen and prone to bleeding. Brush twice daily, floss, and see a dentist if you have pain or bleeding gums.
Newborns’ immune systems are immature. Wash your hands with soap and water:

ul: Before feeding or preparing feeds
After changing nappies
After using the toilet
Before handling your baby, especially after being outside

blocks.p: Ask visitors to wash their hands before holding the baby, and to avoid kissing the baby’s face.

ul: Change clothes and bedsheets more often in the first weeks, since sweating, leaking milk and bleeding are common.
Use cotton fabrics that breathe.

myth: “Bathing after birth causes illness.”
There’s no evidence for this. Showering helps prevent infection.
“Hair washing in the first 40 days causes headaches or joint pain.”
There’s no evidence for this. Dry your hair well and stay warm.
“Brushing your teeth after birth weakens them.”
Dental hygiene is important after birth.

soon: Redness, swelling, pain or discharge from stitches or wound
Sore, cracked or bleeding nipples
Bleeding gums or tooth pain
urgent: Fever or chills
Foul-smelling discharge from the vagina
Heavy bleeding, soaking a pad in an hour
A wound that opens or leaks pus

blocks.p: Feeling clean can make a real difference to how you feel about your body and yourself, especially when everything else feels out of control. If family customs make you uncomfortable, explaining that your doctor recommends showering can help.

takeaway: Showering and washing your hair are safe after birth. Use pads, rinse the perineum with water, care for your wound and breasts, brush your teeth and wash your hands often. Watch for signs of infection and seek help promptly.
prompt: Is there a hygiene custom you’ve been told to follow that you’d like to discuss with your family or doctor?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Understanding Postpartum Hormonal Changes
description: Within hours of birth, your hormone levels shift more dramatically than at almost any other time of life. These changes affect mood, sleep, sweating, hair, skin, vaginal comfort, libido, periods and energy. This guide explains which hormones change and why, how breastfeeding hormones work, how to recognise postpartum thyroid problems, when periods and fertility return, and why “hormone balancing” products aren’t the answer.
glance: Oestrogen and progesterone fall sharply after the placenta is delivered, which contributes to baby blues, night sweats, hair shedding and vaginal dryness.
Prolactin drives milk production; oxytocin releases milk, contracts the uterus and supports bonding.
Postpartum thyroiditis can cause anxiety, a racing heart, fatigue or low mood in the first year. A blood test can identify it.
You can ovulate before your first period, so you can become pregnant before you realise your fertility has returned.

blocks.p: During pregnancy, the placenta produces large amounts of oestrogen and progesterone. When the placenta is delivered, these hormones fall to very low levels within days. This contributes to:

ul: **Mood changes,** including the baby blues around days three to five
**Night sweats** and hot flushes, as the body adjusts and removes extra fluid
**Hair shedding** two to four months later
**Vaginal dryness,** especially while breastfeeding
**Lower libido**

**Prolactin** stimulates milk production. It rises each time your baby feeds or milk is removed, which is why frequent feeding builds supply. Prolactin also suppresses ovulation and can keep oestrogen low.
**Oxytocin** triggers the let-down reflex that releases milk. It also contracts the uterus, which is why you may feel afterpains during feeds, and is linked with feelings of calm and bonding.

Some women feel relaxed or sleepy during feeds; others feel a brief wave of low mood or anxiety as milk lets down (a rare experience called dysphoric milk ejection reflex). If this happens to you, mention it to your doctor or breastfeeding supporter.

blocks.p: Sleep deprivation and stress can keep cortisol and adrenaline levels raised, which may affect mood, appetite and sleep. Rest, support and gentle movement help bring them down.
The thyroid gland controls metabolism. In some women it becomes inflamed in the first year after birth. Typically there is:

ul: **An overactive phase** (often in the first few months): anxiety, irritability, racing heart, feeling hot, weight loss, poor sleep.
**An underactive phase** (often later): tiredness, low mood, feeling cold, constipation, dry skin, weight gain, hair loss.

blocks.p: Not everyone has both phases. Because these symptoms overlap with normal postpartum life, depression and anxiety, it’s often missed. A blood test can check thyroid function. Most women recover within a year, though some need longer-term treatment.

ul: **If you’re not breastfeeding:** periods often return within about six to eight weeks, sometimes sooner.
**If you’re breastfeeding:** prolactin can delay periods for months, especially with frequent feeds day and night.
**Ovulation comes first:** you release an egg about two weeks before a period, so you can become pregnant before your first period.

**Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM):** breastfeeding can be used as contraception only if all three apply: your baby is under six months, you’re exclusively breastfeeding day and night without long gaps, and your periods haven’t returned. If any one changes, you need another method.
**Birth spacing:** the WHO recommends waiting at least 24 months after a birth before trying for another pregnancy, for the health of mother and baby.

blocks.p: Discuss contraception with your doctor before you resume sex, including options compatible with breastfeeding.

Low oestrogen, high prolactin, tiredness, healing tissues and body changes all reduce desire for many women after birth. This is common and often improves over months. See the guide on intimacy and emotional connection after birth.

Many supplements and teas are marketed for balancing hormones after birth. There is little evidence that they work, and some may not be safe while breastfeeding. If you’re worried about hormonal symptoms, ask your doctor, who can check for specific problems such as thyroid conditions or anaemia.

soon: Racing heart, anxiety, heat intolerance or weight loss
Persistent fatigue, feeling cold, low mood or weight gain
Periods that are very heavy, very painful or very irregular once they return
Vaginal dryness or pain that affects your comfort
You want to discuss contraception
urgent: Very heavy bleeding when periods return, soaking a pad in an hour
Thoughts of harming yourself
Confusion, very high mood or hallucinations

blocks.p: Understanding that hormones play a big role in how you feel can reduce self-blame. It doesn’t mean your feelings aren’t real or important, and it doesn’t mean you should simply wait. If symptoms persist, ask for a check-up.

takeaway: After birth, oestrogen and progesterone fall sharply while prolactin and oxytocin support feeding. These shifts explain many changes in mood, sweating, hair and libido. Ask for a thyroid test if you have persistent anxiety, fatigue or low mood, and remember that fertility can return before your first period.
prompt: Which change since giving birth would you most like to understand or discuss with your doctor?

title: Understanding Different Feeding Journeys
description: Babies can be fed in different ways: exclusive breastfeeding, expressed breast milk, formula, or a mix. Each path has its own practicalities, and many families move between them. This guide explains what international guidance recommends and why, how mixed feeding and expressing work, how to prepare formula safely, how to bottle-feed responsively, and how to handle feelings and family opinions when your plans change.
glance: The WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, then continued breastfeeding alongside food to two years or beyond.
If you give some formula, there are ways to protect your milk supply if you want to keep breastfeeding.
Formula must be prepared exactly as instructed, with water boiled first. Never dilute or concentrate it.
Babies under six months who are exclusively breastfed don’t need extra water, even in hot weather.

blocks.h: What the guidance says and why

blocks.p: The WHO and UNICEF recommend starting breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, exclusive breastfeeding for six months, and continued breastfeeding with complementary food up to two years or beyond. Breast milk contains antibodies and other protective factors that reduce the risk of infections such as diarrhoea and pneumonia, which matters especially where clean water and healthcare access can be limited. Many Muslim families also know the Quranic reference to nursing for two full years.
Guidance describes what’s best at a population level. Individual circumstances vary, and every family deserves accurate information and support, not judgement.

ul: **Exclusive breastfeeding:** only breast milk, directly from the breast, with no water, ghutti, honey or other liquids, except medicines prescribed by a doctor.
**Expressed breast milk:** milk removed by hand or pump and given by bottle, cup or spoon. Useful when a baby can’t latch, is in the NICU, or when you’re away.
**Mixed feeding:** breast milk plus some formula.
**Formula feeding:** infant formula as the main or only food.

blocks.p: Milk supply depends on how often and how well milk is removed. Each formula feed that replaces a breastfeed means less stimulation. If you want to keep breastfeeding:

ol: Breastfeed first, then offer formula if needed.
Keep breastfeeding frequently, including at night, when prolactin levels are higher.
If you skip a breastfeed, consider expressing at around that time.
Use paced bottle feeding (see below) so the baby doesn’t come to prefer the faster flow of a bottle.
Get help with any underlying problems, such as latch, that led to formula use.

ul: **Hand expression:** useful in the early days when colostrum volumes are small. Gently massage the breast, then place your thumb and finger in a C shape a few centimetres behind the nipple, press back toward the chest, then compress and release rhythmically.
**Pumps:** manual or electric. Clean all parts thoroughly after each use.

**Storing milk:** use clean containers, label them with the date, and refrigerate at the back of the fridge, not the door. Freshly expressed milk keeps for only a few hours at room temperature, and less in hot weather. Ask your health provider for storage guidance that fits your fridge and climate.
**Warming:** stand the container in warm water. Don’t microwave it, since this creates hot spots.

blocks.p: Powdered formula isn’t sterile, and babies’ immune systems are immature, so preparation matters:

ol: Wash hands and clean the surface.
Wash and sterilise bottles, teats and caps, by boiling or using a steriliser.
Boil fresh water, then let it cool for no more than about 30 minutes, so it’s still at least 70°C. This kills bacteria in the powder.
Pour the water into the bottle first, then add the exact number of level scoops stated on the tin.
Shake well, cool quickly under running water, and test on your wrist.
Discard any formula left after a feed, and any made-up formula not used within two hours.

blocks.p: **Never** add extra powder or extra water. Too concentrated can dehydrate a baby; too dilute can leave them underfed. Don’t add sugar, honey, cereal or anything else.

ol: Hold your baby fairly upright, supporting the head.
Hold the bottle more horizontally so milk only just fills the teat.
Let the baby draw the teat into their mouth rather than pushing it in.
Pause every few minutes, tilting the bottle down to give a rest.
Watch for fullness cues: slowing down, turning away, relaxed hands. Don’t push them to finish the bottle.
If others feed your baby, ask them to follow the same approach.

ul: Exclusively breastfed babies under six months don’t need water, even in Pakistan’s summer heat. Breast milk is mostly water. Feed more often in hot weather instead.

Giving water, ghutti, gripe water, honey or sugar water to newborns can introduce infections, reduce breastfeeding, and in the case of honey, carry a risk of infant botulism. Honey should not be given before one year.
Formula-fed babies may need some cooled boiled water in hot weather; ask your doctor.

blocks.p: Many mothers start with one plan and end up with another, because of a baby’s health, low supply, pain, returning to work or personal circumstances. Grief, guilt, relief and frustration are common reactions. Whatever path you take, responsive feeding, holding your baby close and eye contact during feeds support bonding.

soon: Concerns about your baby’s weight gain or number of wet nappies
You want to increase your milk supply or reduce formula
Pain or difficulty with breastfeeding or expressing
You’re unsure how to prepare formula or which type to use
urgent: Your baby has fewer than six wet nappies a day after day five, very dark urine, a sunken soft spot or is very sleepy (possible dehydration)
Your baby refuses feeds, vomits repeatedly, or has a fever

blocks.p: In Pakistan, feeding choices are often a family matter. Some women feel pressure to breastfeed against difficulty; others are pressured to add formula or ghutti. Knowing the evidence and your options helps you make decisions with confidence, and lets you explain them to others.

takeaway: Exclusive breastfeeding for six months is the international recommendation, and mixed feeding, expressing and formula are all paths that can be done safely. Protect supply if you want to keep breastfeeding, prepare formula exactly as instructed with water boiled first, bottle-feed responsively, and avoid giving water, ghutti or honey to young babies.
prompt: What feeding path feels right for you at the moment, and what support would help you with it?

title: Breastfeeding: Expectations and Emotional Adjustment
description: Breastfeeding is natural, but it is also a skill that you and your baby learn together. This guide explains how milk is made and released, what happens to your body in the first hours, days and weeks, what colostrum is and why it matters, how a good latch works, what cluster feeding is, how to tell if your baby is getting enough, how to manage sore nipples, engorgement, blocked ducts and mastitis step by step, and when to seek help.
glance: Milk supply works on demand: the more often and effectively milk is removed, the more your body makes.
Colostrum, the first milk, comes in small amounts that match a newborn’s tiny stomach, and it’s rich in antibodies.
Mature milk usually “comes in” between days two and five, often with fullness and tenderness.
Feeding 8 to 12 or more times in 24 hours is normal. Wet and dirty nappies and weight gain are the best signs your baby is getting enough.

blocks.p: Breastfeeding relies on two hormones and a simple feedback system:

ul: **Prolactin** tells the milk-producing cells (alveoli) in your breasts to make milk. It rises every time your baby feeds or milk is removed. Levels are higher at night, which is one reason night feeds matter for supply in the early weeks.

**Oxytocin** causes the cells around the alveoli to squeeze milk into the ducts and toward the nipple. This is the **let-down reflex**. You may feel tingling, pressure or a sudden fullness, or you may notice your baby’s sucking change from quick sucks to slower, deeper swallows. Oxytocin is released more easily when you feel calm and comfortable, and pain, stress and embarrassment can slow it down.

**Supply and demand:** milk that stays in the breast sends a signal to slow production. Milk that is removed frequently signals the body to make more. This is why frequent, effective feeding builds supply, and why long gaps or skipped feeds can reduce it.

blocks.p: If you and your baby are well, holding your baby skin-to-skin straight after birth helps regulate their temperature, heart rate and blood sugar. Many babies, if left skin-to-skin, will search for the breast and begin feeding within the first hour. The WHO recommends starting breastfeeding within this first hour. After a caesarean, skin-to-skin and early feeding are usually still possible with help.

Colostrum is the first milk, usually thick and yellowish. It comes in small amounts, often only teaspoons per feed, and this is exactly right: on day one, a newborn’s stomach is roughly the size of a cherry or a marble. Colostrum:

ul: Is rich in antibodies and immune cells that help protect your baby from infection
Coats the baby’s gut, supporting healthy digestion
Helps your baby pass meconium (the first dark stools), which helps clear the substance that causes jaundice

blocks.p: Many families worry that “the milk hasn’t come yet” and want to give ghutti, honey, water or formula. Colostrum is enough for a healthy term baby. Prelacteal feeds can introduce infections and reduce the baby’s interest in the breast. Honey can cause infant botulism and should not be given before one year.

blocks.h: When milk comes in: days two to five

blocks.p: Around days two to five, milk volume increases significantly and changes to “transitional” milk, then gradually to mature milk over the next couple of weeks. You may notice:

ul: Breasts becoming fuller, heavier, warmer and firmer
Milk leaking
More swallowing sounds during feeds
Emotional changes, which often coincide with the baby blues

blocks.p: This can come later after a caesarean, a difficult birth, heavy blood loss or with some health conditions such as diabetes. Frequent feeding and skin-to-skin help.
A good latch is the foundation of comfortable, effective breastfeeding.

ol: **Get comfortable.** Sit or lie with your back supported. Use pillows to support your arms and the baby.
**Hold your baby close,** with their whole body facing you, and their head and body in a straight line.
**Nose to nipple.** Start with the baby’s nose level with your nipple, so they tilt their head back slightly to reach the breast.
**Wait for a wide mouth.** Brush your nipple against the baby’s upper lip until they open wide, like a yawn.
**Bring the baby to the breast,** not the breast to the baby, chin first.
**Aim for a deep latch:** the baby takes a large mouthful of breast, with more areola visible above the top lip than below the bottom lip.

blocks.p: **Signs of a good latch:**

ul: The baby’s chin touches the breast, and the nose is free
Lips are flanged outward
Cheeks are full and rounded, not sucked in
You hear or see swallowing
Feeding is comfortable after the first few seconds
The nipple looks rounded, not flattened or pinched, when it comes out

blocks.p: **If it hurts beyond the first few seconds,** slide a clean finger into the corner of the baby’s mouth to break the suction, and try again.

ul: **Cradle hold:** the baby lies across your lap, head in the crook of your arm.
**Cross-cradle hold:** you support the baby’s head with the hand opposite to the breast, which gives more control for newborns.
**Football (rugby) hold:** the baby is tucked under your arm along your side. Useful after a caesarean or with large breasts.
**Side-lying:** you and your baby lie facing each other. Helpful for night feeds and recovery.
**Laid-back:** you recline and place the baby on your chest, letting them find the breast.
**8 to 12 or more feeds in 24 hours** is normal in the early weeks, counted from the start of one feed to the start of the next.
**Feeds vary in length,** from 10 minutes to 40 minutes or more.
**Offer both breasts** at each feed, letting the baby finish the first before offering the second.
**Watch the baby, not the clock.** Feed when you see early cues: stirring, rooting, sucking on hands. Crying is a late cue.
**Sleepy newborns,** especially if jaundiced, may need waking for feeds. Ask your doctor or midwife how often.

blocks.p: Cluster feeding is when a baby feeds very frequently, sometimes almost continuously, for a few hours, often in the evening. It’s common in the early weeks and during growth spurts. It doesn’t mean you don’t have enough milk. It’s how babies increase supply and fill up before a longer sleep. Prepare for it by keeping water, snacks and something to watch or listen to nearby, and asking someone else to handle cooking and visitors in the evenings.
These signs are more reliable than how full your breasts feel or how long feeds last:

ul: **Wet nappies:** increasing daily in the first days, then at least six heavy wet nappies a day from around day five, with pale yellow urine.
**Dirty nappies:** meconium in the first days, changing to greenish, then yellow, seedy stools by around day five. In the first weeks, many babies have at least two yellow stools a day.
**Weight:** most babies lose some weight in the first days, then start gaining and are usually back to birth weight by around two weeks. Your doctor or Lady Health Visitor will check this.
**Feeding behaviour:** audible swallowing, the baby seeming content after most feeds, and coming off the breast on their own.
**Alertness:** your baby is awake and alert at times, with good skin colour and tone.

blocks.h: Common difficulties and what to do

blocks.p: **Sore or cracked nipples**
Some tenderness in the first days is common, but pain that lasts throughout feeds, or cracked, bleeding nipples, usually means the latch needs adjusting.

ol: Check the latch and try a different position.
Start on the less sore side.
After feeds, express a little milk and let it dry on the nipple.
Let nipples air-dry and change damp breast pads.
Get help from a breastfeeding supporter. Persistent pain may also be caused by tongue-tie or infection, which a doctor can assess.

blocks.p: **Engorgement**
When milk comes in, breasts can become very full, hard, swollen and painful, making it harder for the baby to latch.

ol: Feed frequently, at least 8 to 12 times a day.
If breasts are too firm to latch, hand-express a little milk first to soften the areola.
Try reverse pressure softening: press gently around the areola with your fingertips for a minute to push swelling back.
Use cold compresses between feeds to reduce swelling.
Wear a supportive but not tight bra.

blocks.p: Engorgement usually eases within 24 to 48 hours as supply adjusts.
**Blocked ducts**
A tender, firm lump in the breast, sometimes with redness, caused by inflammation and narrowing in an area of the breast.

ol: Keep feeding normally from that breast.
Avoid deep, aggressive massage, which can increase inflammation. Use gentle, light strokes toward the armpit instead.
Use cold compresses for comfort.
Check that bras and clothing aren’t pressing on the breast.
Rest and drink fluids.

blocks.p: If it doesn’t improve within a day or two, or you develop fever, see a doctor.
**Mastitis**

Inflammation of the breast, sometimes with infection, causing a red, hot, painful area, often with flu-like symptoms, fever and chills. Continue breastfeeding, rest, drink fluids and see a doctor promptly, since treatment may be needed.
**Low supply worries**

Many mothers worry about supply, but most produce enough when feeding is frequent and effective. True low supply can occur, for example after heavy blood loss, with some hormonal conditions, or when feeds are limited. See the guide on managing feeding-related stress, and get support early.
**A sleepy baby or difficult latch**
Skin-to-skin, undressing the baby down to a nappy, switching sides, breast compression (gently squeezing the breast during feeds), and hand expressing into the baby’s mouth can help. Get help early.

ul: Create a feeding spot with good back support, pillows, water, snacks and your phone.
Wear front-opening or side-zip clothing and a large dupatta for privacy.
Ask family to give you privacy and calm during feeds.
Eat regularly and drink to thirst.
Rest when you can.

myth: “Small breasts make less milk.”
Breast size reflects fatty tissue, not the glandular tissue that makes milk.
“Your milk is thin or weak.”
Breast milk can look watery at the start of a feed and creamier later. This is normal and nutritious.
“If the baby feeds often, you don’t have enough milk.”
Frequent feeding is normal and builds supply.
“You must avoid certain foods.”
Most mothers can eat a normal varied diet. If you notice a pattern of fussiness after a particular food, discuss it with your doctor.
“Breastfeeding should hurt.”
Early tenderness is common, but ongoing pain is a sign that something needs adjusting.

soon: Pain that continues throughout feeds, or cracked, bleeding nipples
Engorgement that isn’t improving after 48 hours
A lump that doesn’t improve within one to two days
Concerns about your baby’s weight gain, feeding or nappies
Your baby seems unsettled after most feeds, or feeds continuously for hours every day
urgent: Red, hot, painful breast with fever, chills or flu-like symptoms
Your baby has fewer than six wet nappies a day after day five, dark urine, a dry mouth, a sunken soft spot, or is very sleepy and hard to wake
Yellow skin in the first 24 hours, or jaundice that is spreading with poor feeding
Your baby refuses feeds or has a fever

blocks.p: Breastfeeding can bring deep closeness, pride and calm. It can also bring frustration, pain, exhaustion and doubt, especially in the first weeks and when family members question your milk. Many women feel they’ve failed if breastfeeding is hard. Difficulties are common, they’re not a sign of failure, and most can be improved with skilled help. Whatever happens, your worth as a mother isn’t measured in millilitres.

takeaway: Breastfeeding works on supply and demand, starting with small amounts of protective colostrum and building as milk comes in around days two to five. A deep latch, frequent feeding and watching nappies and weight are the keys. Most difficulties, including sore nipples, engorgement and blocked ducts, can be improved, and mastitis with fever or a baby who isn’t feeding well needs prompt care.
prompt: What do you wish you’d known about breastfeeding before you started, and what support would help you most now?

title: Managing Feeding-Related Stress
description: Feeding a baby is often the biggest source of stress in the early months: worries about supply, painful feeds, conflicting advice, family comments about your milk, and pressure to feed a certain way. This guide explains why feeding stress is so common, the most frequent worries and what usually lies behind them, how to check objectively whether feeding is going well, how to respond to family pressure, and how to reduce stress around feeding.
glance: Most worries about supply come from normal newborn behaviour, such as frequent feeding, cluster feeding and soft breasts after the first weeks.
Wet and dirty nappies and weight gain are the most reliable signs of adequate feeding.
Growth spurts, often around two to three weeks, six weeks and three months, temporarily increase feeding.
Stress doesn’t directly stop milk production, but it can slow let-down. Feeling calm and supported helps.

blocks.h: Why feeding stress is so common

ul: You can’t see how much milk your baby gets.
Feeding feels like a measure of whether you’re a good mother.
Newborn feeding patterns are irregular and often frequent.
Family members may have strong opinions based on their own experiences.
Pain, exhaustion and recovery make everything harder.
Social media often shows idealised feeding.

blocks.h: Common worries and what usually lies behind them

ul: **“The baby wants to feed all the time.”** Frequent feeding and cluster feeding are normal, especially in the evening and during growth spurts.
**“My breasts feel soft now.”** After the first few weeks, supply adjusts to the baby’s needs and breasts often feel softer. This doesn’t mean supply has dropped.
**“My milk looks thin.”** Milk at the start of a feed is more watery, and becomes creamier as the feed continues.
**“The baby cries after feeds.”** Crying can be due to wind, tiredness, overstimulation or wanting closeness, not necessarily hunger.
**“I can’t pump much.”** Pumping output isn’t a reliable measure of supply. Babies are usually more efficient than pumps.
**“The baby fed for only five minutes.”** Some babies feed efficiently and quickly.
**Nappies:** at least six heavy wet nappies a day after day five, and regular yellow stools in the early weeks.
**Weight:** back to birth weight by around two weeks, then gaining steadily.
**Behaviour:** alert periods, good skin colour, and content after most feeds.

blocks.p: If these are on track, feeding is likely going well.

ul: **“Your milk isn’t enough, give the baby formula.”** “The doctor checked the baby’s weight and nappies, and they’re fine.”
**“Give the baby ghutti or water.”** “The doctor advised only breast milk for the first six months, even in summer.”
**“You’re feeding too often.”** “Frequent feeding is normal for newborns and helps build milk.”
**“Don’t breastfeed in front of people.”** “I’ll feed in a quiet room.”

blocks.p: Ask your husband or doctor to support you in these conversations.
Babies often feed more frequently for a few days during growth spurts, commonly around two to three weeks, six weeks and three months. Supply adjusts within a few days.

ol: Focus on nappies and weight rather than feed length or breast fullness.
Create a calm, comfortable feeding space.
Limit people who comment on your feeding.
Get help early with pain or latch problems.
Rest and eat regularly.
Remember that feeding becomes easier for most mothers by six to eight weeks.

soon: Concerns about your baby’s weight gain, nappies or feeding
Pain during feeds
Feeling anxious about feeding most of the time
urgent: Signs of dehydration in your baby: fewer wet nappies, dark urine, dry mouth, sunken soft spot, very sleepy
Your baby refuses feeds or has a fever

blocks.p: Feeding stress can make you feel judged, anxious and inadequate. Many mothers feel their worth is tied to feeding success. Feeding is one part of caring for your baby, and support makes a real difference.

takeaway: Most feeding worries come from normal newborn behaviour. Use nappies and weight to check how feeding is going, expect growth spurts, respond to family pressure with facts, and get help early with pain or latch problems.
prompt: Which feeding worry comes up most often for you, and what objective sign could reassure you?

title: Understanding Your Baby's Crying
description: Crying is your baby’s main way of communicating, and in the first months it can be intense, frequent and hard to interpret. This guide explains why babies cry, the normal pattern of crying in the first three months, how to work through possible causes, specific soothing techniques, what colic is, how to cope when the crying won’t stop, and which cries signal illness.
glance: Crying often increases from around two weeks, peaks around six to eight weeks, and usually reduces by three to four months.
Common causes include hunger, wind, tiredness, overstimulation, discomfort, and wanting to be held.
Some babies cry for long periods even when nothing is wrong. This is often described as colic.
Never shake a baby. If you feel overwhelmed, put your baby down safely and step away for a few minutes.

blocks.p: Crying is how babies tell you they need something. It’s a survival mechanism designed to make adults respond. In the first weeks, babies have limited ways to settle themselves, and their nervous systems are still developing, so they rely on you.

Many babies cry more from around two weeks of age, with a peak around six to eight weeks, often in the late afternoon and evening. Crying usually becomes less frequent by three to four months. Knowing this pattern can help you feel less alarmed during the peak.

ol: **Hunger:** offer a feed, especially if it’s been a while or you see feeding cues.
**Wind:** try burping, or holding your baby upright.
**Nappy:** check if it’s wet or dirty.
**Temperature:** check the back of the neck or chest for overheating or coldness.
**Tiredness:** newborns tire quickly. Look for yawning, staring, or jerky movements.
**Overstimulation:** too much noise, light, handling or visitors.
**Wanting closeness:** many babies settle when held, rocked or carried.
**Discomfort:** tight clothing, a hair wrapped around a toe, or illness.

ul: **Swaddling:** wrap your baby snugly in a light cloth, leaving room for hips and legs to bend. Stop swaddling once your baby starts trying to roll.
**Holding on the side or tummy:** hold your baby on their side or tummy in your arms to calm them, then place them on their back to sleep.
**Shushing:** a steady “shhh” sound or white noise.
**Rocking or swaying:** gentle, rhythmic movement.
**Sucking:** feeding, or a clean finger or dummy.
**Skin-to-skin contact.**
**A change of scene:** a walk outside or in another room.
**Warm bath,** if your baby enjoys it.

blocks.p: Colic is often described as crying for more than three hours a day, more than three days a week, for at least three weeks, in an otherwise healthy, feeding and growing baby. The cause isn’t fully understood. It usually improves by three to four months. Remedies such as gripe water, ghutti or herbal mixtures haven’t been proven to help, and some can be harmful. Ask your doctor before giving anything.
Persistent crying is one of the hardest parts of early parenthood.

ol: Make sure your baby is safe, fed, clean and comfortable.
If you feel overwhelmed or angry, put your baby down on their back in a safe place, such as their cot, and step away for a few minutes.
Take slow breaths, drink water, or call someone.
Return when you feel calmer.
Share the load: take turns with your husband or family.

blocks.p: **Never shake a baby.** Shaking can cause serious brain injury or death.
Seek medical advice if your baby’s cry sounds different, such as high-pitched, weak or moaning, or if crying comes with other symptoms.

soon: Crying that seems excessive or unusual for your baby
Crying with poor feeding, poor weight gain or frequent vomiting
You’re struggling to cope with the crying
urgent: A high-pitched, weak or moaning cry
Crying with fever, difficulty breathing, green vomit, a bulging soft spot, or a rash that doesn’t fade under pressure
Your baby is very sleepy, floppy or hard to wake
You feel you might harm your baby

blocks.p: Constant crying can make you feel helpless, frustrated or like a failure. These feelings are common. Crying isn’t a sign that you’re doing something wrong. Asking for help and taking breaks are important for you and your baby.

takeaway: Crying is your baby’s way of communicating, and it often peaks around six to eight weeks. Work through possible causes, try soothing techniques, and take breaks when you need to. Never shake a baby, and seek help if crying sounds unusual or comes with signs of illness.
prompt: Which soothing technique seems to work best for your baby, and who could help you during the hardest hours?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Bonding With Your Baby
description: Bonding is the emotional connection that grows between you and your baby through everyday moments of care: feeding, holding, eye contact, talking and responding. This guide explains what bonding and attachment actually are, the biology behind them, what your newborn can see, hear and recognise, specific ways to build connection week by week, how fathers and family can bond, and why you don’t need to be perfect.
glance: Bonding usually develops over weeks and months through repeated care, not in a single moment.
Newborns see most clearly at about 20 to 30 cm, roughly the distance to your face during a feed, and they already recognise your voice and smell.
Responding to your baby’s sounds and expressions, sometimes called “serve and return”, helps build the brain connections for communication and emotional security.
Babies don’t need perfect parents. Researchers find that responding well much of the time, and repairing after missed moments, is what supports secure attachment.

blocks.h: Bonding and attachment: what’s the difference?

ul: **Bonding** describes your feelings toward your baby: love, protectiveness, tenderness and connection.

**Attachment** describes your baby’s developing relationship with you. When a baby’s needs are met reliably, they come to trust that you’ll comfort and protect them. This sense of security supports their emotional development, confidence and later relationships.

blocks.p: Both grow from the same everyday interactions.

ul: **Oxytocin** is released during touch, skin-to-skin contact, feeding and gazing at your baby. It’s associated with feelings of calm, trust and closeness, in both mothers and fathers.
**Your baby’s stress system** is still developing. When you soothe your baby, you help regulate their heart rate, breathing and stress hormones. Over time, this helps them learn to calm themselves.
**Your brain adapts:** research shows parents’ brains change in response to caring for a baby, becoming more attuned to the baby’s cues.
**See:** newborns see best at about 20 to 30 cm and are drawn to faces, especially eyes, and to high-contrast patterns. Their vision develops rapidly over the first months.
**Hear:** your baby has heard your voice from inside the womb and often turns toward it. Babies tend to prefer higher-pitched, sing-song speech.
**Smell:** within days, babies can recognise their mother’s smell.
**Feel:** skin-to-skin contact and gentle touch calm babies.
**Communicate:** through crying, facial expressions, movements and, within weeks, cooing. Many babies begin social smiling around six to eight weeks.

blocks.p: **In the first days:**

ul: Skin-to-skin contact: hold your baby wearing only a nappy against your bare chest, covered with a blanket.
Breastfeeding or holding your baby close during bottle feeds.
Looking at your baby’s face and letting them look at yours.

blocks.p: **In the first weeks:**

ul: Talk to your baby during care: “Now I’m changing your nappy... now your clean clothes.”
Sing lullabies, nursery rhymes, naats or recitation, in your own language.
Respond to cues: notice when your baby is hungry, tired or wants closeness.
Carry your baby close in your arms or a carrier.

blocks.p: **From about six weeks:**

ul: Respond to smiles and coos with your own, and wait for your baby to respond back.
Copy your baby’s sounds and expressions.
Play simple face-to-face games during alert times.

blocks.p: When your baby “serves” with a sound, look or movement, and you “return” with a smile, words or touch, you’re having a conversation. These exchanges, repeated thousands of times, help build the brain pathways for language, emotional understanding and relationships. You don’t need special toys or programmes; everyday interaction is enough.
Gentle massage can be a calm way to connect. Massaging babies with oil is a long tradition in Pakistan.

ul: Choose a quiet time when your baby is awake and content, not right after a feed.
If you use oil, choose a plain, gentle oil, test it on a small patch of skin first, and avoid the nose, ears and eyes.
