Use slow, gentle strokes, and stop if your baby seems unhappy.
Wash your hands first and keep the room warm.

blocks.p: Bonding isn’t only for mothers. Fathers, grandparents and siblings can build connection through:

ul: Skin-to-skin contact
Bathing, changing, dressing and settling
Carrying, rocking and walking with the baby
Talking, singing and reading
Taking a regular “shift” of care

blocks.p: When a husband takes an active role in care, it can support the mother’s rest and the baby’s relationships.

blocks.h: You don’t need to be perfect

blocks.p: Responding well much of the time, noticing when you’ve missed a cue, and reconnecting is what helps babies feel secure. Every parent sometimes misreads cues, gets frustrated or needs a break. Repair, coming back and comforting, is part of building trust.

soon: You feel disconnected or numb toward your baby for several weeks
Low mood or anxiety most days for two weeks or more
Your baby rarely makes eye contact or responds to sounds over the first few months (mention this at check-ups)
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby

blocks.p: Some mothers feel a rush of love immediately; others feel it grow over weeks or months. Both are normal. If bonding feels slow, see the guide on when bonding takes time.

takeaway: Bonding grows through everyday care: skin-to-skin, eye contact, talking, singing and responding to cues. Newborns already know your voice and smell, and back-and-forth “serve and return” interaction helps build their brains. You don’t need to be perfect; responding much of the time and repairing missed moments is enough.
prompt: When does your baby seem most alert and interested in your face, and how could you use that time for connection?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: When Bonding Takes Time
description: Not every mother feels an instant rush of love. For many, the feeling grows gradually over weeks or months, especially after a difficult birth, a NICU stay, depression, exhaustion or a hard start to feeding. This guide explains why bonding can take time, why loving actions can come before loving feelings, practical steps to nurture connection, how depression can affect bonding, and when it’s time to seek help.
glance: Delayed bonding is common and doesn’t predict how close you’ll be to your child in the long term.
A traumatic birth, separation, depression, anxiety, exhaustion, pain and family pressure can all slow bonding.
You don’t need to feel love to give loving care. Consistent care often leads the feelings to follow.
Feeling persistently numb, resentful or detached can be a symptom of postpartum depression, which is treatable.

ul: **A difficult or traumatic birth:** if you were frightened, in severe pain or had an emergency, your mind may be focused on processing what happened.
**Separation:** if your baby was in the NICU, or you were unwell, early contact may have been limited.
**Exhaustion and pain:** recovering from birth while caring for a baby leaves little emotional energy.
**Postpartum depression or anxiety:** can cause numbness, worry or difficulty feeling joy.
**Feeding difficulties:** pain or worry about feeding can make feeds feel stressful rather than connecting.
**Your circumstances:** an unplanned pregnancy, money worries, relationship problems or family conflict.
**Family pressure:** disappointment about the baby’s sex, or relatives taking over care, can leave you feeling sidelined.
**Your own history:** if your own childhood was difficult, becoming a mother can bring up complicated feelings.
**Unrealistic expectations:** expecting instant love can make gradual feelings seem like a problem.

blocks.h: What delayed bonding can feel like

ul: Feeling like you’re caring for someone else’s baby
Going through the motions without feeling much
Feeling irritated or resentful at times
Feeling guilty that you don’t feel what others seem to feel
Feeling closer on some days than others

blocks.p: Loving actions build connection, even when feelings are slow. Feeding, holding, comforting, talking and responding to your baby are all part of bonding. Your baby benefits from your care, regardless of how you feel in the moment, and many mothers find feelings grow as they keep caring.

ol: **Skin-to-skin contact:** spend time each day with your baby against your bare chest. This can help both of you feel calmer.
**Quiet time together:** away from visitors and noise, even for 10 minutes.
**Look and notice:** watch your baby’s expressions, hands and movements. Notice one new thing about them each day.
**Talk or sing:** even if it feels awkward at first.
**Do some care yourself:** if relatives are doing most of the care, ask to do some feeds, baths or settling yourself.
**Rest:** exhaustion makes connection harder.
**Talk to someone:** share how you feel with a trusted person or professional.
**Process the birth:** if your birth was difficult, a birth debrief or counselling may help.

ul: Ask the NICU team about skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care) and how you can be involved in care.
Express milk if you’re planning to breastfeed; it can be a way to feel connected.
Talk to staff about your baby’s progress.
Expect bonding to continue to grow once you’re home.

blocks.p: Talk to your doctor if:

ul: You feel disconnected, numb or resentful most of the time for several weeks
You have persistent low mood, anxiety or loss of interest
You have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
You feel your baby would be better off without you

blocks.p: These can be symptoms of postpartum depression or anxiety, which are treatable. Treatment often helps bonding improve too.

soon: Persistent disconnection, numbness or resentment toward your baby
Persistent low mood or anxiety for two weeks or more
Flashbacks or nightmares about the birth
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
Feeling your baby would be better off without you

blocks.p: Many mothers feel deep shame when bonding is slow, and keep it secret. Delayed bonding is common and doesn’t make you a bad mother. Talking about it is often the first step to feeling closer.

takeaway: Bonding can take time, especially after a difficult start. Keep providing loving care, spend quiet skin-to-skin time with your baby, and talk to someone you trust. If disconnection or low mood persists, it may be postpartum depression, which is treatable.
prompt: What has made it harder to feel close to your baby, and what is one small step that might help?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Adjusting to Newborn Sleep Patterns
description: Newborn sleep is nothing like adult sleep: short cycles, lots of noisy “active” sleep, no sense of day and night, and frequent waking to feed. This guide explains how newborn sleep works and changes over the first months, how to read sleep cues and use short awake windows, how to help your baby learn day from night, safe sleep essentials, and what isn’t realistic yet.
glance: Newborns often sleep around 14 to 17 hours in 24 hours, but in short stretches spread across day and night.
Newborns spend a lot of time in light, active sleep: twitching, grunting and even opening their eyes. Pause before picking them up.
Babies don’t develop a day-night rhythm until around two to four months. Bright days and dim, quiet nights help it develop.
Always place your baby on their back to sleep, on a firm, flat surface, with nothing else in the sleep space.

ul: **Total sleep:** newborns often sleep 14 to 17 hours in 24 hours, but it varies widely between babies.
**Short stretches:** usually one to three hours at a time, because they need frequent feeds.
**Short sleep cycles:** around 40 to 60 minutes, compared with about 90 minutes in adults.

**Active sleep:** newborns spend about half their sleep in active (REM-like) sleep. They may twitch, grunt, smile, make sucking movements, breathe irregularly or briefly open their eyes. This is normal. Many parents pick up a baby who would have settled alone, so it can help to watch and wait a moment.
**Quiet sleep:** deeper sleep with regular breathing and little movement.

blocks.p: In the womb, your movements during the day often rocked your baby to sleep, so many newborns are more wakeful at night. The body clock that tells us to sleep at night develops over the first few months. You can help it develop:

ul: **During the day:** open curtains, keep normal household sounds, take your baby outside, talk and play during awake times.
**During the night:** keep lights dim, voices soft, interaction minimal. Change nappies only when needed.

blocks.p: Newborns can only stay awake comfortably for short periods, often around 45 to 60 minutes including feeding in the first weeks, gradually increasing.

ul: **Early sleepy cues:** staring into space, slower movements, quietening, yawning.
**Later cues:** rubbing eyes, pulling ears, jerky movements, fussing.
**Overtired:** crying, arching, difficulty settling.

blocks.p: Responding to early cues often makes settling easier.

ul: Feeding, rocking, holding, shushing, swaddling (with hips free) and white noise can all help.
In the early weeks, it’s normal and safe for babies to fall asleep while feeding or being held. You can’t spoil a newborn.
Some parents try placing the baby down drowsy but awake sometimes. It may or may not work in the early weeks, and that’s fine.
**Back to sleep:** place your baby on their back for every sleep, including naps.
**Firm, flat surface:** a cot, crib or basket with a firm, flat mattress.
**Clear sleep space:** no pillows, bumpers, soft toys, loose blankets or quilts.
**Room-share:** keep your baby in the same room as you for the first six months.
**Avoid overheating:** dress the baby appropriately for the room temperature, keep their head uncovered, and avoid heavy blankets.
**Never sleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair.**
**No smoking** around your baby.
**Bed-sharing** carries higher risks, especially if anyone in the bed smokes, has taken alcohol or drowsy medication, if the baby was premature or small, or if you’re extremely tired.

blocks.h: How sleep changes over the first months

ul: **Weeks 0 to 6:** short stretches, frequent feeds, day-night confusion.
**Weeks 6 to 12:** longer awake periods, more distinct night sleep, often one longer stretch at night.
**Months 3 to 4:** more regular patterns emerge for many babies, though night waking for feeds is still common.
Sleeping through the night
Following a strict schedule
Sleep training (generally not recommended for babies under around six months)

soon: Your baby is very difficult to wake for feeds, or sleeps much more than usual
Snoring, pauses in breathing, or noisy breathing during sleep
Concerns about weight gain alongside sleepiness
urgent: Breathing difficulties, blue or grey colour, or pauses in breathing
Your baby is floppy, unusually sleepy or hard to wake
Fever with sleepiness

blocks.p: Comments like “Does the baby sleep through the night yet?” can make you feel you’re doing something wrong. Frequent waking is biologically normal in the early months. Your baby’s sleep doesn’t measure your parenting.

takeaway: Newborn sleep is short, light and not yet organised by day and night. Watch for early sleep cues, keep days bright and nights dim, expect frequent waking, and always follow safe sleep guidance.
prompt: What pattern have you noticed in your baby’s sleep, and what could you adjust to make nights calmer?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Building a Flexible Daily Routine
description: Strict schedules rarely work with a newborn, but a flexible daily rhythm can bring predictability, calm and a sense of control. This guide explains the difference between a schedule and a rhythm, how to build a gentle “feed, awake, sleep” flow around your baby’s cues, which daily anchors help, what a sample day might look like at different ages, and how to fit your own needs and a busy household into the day.
glance: Newborns can’t follow a clock, but they benefit from activities happening in a predictable order.
A common rhythm is feed, then a short awake time, then sleep, repeated through the day.
Anchors such as a morning wake-up, a daily walk and a bedtime routine add structure without rigid timing.
A good routine includes your meals, rest and personal time, not just the baby’s.

ul: **A schedule** sets activities at fixed times: feed at 9, sleep at 10. In the early weeks, this usually conflicts with a baby’s hunger and sleep cues, and can interfere with breastfeeding, which depends on feeding responsively.
**A rhythm** sets activities in a predictable order, guided by your baby’s cues. Times shift from day to day, but the sequence stays similar.

blocks.p: Rhythms give babies a sense of predictability and give you a framework, while staying flexible.

blocks.h: The basic flow: feed, awake, sleep

ol: **Feed** when your baby shows early hunger cues.
**Awake time** after the feed: change the nappy, cuddle, talk, look at faces, and give some supervised tummy time when your baby is alert.
**Sleep** when you see early sleepy cues, such as staring, quietening or yawning.
**Your time** while the baby sleeps: eat, drink, rest, or do something for yourself.

blocks.p: This flow isn’t a rule. Many newborns fall asleep while feeding, especially in the first weeks, and that’s fine. As babies grow, they naturally stay awake a little longer after feeds.
Anchors are a few consistent moments that frame the day:

ul: **Morning start:** around the same time each day, open the curtains, change your baby’s clothes, and say “good morning”. This signals the start of the day.
**Daylight time:** a short walk outdoors, time on a balcony or near a window. Daylight helps your baby’s body clock and your mood.
**Afternoon calm:** a quieter time if your baby gets fussy in the late afternoon or evening.

**Bedtime routine:** a short, calm sequence each evening, such as a warm wash or bath, a change into night clothes, a feed in dim light, a lullaby or recitation, then sleep. From around six to eight weeks, a consistent bedtime routine can help babies settle.

blocks.h: A sample day at different ages

blocks.p: These are examples, not targets.
**Around 2 weeks:**

ul: Feeds every two to three hours, day and night
Awake time often only enough for a feed and nappy change
Lots of sleep, often in short stretches

blocks.p: **Around 8 weeks:**

ul: Feeds every two to four hours
Awake times of around an hour or a little more
Several naps, and often one longer stretch at night

blocks.p: **Around 4 months:**

ul: More predictable feeds and naps for many babies
Longer awake periods with play
A clearer bedtime and morning wake time

blocks.p: Your routine should keep you going too:

ul: **Meals:** eat at regular times, ideally when someone else can hold the baby, or keep easy snacks within reach.
**Water:** a glass at every feed.
**Rest:** at least one daily rest while someone else watches the baby.
**Personal care:** a daily shower, getting dressed, brushing hair.
**Something for you:** prayer, a short call with a friend, a few pages of a book.

blocks.p: In joint families or busy homes, the day may revolve around meal times, prayer times, guests, and other people’s schedules.

ul: Share your baby’s rhythm with the family, especially naps and bedtime.
Agree on quiet times, for example lower volume TV during naps.
Ask for help at the busiest times, such as when meals are being prepared.
Keep visits to times that suit your baby’s rhythm when possible.

blocks.p: Growth spurts, illness, vaccinations, travel, weddings and visitors can disrupt any rhythm. This is normal. Return to your usual pattern gradually once things settle.

soon: Concerns about your baby’s feeding, weight gain or sleep
Feeling anxious when the day doesn’t go to plan
urgent: Newborn danger signs, such as poor feeding, fever, breathing difficulty or unusual sleepiness

blocks.p: Routines can make days feel calmer and more manageable. But trying to force a strict schedule can increase stress and make you feel like you’re failing. Aim for predictability, not perfection.

takeaway: Use a flexible rhythm of feeding, awake time and sleep guided by your baby’s cues, add a few daily anchors such as a morning start, daylight and a bedtime routine, and build your own meals, rest and personal time into the day.
prompt: Which daily anchor would make the biggest difference to how your day feels?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Coping With the Demands of Newborn Care
description: Caring for a newborn means a constant stream of tasks: feeding, changing, burping, settling, washing and watching, often while you’re healing and sleeping in fragments. This guide makes the real workload visible, explains why it’s so draining, and offers practical ways to share tasks, set up your home to save effort, handle the feeling of being “touched out”, and recognise when it’s too much.
glance: A newborn may need 8 to 12 feeds and 6 to 10 or more nappy changes a day, plus burping, settling, clothes changes and laundry.
Feeding alone can take many hours a day in the early weeks.
The physical workload is matched by a mental load of tracking, planning and worrying.
Feeling “touched out”, overwhelmed by constant physical contact, is common and doesn’t mean you love your baby less.

blocks.p: In a typical 24 hours with a newborn:

ul: **Feeding:** 8 to 12 or more feeds, each 10 to 40 minutes or longer
**Nappy changes:** 6 to 10 or more
**Burping and settling:** after many feeds, sometimes taking as long as the feed
**Clothes changes:** after spit-up, leaks and nappy accidents
**Laundry:** clothes, cloths, blankets and sometimes cloth nappies
**Bathing and cleaning**
**Comforting crying**
**Monitoring:** checking temperature, breathing, nappies and feeding
**Your own care:** eating, drinking, showering, healing

blocks.p: This adds up to most of the day and part of the night. When people ask, “What do you do all day?”, this is the answer.

ul: **It never stops:** unlike most work, there are no fixed breaks.
**It’s repetitive:** the same tasks over and over, which can feel monotonous.
**It’s urgent:** a crying baby demands immediate response.
**You’re healing:** physical recovery uses energy.
**You’re sleep-deprived.**
**The mental load:** tracking feeds, nappies, appointments and supplies.

blocks.p: Even if you’re breastfeeding, almost every other task can be shared:

ul: **Nappy changes** day and night
**Burping and settling** after feeds
**Bathing and dressing**
**Laundry,** including baby clothes
**Bringing you water and snacks** during feeds
**Holding the baby** while you eat, shower or rest
**Tracking supplies** and buying nappies, wipes and other essentials

blocks.p: Share specific tasks with your husband and family, and agree on times. For example: “You do the 10 p.m. nappy change and settling every night.”

blocks.h: Setting up your home to save effort

ul: **Feeding station:** a comfortable chair or bed spot with pillows, water, snacks, phone charger, muslin cloths and burp cloths.
**Changing stations:** a changing mat, nappies, cloths, water and a change of clothes in the room you use most, and a smaller kit in another room.
**Night kit:** a dim light, nappies, cloths and spare clothes near where you sleep.
**Laundry system:** a basket for baby laundry, washed every day or two.
**Supply list:** a shared note on your phone listing what’s running low.

blocks.p: After hours of holding, feeding and being needed, many mothers feel overwhelmed by physical contact and want space, even from their husband or older children. This is common and doesn’t mean you love your baby less.

ul: Take short breaks when someone else can hold the baby, even 10 to 15 minutes alone.
Let your husband know you may need space at times.
Do something that feels like yours: a shower, a short walk, time with a book.

blocks.p: Signs the load may be too much:

ul: Feeling overwhelmed most days
Resentment or irritability that’s hard to manage
Exhaustion that doesn’t improve
Low mood or anxiety
Feeling detached from your baby

blocks.p: Ask for more help, reduce other demands, and talk to your doctor if these feelings persist.

soon: Feeling overwhelmed, exhausted or detached most days for two weeks or more
No one available to share care
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
Feeling you can’t keep your baby safe

blocks.p: Newborn care is important, demanding work that often goes unrecognised. You may feel invisible or undervalued, especially if others focus on the baby and not on you. Your work and your needs matter.

takeaway: Newborn care is a full-time job of feeding, changing, settling and watching. Make the workload visible, share specific tasks, set up care stations to save effort, take breaks when you feel touched out, and get support if you’re overwhelmed.
prompt: If you wrote down every task you did yesterday, which one could someone else take over starting today?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Adjusting to Your New Identity as a Mother
description: Becoming a mother changes how you see yourself, how others see you, and what you value, a transition researchers call matrescence. This guide explains what shifts in your identity and why, why the transition can feel disorienting, how culture and family shape the experience in Pakistan, and practical ways to integrate your new role with the person you’ve always been.
glance: Matrescence is the transition into motherhood. Like adolescence, it involves physical, emotional, social and identity changes, and it takes time.
Ambivalence, feeling love and loss at the same time, is a normal part of this transition.
Your identity as a mother adds to who you are; it doesn’t have to replace it.
Family roles and expectations in Pakistan can shape how you see yourself as a mother.

blocks.p: The anthropologist Dana Raphael used the term matrescence in the 1970s to describe the process of becoming a mother, and the idea has since been developed by psychologists. It recognises that becoming a mother is not just giving birth; it’s a developmental transition that unfolds over months and years.

ul: **Your priorities:** your baby’s needs come first for much of the time, and your values may shift.
**Your time:** you have less control over how you spend your days.
**Your body:** it may look, feel and function differently.
**Your relationships:** with your husband, parents, in-laws and friends.
**Your work or studies:** your ambitions may stay the same, change, or be paused.
**Your sense of self:** you may feel unsure who you are beyond being a mother.
**Speed:** the change happens quickly, without time to adjust.
**Loss:** of freedom, time, independence and parts of your old life.
**Ambivalence:** loving your baby while missing your old life.
**Invisibility:** others may focus on the baby and see you mainly as “the mother”.
**Expectations:** of what a good mother should be, from family, culture and social media.
**Respect and status:** becoming a mother, especially of a first child, often brings new status and respect.
**Expectations:** of sacrifice, selflessness and putting family first.
**Family roles:** your role may be shaped by elders’ expectations, particularly in joint families.
**Gender pressures:** pressure around having a son, or about your baby’s sex.
**Your mother’s influence:** you may reflect on how you were raised, and what you want to repeat or change.

ol: **Notice what you miss** and what you’d like to bring back, even in a small way.
**Keep some threads of your old life:** friendships, interests, faith practices, or work.
**Define your own version of motherhood,** rather than following someone else’s script.
**Talk to other mothers** about how their identities have changed.
**Be patient:** many mothers say it takes a year or more to feel settled in their new identity.
**Write about it:** “Before I became a mother, I was... Now I am... I want to be...”

soon: Feeling persistently lost, numb or unlike yourself
Persistent low mood or anxiety
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: It’s possible to love your baby deeply and still grieve the life you had before. Both can be true. Giving yourself permission to feel this mix can make the transition easier.

takeaway: Becoming a mother is a major identity transition, known as matrescence. Expect shifts in priorities, relationships and sense of self, allow ambivalence, keep threads of your old life, and give yourself time to find your own version of motherhood.
prompt: What part of who you were before motherhood would you most like to keep?

title: Missing Your Pre-Motherhood Life
description: Missing your life before motherhood, your sleep, freedom, work, friends, spontaneity or simply time alone, is common and does not mean you regret your baby. This guide explains why the feeling arises, how it relates to grief and ambivalence, how to tell normal longing from depression or burnout, why the feeling is often strongest in particular moments, and practical, realistic ways to reclaim pieces of your old life.
glance: Every major life change involves loss, even a wanted one. Missing your old life is part of adjusting.
Ambivalence, loving your baby while missing your freedom, is common and does not reduce your love.
The feeling is often sharpest at night, when friends post about their lives, or at family events where you can’t take part as before.
Persistent hopelessness, feeling trapped, or loss of all enjoyment may be depression, which is treatable.

ul: **Sleep and rest:** uninterrupted nights, lie-ins, naps when you choose.
**Freedom:** going out on impulse, visiting friends, shopping without planning around feeds.
**Time alone:** even a few minutes without being needed.
**Work or studies:** the structure, achievement, income, adult conversation and identity that came with them.
**Friendships:** easy contact with friends, especially those without children.
**Your body:** how it looked, felt or worked.
**Your marriage:** time as a couple, conversations that aren’t about the baby.
**Interests:** reading, cooking for pleasure, sport, art, faith practices you used to have time for.
**Your place in the family:** for example, being the daughter who was cared for, rather than the mother caring for others.

blocks.p: Psychologists who study life transitions note that change, even welcome change, involves leaving something behind. Becoming a mother changes your time, body, relationships and identity at once, and quickly. Missing your old life is how the mind registers the size of that change. It usually softens as you build a new rhythm and find ways to reconnect with what matters to you.

Ambivalence means holding two opposite feelings at once: “I love my baby” and “I miss my old life”. Many mothers feel both on the same day, sometimes in the same hour. In many cultures, including in Pakistan, there can be pressure to feel only gratitude, which makes ambivalence feel shameful. Researchers who study motherhood describe it as an ordinary part of the experience.

ul: **At night,** when you’re exhausted and others are asleep
**When scrolling social media** and seeing friends travelling, working or socialising
**At weddings and family gatherings,** where you spend the evening feeding in a back room
**When your husband leaves for work or goes out,** and your day looks the same as yesterday
**On anniversaries** of things you used to do

blocks.p: Noticing these patterns can help you plan small supports around them.

ul: **Normal longing:** comes and goes, coexists with moments of enjoyment, and eases as you adapt.
**Burnout:** you feel exhausted, detached and empty mainly in your parenting role, usually linked to too much load and too little support (see the guide on burnout).
**Depression:** persistent low mood, hopelessness, loss of interest in almost everything, feeling trapped, or thinking your family would be better off without you.

blocks.h: Reclaiming parts of your old life

ol: **Name what you miss most.** Be specific: not “my freedom” but “walking alone to the market” or “reading for an hour”.
**Find the smallest version.** A 20-minute walk, a chapter instead of a book, a video call instead of a visit, an online course module instead of a degree.
**Schedule it.** Put it in the week, and arrange childcare for it, even if only half an hour.
**Ask for help clearly:** “On Saturday mornings, could you take the baby for an hour so I can go for a walk?”
**Bring your baby along** where possible: visit friends with the baby, go to a park, attend a small gathering.
**Plan couple time:** tea together after the baby sleeps, a short walk, a weekly conversation not about the baby.
**Think longer-term:** many things you miss aren’t gone, just paused. Planning a return to work, study or travel in a year can make the present easier.

blocks.p: If social media makes you feel worse, try muting accounts that trigger longing, or limiting scrolling at night.

soon: Persistent low mood, hopelessness, or feeling trapped for two weeks or more
Loss of interest in almost everything, including things you used to enjoy
Exhaustion and detachment that don’t lift
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself
Feeling your family would be better off without you

blocks.p: Missing your old life can bring guilt, especially if others tell you how lucky you are. You can be grateful and still grieve. Many mothers find that as their baby grows and routines settle, they’re able to reclaim much of what they missed, often in new forms.

takeaway: Missing your pre-motherhood life is a normal response to a huge change, and it can coexist with deep love for your baby. Name what you miss, find the smallest version you can bring back, schedule it with help, and seek support if longing turns into persistent hopelessness.
prompt: What is the smallest version of something you miss that you could bring back this week?

title: Maintaining Your Relationship With Your Partner
description: A baby changes a marriage. Couples suddenly share less time, less sleep and more work, and differences in expectations can surface quickly. Research on couples becoming parents finds that many experience more conflict and lower satisfaction in the first years, and that couples who share the load and keep talking cope better. This guide explains why the relationship shifts, the most common flashpoints, how to divide work fairly, communicate under stress, stay connected in a joint family or when your husband works away, and recognise when a relationship is unhealthy.
glance: Many couples report more conflict and less satisfaction in the first year after a baby. This is common, not a sign your marriage is failing.
The biggest flashpoints are sleep, division of work, the mental load, feeling unappreciated, intimacy and family involvement.
Couples who share childcare and housework more fairly and keep up small daily connection tend to cope better.
If you feel afraid, controlled or hurt by your husband, that is not a normal adjustment, and help is available.

ul: **Less time and energy:** almost all of it goes to the baby, and to recovering.
**Sleep loss:** makes both of you more irritable and less patient.
**New roles:** you are now parents as well as husband and wife, and may have different ideas about what each role means.
**Workload:** in many households, mothers take on most of the childcare, housework and mental load, which can lead to resentment.
**Intimacy:** physical and emotional closeness often drop for a while.
**Family:** in Pakistan, both families may become more involved, sometimes helpfully, sometimes adding tension.
**Money:** a new baby can bring financial pressure.
“Why do I always get up at night?”
“You came home and went straight to your phone.”
“You don’t notice how much I do.”
“Your mother is criticising how I care for the baby.”
“We never talk anymore.”
Disagreements about feeding, sleep, visitors or how much to follow elders’ advice

ol: **Make the work visible.** List everything: feeds, nappies, night waking, cooking, cleaning, laundry, appointments, supplies, and the mental load of tracking it all.
**Divide areas, not just tasks.** For example, your husband owns bath time and evening settling, or he handles all paediatric appointments and vaccines.
**Plan nights together.** Even if you’re breastfeeding, he can change, burp and settle the baby, bring the baby to you, or take a shift so you can sleep.
**Account for work outside the home.** If he works long hours, agree on what he can realistically take on, such as nights at weekends or the first hour after he’s home.
**Review regularly.** What’s working? What isn’t?

ul: **Choose the moment:** important conversations go better when the baby is asleep and neither of you is hungry or exhausted.
**Start softly:** begin with how you feel rather than criticism. “I feel exhausted and alone at night” lands better than “You never help.”
**Be specific:** “Could you do the 11 p.m. nappy change and settling?” is clearer than “Help me more.”
**Listen to his experience:** he may feel shut out, unsure how to help, or under financial pressure.
**Repair:** after an argument, come back to it calmly. Apologising and reconnecting are part of healthy relationships.
**A daily check-in:** 10 minutes to ask, “How are you really?”
**Appreciation:** say thank you for specific things, and ask for appreciation in return.
**Small touches:** holding hands, a hug, sitting together.
**Couple time:** tea after the baby sleeps, a short walk, a meal together. It doesn’t need to be elaborate.
**Talk about more than the baby:** dreams, plans, news, jokes.
**Privacy:** find time to talk privately, even if it’s a short walk.
**United front:** discuss decisions about the baby between yourselves first, then present them together to the family.
**His role with his family:** a husband speaking to his own parents about boundaries is often more effective than his wife doing so.
**Avoid triangles:** try not to vent about in-laws in ways that force your husband to choose sides. Focus on specific problems and solutions.

blocks.p: See the guide on navigating motherhood in a joint family.
Many Pakistani families live with husbands working in another city or abroad.

ul: Schedule regular calls at times that work for both of you.
Share photos, videos and small updates so he feels part of daily life.
Plan how decisions will be made while he’s away.
Arrange practical support from family.
Plan his visits to include time with you, not only with the wider family.

blocks.h: When a relationship is not healthy

blocks.p: Ordinary conflict is different from abuse. Seek help if your husband or anyone at home:

ul: Hits, pushes, threatens or frightens you
Controls your money, phone, movements or contact with your family
Humiliates or insults you repeatedly
Forces sex
Threatens to take the baby away

blocks.p: Pregnancy and the postpartum period can be a time when abuse begins or gets worse. You can talk to your doctor, a trusted relative, or a women’s support organisation. If you’re in immediate danger, contact emergency services.

soon: Frequent conflict that you can’t resolve
Feeling unsupported, isolated or resentful most of the time
Persistent low mood or anxiety affecting your relationship
urgent: You feel unsafe at home, or you or your baby have been hurt or threatened
Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: It’s common to feel disappointed in your marriage after a baby: that your husband isn’t helping as much as you hoped, or that you’ve lost closeness. Many couples find their way back, often to a deeper partnership, by naming the problems and working on them together.

takeaway: A baby changes a marriage, and more conflict in the first year is common. Make the work visible, divide areas of responsibility, communicate gently and specifically, protect small daily moments of connection, and seek help if your relationship feels unsafe.
prompt: What is one specific responsibility you’d like your husband to take on fully, and how could you ask him?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Intimacy and Emotional Connection After Birth
description: Intimacy after birth involves physical healing, hormones, exhaustion, body confidence and emotional connection. This guide explains when couples commonly resume sex and why, what physical changes to expect including dryness and discomfort, how quickly fertility can return and what to know about contraception and birth spacing, how to rebuild emotional closeness, and when pain or low desire needs a doctor.
glance: Many couples wait until bleeding has stopped and the body has healed, often around six weeks. For many Muslim couples, the nifas period also guides timing.
Low oestrogen, especially while breastfeeding, commonly causes vaginal dryness. A water-based lubricant can help.
You can become pregnant before your first period returns. Discuss contraception before resuming sex.
Pain that persists, or low desire that is distressing you, is worth discussing with a doctor.

blocks.p: There’s no single right time. Many doctors suggest waiting until:

ul: Postpartum bleeding has stopped, which often takes up to around six weeks
Any tear, episiotomy or caesarean wound has healed
You feel physically and emotionally ready

blocks.p: For many Muslim couples, intercourse is avoided during nifas, the postpartum bleeding period of up to 40 days. Some women feel ready soon after; many take longer. Readiness is about your body and your feelings, not a date.

ul: **Dryness:** after birth, oestrogen levels are low, and breastfeeding keeps them low. This can make the vagina dry and sex uncomfortable. A water-based lubricant can help significantly.
**Tenderness:** scar tissue from a tear or episiotomy may feel tight or sensitive at first.
**Caesarean recovery:** abdominal tenderness may affect which positions are comfortable.
**Leaking breasts:** milk may leak during intimacy because oxytocin triggers let-down. A bra with pads can help if this bothers you.
**Pelvic floor:** may feel different. Pelvic floor exercises help restore tone.
**Tiredness:** often the biggest barrier.

ol: Go slowly and communicate.
Use plenty of water-based lubricant.
Try positions that give you control over depth and pressure, such as being on top or side-lying.
Choose a time when you’re less tired, not necessarily at night.
Stop if it hurts, and try again another time.

ul: **Ovulation can return before your first period,** so you can become pregnant without realising your fertility has returned.
**If you’re not breastfeeding,** fertility can return within weeks.

**Breastfeeding as contraception (LAM)** only works if all three conditions apply: your baby is under six months, you’re exclusively breastfeeding day and night without long gaps, and your periods haven’t returned.
**Birth spacing:** the WHO recommends waiting at least 24 months after a birth before trying for another pregnancy, to support the health of mother and baby.
Discuss contraception options with your doctor before resuming sex, including methods compatible with breastfeeding.

blocks.p: Low desire after birth is common and has many causes: hormones, tiredness, pain, body image, feeling “touched out”, stress, and relationship tension. It often improves over months. Talking openly with your husband about this can reduce pressure on both sides.
Intimacy isn’t only sex. Emotional closeness can grow through:

ul: Talking about your feelings and experiences
Physical affection without expectation: hugs, holding hands, massage
Time alone together, even briefly
Appreciation and kindness
Sharing the load of caring for the baby

blocks.p: Many couples find it hard to talk about sex, especially in households with little privacy. It can help to:

ul: Choose a private, calm moment
Explain what your body is going through
Say what would help: “I’d like us to be close, but I need us to go slowly”
Listen to how he feels, including any worries about hurting you

soon: Pain during sex that persists beyond the first few attempts or doesn’t improve
Bleeding after sex
Low desire that is distressing you or your relationship
You want to discuss contraception
urgent: Heavy bleeding or severe pain
Being pressured or forced into sex

blocks.p: It’s common to feel unsure, anxious or disconnected from your body after birth. Some women feel pressure to resume sex before they’re ready. Your readiness matters, and a caring partner will want you to feel comfortable.

takeaway: Resume sex when you’re healed and ready, often after bleeding stops. Expect dryness and use lubricant, go slowly, and discuss contraception first, since fertility can return before your first period. Emotional closeness is part of intimacy too, and persistent pain deserves a doctor’s attention.
prompt: What would help you feel closer to your husband right now, physically or emotionally?

title: Managing Family Expectations
description: Families in Pakistan often hold strong expectations about pregnancy, birth, feeding, chilla, raising children, the baby’s sex and when to have the next child. This guide explains why these expectations arise, which are helpful and which may need questioning, how to negotiate respectfully, how to work as a team with your husband, and how to protect your wellbeing when expectations clash with your needs or medical advice.
glance: Family expectations usually come from love, tradition and elders’ own experiences.
Some customs are supportive; others conflict with current medical advice.
Discussing decisions with your husband first and presenting a united front helps.
You can respect elders while still making choices for your baby and your health.

ul: **Pregnancy:** food rules (“garam” and “thanda”), rest, rituals, and predictions about the baby’s sex
**Birth:** which hospital, who attends, and attitudes to caesareans
**The baby’s sex:** pressure or disappointment about having a girl, or expectations to have a son
**Chilla:** where you stay, food, bathing, visitors and your role in the household
**Feeding:** ghutti, water, formula, or comments about your milk
**Baby care:** swaddling, oil massage, surma, sleeping arrangements
**Your role:** returning to housework, hosting guests and caring for elders
**The next child:** pressure to have another baby soon
Love and a wish to protect you and the baby
Tradition and cultural identity
Elders’ own experiences, which may have worked for them
Social expectations from the wider community
Different access to medical information in previous generations

blocks.p: **Often supportive:**

ul: Rest and being freed from duties during chilla
Nourishing food prepared by others
Practical help with the baby
Emotional care and company

blocks.p: **Worth questioning, because they conflict with current medical advice:**

ul: Giving ghutti, honey, water or sugar water to newborns
Applying surma or kajal to babies’ eyes
Putting substances on the umbilical cord
Not bathing for weeks
Avoiding fruit and vegetables
Pressure to have another baby before your body has recovered (the WHO recommends at least 24 months between birth and the next conception)

ol: **Acknowledge their care:** “I know you want what’s best for the baby.”
**Share the reason:** “The doctor advised only breast milk for six months, because water can cause infections.”
**Offer an alternative:** “Instead of ghutti, could you help me by burping the baby?”
**Use your doctor:** “The doctor specifically told us not to use surma.”
**Choose your battles:** decide which customs matter most to you and which you can accept.

blocks.h: Working as a team with your husband

ul: Discuss expectations and decisions privately first.
Agree on which issues matter most.
Ask him to speak to his family about concerns.
Present decisions together.

blocks.p: Pressure about the baby’s sex is common in Pakistan and can be painful. The baby’s sex is determined by chance, not by anything you did. If comments about having a daughter are affecting you, talk to your husband and a trusted person.

soon: Family pressure is causing ongoing distress
Disagreements are affecting your relationship
You feel unable to follow medical advice because of family pressure
urgent: You feel unsafe, threatened or are being hurt at home
Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: It can be hard to balance respect for elders with your own needs and beliefs. Many women feel caught between their husband’s family and their own wishes. It’s possible to be respectful and still make decisions for your baby and your health.

takeaway: Family expectations often come from love and tradition. Keep supportive customs, question those that conflict with medical advice, negotiate respectfully, and work as a team with your husband.
prompt: Which family expectation feels hardest for you right now, and how could you approach it with your husband?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Setting Boundaries With Relatives and Visitors
description: After a birth in Pakistan, visitors arrive quickly and often, bringing congratulations, gifts and advice. Visits can be loving, but they can also interrupt feeding and sleep, exhaust a healing mother, and expose a newborn to infection. This guide explains why newborns are vulnerable to infection, how to plan visits, who can help enforce boundaries, and specific phrases to use politely.
glance: Newborns have immature immune systems, so infections such as colds, flu, whooping cough and RSV can be serious.
Asking visitors to wash their hands, avoid kissing the baby’s face, and postpone visits when unwell protects your baby.
Planning visiting times, keeping visits short, and choosing a “visitor manager” can protect your rest.
You can be warm and hospitable while still setting limits.

ul: **Infection risk:** newborns’ immune systems are still developing. Respiratory infections can be more serious in young babies, and whooping cough (pertussis) and RSV can cause severe illness. Cold sores (herpes virus) can be dangerous for newborns if passed on through kisses.
**Your recovery:** hosting, sitting up for long periods and talking can exhaust you.
**Feeding:** frequent visitors can interrupt feeding or make you feel uncomfortable breastfeeding.
**Baby’s sleep and settling:** being passed around and noise can overstimulate newborns.
**Your emotional wellbeing:** constant advice and comments can be draining.

ol: **Decide on visiting times:** for example, afternoons only, or certain days.
**Keep visits short:** 20 to 30 minutes in the first weeks.
**Stagger visitors** rather than having many at once.
**Choose a “visitor manager”:** your husband, mother or a sibling who greets guests, manages time and ends visits politely.
**Delay non-essential visits** until after the first few weeks or after chilla.
**Ask people to message first.**

ul: Wash hands with soap before holding the baby.
Don’t kiss the baby’s face or hands.
Stay home if unwell, with a cough, cold, fever, diarrhoea or cold sores.
Avoid smoking before visiting, and never smoke near the baby.
Don’t pass the baby around too much.
“We’re so happy you came. The baby needs to feed and sleep now, so we’ll wrap up shortly.”
“The doctor asked us to keep visits short for the first few weeks.”
“Please wash your hands before holding the baby, it’s what the doctor advised.”
“We’re not kissing the baby’s face for now, to keep away infections.”
“If anyone has a cold, could you visit when you’re feeling better?”
“I need to rest now. My husband will sit with you.”
Excuse yourself to feed in another room.
Use a dupatta or shawl if you prefer.
Ask someone to bring you water and keep visitors entertained.
Others in the family can serve tea and snacks.
Keep simple refreshments ready.
You don’t need to host while recovering.

soon: Visitors are causing ongoing stress or exhaustion
Family members ignore your requests
urgent: Your baby develops fever, breathing difficulty, poor feeding or unusual sleepiness, especially after visitors who were unwell

blocks.p: Setting boundaries with relatives can feel uncomfortable, especially when hospitality is valued and elders may feel offended. Boundaries protect your baby’s health and your recovery. Most people will understand, especially when you explain the reasons.

takeaway: Visitors can be loving but exhausting and can expose your newborn to infection. Plan visiting times, keep visits short, ask for handwashing and no kissing, and choose someone to help manage guests.
prompt: Who could act as your “visitor manager”, and what would you like them to do?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Dealing With Unsolicited Parenting Advice
description: New mothers in Pakistan often receive a constant stream of advice from mothers, mothers-in-law, aunts, neighbours and strangers, about feeding, sleep, clothing, crying, food and remedies. Some of it is wise, some is outdated, and some can be harmful. This guide gives you a simple way to sort advice, explains the specific practices that current medical guidance advises against and why, offers responses for different relationships, and helps you build trust in your own judgement.
glance: Most advice comes from love and experience, even when it’s unwelcome or outdated.
Sort advice into three groups: helpful, harmless but not for you, and potentially harmful.
Practices to politely decline include ghutti, honey or water for young babies, surma on the eyes, putting babies to sleep on their tummies, tight leg swaddling, and baby walkers.
Short, warm responses and referring to your doctor tend to work better than debate.

ul: **Love and concern:** relatives want the baby to thrive.
**Experience:** they’ve raised children and want to pass on what worked.
**Tradition:** many practices carry cultural or religious meaning.
**Hierarchy:** in many families, elders are expected to guide new mothers.
**Changing knowledge:** guidance on safe sleep, feeding and remedies has changed since many elders raised their children.

blocks.p: **1. Helpful, and worth accepting**

ul: “Rest while the baby sleeps, I’ll cook.”
“Feed the baby whenever they’re hungry.”
“Keep the baby warm but not too wrapped up.”
Practical tips for burping, holding or soothing.

blocks.p: **2. Harmless, but you can choose**
Advice about clothing styles, how often to bathe the baby, names, rituals, or how to arrange the room. These don’t affect safety, so you can follow them to keep peace, or politely do things your way.
**3. Potentially harmful: worth politely declining**

ul: **Ghutti, honey, sugar water, gripe water or plain water for babies under six months.** These can carry infections and reduce breastfeeding. Honey can cause infant botulism and shouldn’t be given before one year. Exclusively breastfed babies don’t need water, even in summer heat.
**Surma or kajal on the eyes.** Some products contain lead, and applying anything to a baby’s eyes can cause infection.
**Oil, ghee, ash or other substances on the umbilical cord.** Keep it clean and dry, following your health provider’s advice.
**Putting babies to sleep on their tummy or side.** Sleeping on the back lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
**Pillows, soft mattresses or heavy quilts in the baby’s sleep space.**
**Tight swaddling with legs straight.** This can affect hip development.
**Putting oil in the baby’s ears or nose.**
**Adding cereal, biscuits or other food to bottles before six months.**
**Baby walkers,** which are linked to falls and injuries.
**Cough syrups, herbal mixtures or medicines** without a doctor’s advice.
**Shaking or vigorously jiggling a crying baby.**

blocks.p: **To acknowledge without agreeing:**

ul: “Thank you, I’ll keep that in mind.”
“That’s interesting, I hadn’t heard that.”

blocks.p: **To refer to your doctor:**

ul: “The doctor told us specifically not to give water or ghutti before six months.”
“Our paediatrician asked us to put the baby to sleep on her back.”

blocks.p: **To explain briefly:**

ul: “Doctors now say honey can make babies very ill before one year.”
“We’ve learned that surma can contain lead, so we’re avoiding it.”

blocks.p: **To redirect to real help:**

ul: “What would really help is if you could hold the baby while I eat.”
“You’re so good at burping her. Could you do that after this feed?”

blocks.p: **To set a firm limit:**

ul: “I know you mean well. We’ve decided on this, and I’d like us to leave it there.”
Speak privately rather than correcting someone in front of others.
Acknowledge their experience: “You’ve raised wonderful children.”
Ask your husband to speak to his own parents about safety issues.
Accept harmless customs where you can, so you have more goodwill for the issues that matter.
Get information from reliable sources: your doctor, a Lady Health Visitor, a trained breastfeeding supporter or reputable health websites.
Notice what works for your baby. You see them every day.
Remember that changing your mind is fine as you learn.

soon: Pressure to follow advice is causing ongoing distress or conflict
You feel unable to follow medical advice because of family pressure
You’re unsure whether a remedy or practice is safe
urgent: Your baby becomes unwell after being given a remedy, honey, herbal mixture or medicine
Your baby has a fever, difficulty breathing, is very sleepy or refuses feeds

blocks.p: Constant advice can leave you doubting yourself, especially when it implies you’re doing something wrong. You’re learning, and so is everyone who becomes a mother. Being respectful doesn’t require following every suggestion.

takeaway: Sort advice into helpful, harmless and harmful. Accept the helpful, choose freely on the harmless, and politely decline practices such as ghutti, honey, water, surma, cord substances, tummy sleeping and walkers. Use short, warm responses, refer to your doctor, and involve your husband with his family.
prompt: Which piece of advice do you hear most often, and which of the three groups does it belong to?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Navigating Motherhood in a Joint Family
description: Many Pakistani mothers raise their babies in joint families. That can mean more hands, company and experience, and also less privacy, expectations about housework, decisions made by elders, and conflicting advice. This guide explains the benefits and pressures, and gives practical ways to use family support well, protect space for feeding and rest, negotiate household duties after birth, handle disagreements with in-laws, and work as a team with your husband.
glance: Practical and emotional support from family is a real protective factor for mothers after birth.
The most common pressures are limited privacy, early return to housework, elders’ decision-making and conflicting childcare advice.
Specific requests and a united front with your husband reduce conflict.
If tension is harming your mental health, or you feel unsafe or controlled, seek support.

ul: **More hands:** help with cooking, cleaning, laundry and older children.
**Company:** less isolation during long days at home.
**Experience:** elders who have cared for many babies.
**Night and nap support:** someone to hold the baby while you sleep.
**Security:** financial and emotional stability for many families.
**Privacy:** little space to feed, rest, cry or talk privately with your husband.
**Housework:** expectations to cook, clean or host soon after birth, sometimes even during chilla.
**Decision-making:** elders may expect to decide on feeding, sleep, names, remedies or when you go out.
**Conflicting advice:** different views on almost everything.
**Comparisons:** with other daughters-in-law, sisters-in-law or relatives’ babies.
**Your position:** feeling like a junior member in decisions about your own child.

ol: **Be specific:** “Could you hold the baby from 3 to 5 p.m. so I can sleep?” works better than “Please help.”
**Divide tasks clearly:** who cooks, who does laundry, who manages visitors.
**Notice and thank:** acknowledging help builds goodwill for when you need to disagree.
**Let others bond with the baby:** grandparents holding, bathing or singing to the baby can be a gift to everyone.

ul: **Before birth,** agree with your husband how long you’ll be off household duties, ideally at least the first six weeks.
**Use the chilla tradition:** many families already accept that a new mother rests for 40 days.
**Use medical advice:** “The doctor told me not to lift heavy things or do floor-level work for six weeks.”
**Return gradually:** start with light, seated tasks.
**Ask your husband** to take on or reassign the tasks you normally do.
Choose a room or corner for feeding and rest.
Use a curtain, screen or dupatta.
Agree on quiet times when you’re not disturbed.
Ask your husband to help protect this space.
Find a private moment each day to talk with your husband, even a short walk on the roof.

ol: **Pick your priorities.** Safety issues, such as safe sleep, ghutti, surma or remedies, matter more than preferences, such as clothes or bath timing.
**Accept harmless customs** where you can.
**Refer to medical advice** for safety issues.
**Choose your moment:** talk calmly, privately, not in the heat of an argument.
**Let your husband lead** conversations with his own parents.
**Look for compromise:** “We’ll do the massage, but without oil in her nose and ears.”

blocks.h: Working as a team with your husband

ul: Discuss issues privately first, and agree on your non-negotiables.
Present decisions together.
Avoid forcing him to choose sides. Focus on the specific problem and a solution.
Recognise that he may feel caught between you and his parents.

blocks.p: Signs that joint family stress is harming your wellbeing:

ul: Constant criticism or comparison
Feeling you have no say over your baby
Being prevented from resting, eating or seeing your own family
Persistent low mood, anxiety or tearfulness

blocks.p: Ordinary family tension is different from control or abuse. Seek help if you’re being hit, threatened, humiliated, prevented from seeing a doctor or your family, or having your money or phone controlled. You can talk to your doctor, a trusted relative or a women’s support organisation, and contact emergency services if you’re in immediate danger.

soon: Ongoing conflict that’s affecting your sleep, eating or mood
Feeling isolated, or unable to make decisions for your baby
Persistent low mood or anxiety for two weeks or more
urgent: You feel unsafe, threatened or are being hurt
Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: A joint family can be a source of warmth and frustration at the same time. Many women feel caught between gratitude and a longing for autonomy. Both feelings are valid, and with clear communication many families find a workable balance over time.

takeaway: Joint families offer real support. Use it with specific requests, agree on rest and housework before birth, protect privacy for feeding and rest, prioritise safety issues in disagreements, and work as a team with your husband. Seek help if stress harms your wellbeing or you feel unsafe.
prompt: What is one specific request you could make to a family member this week that would make the biggest difference to you?

title: Managing Comparisons With Other Mothers
description: Comparing yourself with other mothers, on Instagram, in the family WhatsApp group, at weddings or among friends, is almost universal, and it often leaves you feeling behind or inadequate. This guide explains why the mind compares, why comparisons in motherhood are especially misleading, how widely babies vary in sleep, feeding, weight and milestones, how to respond when relatives compare your baby, and practical ways to step out of the comparison trap.
glance: Comparing is a natural human habit, but in motherhood it is usually based on partial, curated information.
Babies vary widely in sleep, feeding, growth and when they reach milestones. Doctors look at progress over time, not exact dates.
Comparisons from relatives often reflect their own anxieties or traditions, not your baby’s health.
Comparing yourself with your own past progress is more useful and more accurate.

blocks.p: Psychologists describe social comparison as a basic way humans judge how they’re doing, especially when something is new and there are no clear standards. Motherhood is exactly that: unfamiliar, high-stakes and full of uncertainty, so the mind looks around for reference points.

ul: **You see their highlights and your behind-the-scenes.** Social media shows the good moments; your own life includes every hard one.
**Babies are different.** Temperament, sleep needs, appetite and pace of development vary widely between healthy babies.
**Circumstances are different.** Support at home, money, health, birth experience and work all differ.
**People often don’t share struggles.** The mother who seems effortless may be struggling privately.

blocks.h: Common comparisons, and what’s actually true

ul: **“Her baby sleeps through the night.”** Night waking is normal for months. Some babies sleep longer stretches earlier, often for reasons that have nothing to do with their parents.
**“Her baby is bigger.”** Healthy babies grow along different curves. What matters is steady growth along your baby’s own curve, which your doctor checks.
**“Her baby is already rolling or sitting.”** Milestones fall within wide ranges. A few weeks’ difference is normal.
**“She has so much milk.”** Visible milk, leaking or pumping amounts don’t reflect how much a baby gets. Nappies and weight do.
**“She lost her pregnancy weight in two months.”** Recovery varies widely.
**“Her house is always perfect.”** You don’t know what help she has, or what she’s sacrificing to keep it that way.

blocks.p: Babies reach milestones such as social smiling, holding up their head, rolling, sitting, crawling and walking across wide age ranges. Doctors look at whether a baby is progressing steadily, and whether skills are developing across different areas, such as movement, communication and interaction. If you have a genuine concern, for example your baby isn’t making eye contact, isn’t responding to sounds, or has lost a skill they had, ask your doctor rather than comparing with others.

ul: “Every baby has their own pace. The doctor is happy with her growth.”
“We’re following what the paediatrician advised.”
“She’s doing well in her own way.”
Change the subject, or ask your husband to step in if comparisons are frequent.

blocks.h: Stepping out of the comparison trap

ol: **Notice the trigger:** which accounts, groups, people or situations leave you feeling worse?
**Reduce exposure:** mute accounts, leave or mute busy WhatsApp groups for a while, limit scrolling at night.
**Compare with yourself:** how much more confident are you now than in the first week?
**Define your own priorities:** what do you value most as a mother? Measure yourself against that.
**Talk honestly with other mothers:** you’ll often discover they have the same worries.
**Be curious rather than critical:** instead of “Why am I not like her?”, ask “Is there something useful I could learn from her?”
**Practise appreciation:** notice what’s going well, without denying what’s hard.

soon: Concerns about your baby’s growth, feeding or development
Your baby loses a skill they previously had, or isn’t responding to sounds or faces
Comparison is affecting your mood most days
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Comparison can leave you feeling inadequate even when you’re doing well. Every mother and every baby are on their own path. The only fair comparison is with where you started.

takeaway: Comparison in motherhood is natural but usually misleading, because you see others’ highlights and babies vary widely. Reduce triggers, respond calmly to relatives, compare yourself with your own progress, and take genuine developmental concerns to your doctor rather than to the family group.
prompt: Who or what triggers comparison for you most, and what is one change you could make to reduce it?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Balancing Personal Needs and Motherhood
description: Many mothers believe that meeting their own needs is selfish, yet sleep, food, health, connection and a sense of self directly shape how they feel and how they care for their baby. This guide explains which needs matter most and why, how guilt and cultural ideals keep mothers from meeting them, how to define a daily minimum, how to negotiate time and help, and what to do when your needs and your baby’s genuinely clash.
glance: Your needs and your baby’s needs are not in competition. A rested, fed and supported mother has more patience and energy to give.
Core needs include sleep, food and water, physical recovery, connection, some time to yourself, and meaning.
Guilt often comes from cultural ideals of total self-sacrifice, not from anything you’re doing wrong.
A small, non-negotiable daily minimum is easier to protect than an ambitious plan.

ul: **Sleep:** affects mood, patience, memory and decision-making.
**Food and water:** fuel your body and support milk production and healing.
**Physical recovery:** healing from birth needs rest and care.
**Connection:** reduces stress and loneliness.
**Time to yourself:** gives your nervous system a chance to recover.
**Meaning:** faith, values, interests or goals give a sense of purpose beyond daily tasks.

blocks.p: When these needs go unmet for long periods, mothers are more likely to experience exhaustion, irritability, burnout, anxiety and depression. Meeting them is part of looking after your baby.

ul: **Cultural ideals:** the self-sacrificing mother who puts everyone else first is deeply valued in Pakistani culture.
**Family expectations:** to keep up with housework, cooking and hosting.
**Comparison:** with mothers who seem to do everything.
**Fairness worries:** feeling that if you rest, someone else has to work harder.
**Your own upbringing:** watching your mother or grandmother never stop.

blocks.p: Guilt is a feeling, not proof that you’re doing something wrong.
Choose a few small, realistic things that you’ll protect each day, no matter what:

ul: Three meals, and water at each feed
One block of protected sleep, ideally three to four hours
A shower
10 minutes outside or near a window
One conversation with someone who supports you
10 minutes for something you enjoy, or for prayer

blocks.p: Write your minimum down and share it with your husband.

ol: **Make specific requests:** “Could you take the baby from 2 to 4 p.m. so I can sleep?”
**Trade time:** “I’ll do the evening settling if you do the early morning.”
**Reduce other demands:** lower standards for housework, hosting and appearances.
**Use family help well:** let grandparents care for the baby while you rest.
**Review weekly:** what’s working, and what’s missing?

ul: Walk outside with the baby in a carrier or pram.
Listen to a podcast, recitation or music during feeds.
Eat a proper meal while the baby lies safely beside you.
Have a friend visit and talk while you feed.

blocks.p: Sometimes your needs and your baby’s genuinely clash, such as when the baby wants to feed and you’re exhausted. In those moments:

ul: Meet the urgent need first, then plan to meet yours: “After this feed, someone else takes over.”
Look for small ways to meet your need at the same time, like feeding lying down to rest.
Ask for help sooner rather than later.

blocks.p: In joint families or busy homes, your needs can disappear among everyone else’s. Agree on specific rest and help times with your husband and family, and ask him to support you when others expect you to return to duties.

soon: You’re consistently unable to meet basic needs such as sleep or food
Persistent exhaustion, irritability, low mood or anxiety
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Meeting your own needs isn’t selfish. It’s how you sustain the long, demanding work of motherhood. Your baby benefits from a mother who is cared for, too.

takeaway: Your needs for sleep, food, recovery, connection, time and meaning directly affect your wellbeing and your care for your baby. Define a small daily minimum, make specific requests, trade time, lower other standards and let guilt be a feeling rather than a rule.
prompt: What is the one need you’ve been neglecting most, and what specific request would help you meet it tomorrow?

title: Returning to Work or Studies After Childbirth
description: Returning to work or studies after having a baby involves practical planning and complex emotions: childcare, breastfeeding or expressing at work, your rights as an employee, energy, and guilt or relief. This guide explains how to plan the return, continue breastfeeding if you wish, arrange childcare, handle the emotional transition, and look after yourself in the first weeks back.
glance: Maternity leave entitlements in Pakistan depend on your sector, employer and province. Check your contract, HR policy and current law.
Breastfeeding can continue after returning to work by expressing milk and feeding when you’re together.
Plan childcare early and do trial runs before your first day back.
Mixed feelings, guilt, relief, sadness, excitement, are common.

ol: **Check your entitlements:** maternity leave, flexible hours, breastfeeding breaks and any phased return options. Laws and policies vary by sector and province, and have been updated in recent years.
**Talk to your employer or university early:** discuss your return date, flexibility, and space for expressing milk.
**Arrange childcare:** family, a nanny, or daycare. Consider reliability, safety and your baby’s needs.
**Do trial runs:** leave your baby with the caregiver for short periods before you return.
**Plan your routine:** mornings, travel, feeds and evenings.
**Start gradually** if possible, with shorter days or weeks.

ul: **Expressing milk:** start a few weeks before your return to build a small store of milk, if you plan to give expressed milk.
**At work:** ask for a private, clean space and time to express, usually every three to four hours.
**Storage:** use clean containers, label with date, refrigerate. Bring an insulated bag with ice packs if no fridge is available.
**Feeding at home:** feed directly when you’re together, such as before work, after work and at night.
**Caregivers:** teach them paced bottle feeding (see the guide on different feeding journeys).
**Family members:** often trusted and affordable, but agree on expectations about feeding, sleep, and safety.
**Nanny or maid:** check references and agree on responsibilities.
**Daycare:** check hygiene, staff ratios, safety and policies.
**Guilt:** about leaving your baby.
**Relief:** about adult conversation, structure and identity.
**Sadness:** about missing moments.
**Anxiety:** about how your baby will cope.
**Exhaustion:** from managing work and home.

blocks.p: All of these are common. Many mothers find the first few weeks hardest, then adjust.

ul: Prepare meals and clothes the night before.
Share night duties.
Lower standards at home.
Protect sleep.
Talk to other working mothers.

soon: Persistent anxiety, low mood or exhaustion
Difficulty expressing milk or maintaining supply
Concerns about childcare
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Returning to work or study can bring both loss and relief. There’s no right way to feel. Many mothers find meaning in both roles.

takeaway: Plan your return early: check entitlements, arrange childcare, do trial runs and plan for expressing if you’re breastfeeding. Expect mixed emotions and look after yourself in the first weeks.
prompt: What would make your first week back feel more manageable?

title: Rebuilding Your Social Life
description: Social life often shrinks after a baby: friends drift, outings become complicated, and family gatherings feel different when you’re feeding in a back room. This guide explains why friendships change in early motherhood, how to keep important friendships going, how to make new friends who are at the same stage, how to plan outings and weddings with a baby, and how to rebuild your social life gradually.
glance: Friendships often shift after a baby because of time, energy and different life stages. This is common, not a sign of failure.
Low-effort contact, such as voice notes and short visits, keeps friendships alive during the busy months.
Other mothers with babies of similar age can become an important source of support.
Outings and gatherings with a baby are easier with planning: timing around feeds, a quiet space, and ear protection in loud places.

ul: **Time and energy:** feeds, sleep and recovery leave little room.
**Different life stages:** friends without children may not understand your new rhythm, and you may have less in common for a while.
**Practical barriers:** transport, feeding in public, naps and bedtime.
**Your feelings:** you may feel less confident, or not want to be away from your baby.
**Family expectations:** some families expect new mothers to stay home, especially during chilla.

ol: **Use low-effort contact:** voice notes, short messages, sharing photos.
**Invite friends to visit you,** even briefly, rather than going out.
**Be honest:** “I want to stay in touch, but I’m exhausted. Can we do short calls for now?”
**Show interest in their lives,** not only your baby.
**Accept that some friendships will change,** and some may become closer.

ul: Mothers you meet at antenatal or paediatric clinics
Relatives or neighbours with young children
Mother-and-baby groups or classes
Online communities for mothers (choose moderated, respectful ones)
Mothers at the park or mosque, or through older children’s schools

blocks.p: Starting a conversation can be as simple as asking how old their baby is.

ul: **Time it around feeds and naps.**
**Pack a bag:** nappies, wipes, a change of clothes, a burp cloth, a dupatta or shawl for feeding, water and snacks for you.
**Choose baby-friendly places,** with space to feed and change.
**Start short:** a 30-minute visit or walk.
**Have an exit plan** if your baby becomes unsettled.

blocks.p: Shaadi season can be lively but challenging with a baby.

ul: **Loud music:** very loud sound systems can harm babies’ hearing. Keep your baby away from speakers and consider ear protection designed for infants.
**Crowds:** limit passing the baby around, and ask guests to wash hands.
**Feeding:** identify a quiet room in advance.
**Late nights:** consider leaving early or attending only part of the event.
**Your comfort:** wear clothes you can feed in and comfortable shoes.

blocks.p: Your social life may look different for a while. Small, regular connections often matter more than big outings. As your baby grows and routines settle, you’ll likely have more energy and freedom to see people.

soon: Feeling isolated or lonely most of the time
Avoiding people because of anxiety or low mood
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Losing touch with friends or missing out on gatherings can feel lonely and sad. Many mothers find their social circles shift but eventually grow, with new friendships built around shared experiences.

takeaway: Social life often shrinks after a baby, but connection matters for your wellbeing. Keep friendships going with low-effort contact, make new friends at the same stage, and plan outings and gatherings carefully, protecting your baby’s hearing and health.
prompt: Which friend would you like to reconnect with, and what’s the easiest way to reach out this week?
sources: NHS — Baby: caring for a newborn

title: Asking for Help Without Feeling Guilty
description: Many mothers find it hard to ask for help, worrying about being a burden, seeming lazy, or owing people. This guide explains where that guilt comes from, why accepting help is not weakness but the norm across cultures, how to make specific requests that are easy to say yes to, what to ask for at different stages, and how to accept help gracefully.
glance: Across cultures, new mothers have traditionally been supported by family and community. Needing help is normal.
Guilt about asking often comes from ideals of the self-sacrificing mother and fear of being judged.
Specific requests (“Could you cook dinner on Tuesday?”) are easier for people to say yes to than general ones.
Helping is often meaningful for the helper too.

ul: **Cultural ideals:** the good mother copes alone and puts everyone first.
**Comparison:** relatives or friends who seemed to manage without help.
**Fear of judgement:** being seen as lazy, weak or incapable.
**Feeling indebted:** worry about owing people.
**Not wanting to burden others** who are busy.
**Wanting to prove yourself,** especially as a new daughter-in-law.

blocks.p: Human babies have always been raised with help from many people: grandparents, siblings, aunts, neighbours. The chilla tradition itself reflects an understanding that new mothers need care. Accepting help is part of a long tradition, not a sign of failure.
General requests like “Help me” are hard to act on. Specific requests are easier:

ul: “Could you hold the baby for an hour after lunch so I can sleep?”
“Could you cook dinner on Monday and Thursday?”
“Could you take the older children to school this week?”
“Could you bring me water and a snack when I’m feeding?”
“Could you change the baby’s nappy and settle her after the night feed?”

blocks.h: What to ask for at different stages

ul: **Late pregnancy:** heavy housework, shopping, carrying things, transport to appointments.
**First two weeks:** cooking, cleaning, laundry, managing visitors, night help.
**Weeks two to six:** meals, holding the baby while you rest, older children.
**Later months:** time for yourself, help when returning to work, a listening ear.
Say thank you and let it be.
Avoid redoing what others have done.
Let people help in their own way if it’s safe.
Remember that reciprocity can come later, or in other forms.

blocks.p: Keep a list of tasks ready, so when someone says “Let me know if you need anything”, you can answer with a specific request.

soon: You have no one to ask for help
Persistent exhaustion or low mood
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself

blocks.p: Asking for help can feel vulnerable. But many people are glad to be asked, and accepting help allows you to recover and care for your baby well.

takeaway: Needing help as a new mother is normal across cultures. Make specific requests, keep a list ready for when people offer, and accept help gracefully without guilt.
prompt: What is one specific request you could make to someone this week?

title: Finding Time for Yourself
description: Finding time for yourself as a mother can feel impossible, yet even small, regular amounts of personal time restore energy, patience and a sense of who you are. This guide explains why personal time protects against burnout, how to audit your day to find hidden time, how to arrange regular breaks through swaps and specific requests, what to do with short breaks so they truly restore you, and how to handle guilt and household expectations.
glance: Regular time off duty is one of the best protections against exhaustion and burnout.
Fixed, scheduled breaks are far easier to protect than hoping for spare time.
Ten to twenty minutes can help, if it’s genuinely off duty and spent on something restorative.
Scrolling and catching up on chores rarely leave you feeling restored, even though they’re tempting.

ul: **Recovery:** your stress system needs periods of rest to settle.
**Identity:** time for your own interests reminds you that you’re more than your role.
**Patience:** a short break can reset your capacity to respond calmly to your baby.
**Relationships:** you have more to give when you’re not running on empty.
